speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: CANADIAN ENVIRONMENT WEEK AND WORLD ENVIRONMENT DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to draw the attention of the House to two very important events. Today is the first day of Canada's National Environment Week, and June 5 is also World Environment Day.
As a result of its constant urge to create and its desire for economic prosperity, the human race has set off a process that, if allowed to continue in its present form, may well endanger our survival. Everywhere we see signs that our environment is deteriorating: degradation of the ozone layer, global warming, deforestation, declining fish stocks and the desertification of arable land. There are the toxic substances in our lakes and rivers, and air pollution has become so intense in some North American cities that joggers are being advised to train inside during the summer.

The cold facts of science insist we do not have the luxury of another decade of study, delay and inaction. Together with the international community and with the utmost urgency, we must come to terms with the causes of our deteriorating atmosphere which certainly constitutes the most serious pollution threat in the history of the human race.
We must find the means to continue our growth, and the growth of developing nations but we must, at the same time, change the way we grow.
Let me remind all Hon. Members, who, I know, share my concern about global warming, that half of the carbon dioxide added to the atmosphere by human activity has been added just in the last 30 years. Our generation has accelerated the decline of the environment that sustains us. Now we must work to reverse that decline. We must act individually, nationally and globally to set the world on a development pathway that is indeed sustainable.
While the situation is urgent, there is also cause for hope. As a nation and as citizens of this planet, we are capable of change. We can apply the same knowledge and creativity that have so raised our material standards of living, and so harmed our environment, to finding the means to sustain our economies in a manner harmonious with our environment.

Today we should remember the concept of sustainable development as described in the report by the World Commission on Environment and Development, and the need to translate that concept into decisions and concrete action.

I also want to pledge again this Government's commitment to developing the means through which economic development is-by law and regulation as well as by individual morality-harmonized with our environment.
We will continue to address these issues at home and at every international forum in which we participate.

Mr. Speaker, we shall also continue to play a leading role as we did when the Montreal Protocol on protecting the ozone layer was adopted and in several other international conventions and agreements in which Canada participates.
At the international level, we occupy a privileged position. We can show the industrialized world and developing countries that a balanced environment is not synonymous with economic stagnation. We can prove that in the long term, there will be more jobs and better prospects for economic growth in a clean environment then a polluted one. We can show how the various

June 5, 1989
Statements by Ministers
groups in a society as complex as ours can, with a little good will, work together to achieve sustainable development.

Through such new bodies as the Cabinet Committee on the Environment and the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy, we can make significant progress in the 12 months leading up to next year's important sustainable development conferences in Quebec City and Bergen, Norway. We can accelerate the pace in the three years between now and the 1992 United Nations World Conference on Sustainable Development.
All Elon. Members are partners in this national undertaking. Let us all, working within our Parties, our committees, our provinces and our communities, share in the individual and collective efforts that will bring about real environmental change.
Let us, as legislators, be able to look back one day and say we contributed substantially to setting the world on a new path.

On behalf of the Government of Canada, I invite all Canadians to show their determination by their actions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe these comments on Environment Week are an excellent opportunity for us to examine the new Environment Minister's record so far. This is the Minister who took up his duties five months ago, when he said he was going to do some shaking and moving and thoroughly change the Government's approach to certain projects, from megaprojects like Phase 2 of James Bay on down.
Mr. Speaker, looking back five months later, we have had a lot of talk and rhetoric, but one wonders about the actual power the Minister has. Either he is impotent- If we look at all the projects being developed at the federal level, after the Minister's revolutionary or so-called revolutionary statement, we have to say the Government is either hypocritical or impotent.
I would like to look at a number of issues, for instance-
The environment-the Minister says "very positive". I could stand and give all the beautiful words in the world as the Minister has done for the last five months. Instead, I would like to examine his record in the Rafferty-Alameda case. He had an opportunity to revoke the decision of his predecessor to proceed with Rafferty-Alameda. He should have carried out a full federal environmental assessment. Instead, he forced the Canadian Wildlife Federation to take him to court. Is it not time in this country for the Government of Canada and not the courts to exercise the rights of individual Canadians to have a full national environmental assessment? In the Rafferty-Alameda case the Minister showed quite clearly that he was prepared to ignore the fundamental precepts of his own law. He is doing the same thing in the Hydro Quebec-James Bay project.

Mr. Speaker, last week, we heard the Cree explain that almost 25 per cent of the fish now in the waters adjacent to the James Bay Project are no longer fit for human consumption because they contain from two to three, four, five and even six times the amount of mercury they contained at the beginning of Phase 1.
And this is what they asked the Minister, and I think that is perfectly normal: They asked for a federal investigation of the environmental impact of Phase 1 of the James Bay Project.
Last week, the Minister refused to give us. Opposition Members, the assurance in committee that he would order a federal analysis. We know what he said: "Hydro-Quebec takes care of that". However, asking Hydro-Quebec to analyse the environmental impact of Phase 1 of the James Bay Project is completely ridiculous.
I would like to talk about the rain forest. We all know that in the Amazon, there is a serious problem with the disappearance of the-

I was shocked to discover that in British Columbia the rain forest is as old or older than the Amazon rain forest. It is about to disappear because the Government of Canada, together with the Government of British Co-
June 5, 1989

lumbia, has proceeded over overlogging and overcutting. That has created a situation where we do not have time. Within the next 12 years that precious resource which pre-dates civilization, or so-called civilization in our country, which pre-dates the arrival of Christopher Columbus, and which pre-dates even the arrival of Christ is about to disappear in our own country. It is fine to lecture about the Brazilian rain forests, but we have a job to do in our own country that is not being done.
We have heard a lot about water policy. Yet to date we have no firm water policy coming from the Government. I appreciate the Minister's concern about implementing the Montreal Protocol. It is unfortunate that after he announced in February that he was going to be working immediately on regulations for the Montreal Protocol that he has not done so. We are now in a situation where the Montreal Protocol implementation is at risk because of the negligence of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) in so far as the regulations are concerned.
This week alone the Minister of Energy, who is sitting two or three seats away from the Minister of the Environment, made a statement in support of megaproject subsidies. Time and again we have heard the Government state that it cannot afford to pay senior citizens' pensions. It cannot afford to pay family allowances, and it brought forward a taxation policy which discriminates against families. Yet the Government has no problem in coming up with $5 billion to subsidize megaprojects which are putting the air we breathe and our atmosphere at risk. The Minister continues to defend this stand, along with his partner in crime, the Minister of Energy, at the same time as they are closing down the only offices in the Ministry of Energy that are looking toward the development of alternative energy resources.
I could go on, but I have very little time. It is about time that the Minister of the Environment was called upon to put his money where his mouth is. Next week some national organizations will be coming to Ottawa. They have heard the rhetoric and they have been impressed with the vast promises and the anticipation of the Minister of the Environment, but he has not delivered the goods on every single major issue, including the importation of legal and illegal waste into the country.
Statements by Ministers
On Thursday, the very day that I was questioning the Minister in the House, his own officials and his own Government were trying to put the boots to a Washington initiative to put limitations on the exportation of hazardous waste into Canada.
Therefore, let us not only talk about the environment and not only celebrate Environment Week, but also make sure that government policy reflects the type of sustainable development commitment that was originally enshrined in the Brundtland report, and which the Minister is talking about on an ongoing basis.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on June 5, the World Environment Day and also the first day of Canada's National Environment Week.
Many Members of the House wanted Our Common Future to be played on every broadcasting system in the country on Saturday. Many Canadians could have benefited from an opportunity to view Our Common Future. I would hope if another opportunity does arise that the Ministers of the Crown will ensure that such broadcasting is made widely available from East to West and North to South.
The Minister touched on a couple of matters. I would like to touch on some specifics. There is a great deal that the Minister and the Government can and must do. I issue two challenges today on the first day of Canada's Environment Week, one to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) and to Canada, and one to you, Mr. Speaker, that I will come to in a moment.
In terms of legislation there are a number of things that the Minister of the Environment must do. One is an environmental Bill of Rights. There must be amendments to Canada's Constitution on aboriginal rights to recognize the First Nations as founding nations of Canada. The Access to Information Act must be changed. There is no other field in greater need of access to information under federal law than in the environment. I would hope that the Minister of the Environment will see that the more than 100 unanimously recommended amendments that were made in the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General two years ago are brought before the House this month.

June 5, 1989
Statements by Ministers
There must be a full environmental assessment and review. We know that the Environmental Assessment Review Process legislation is complete. It is sitting over at the federal environmental assessment review office and I would hope that the Minister will make it publicly available for assessment and review before bringing it before the House.
On crimes against the environment, Canada's Criminal Code must be amended to take into account the web of offences such as we have learned recently in terms of the addition of things like PCBs into fuel. There were nine million litres blended with gas in the U.S. and Canada and sold to unsuspecting consumers and buyers over the last year and a half.
There must be an environmental auditor. I would hope the Minister would ensure that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) openly supports that very soon. There should be a toxic substances inventory. There are now a 100,000 chemicals moving around in our enviornment. The 44 members on the toxic substances list are not enough. There must be a national inventory.
There must also be a national resources inventory of everything from forests and plants to mammals and fish. That is absolutely fundamental. A store cannot be run without knowing what the inventory is. A country must have a national inventory.
There must be fine-splitting in all forms of federal legislation. It is in the Fisheries Act and it should be introduced into CEPA and into all other federal regulations and law in order that the public knows there is a benefit, whether they are a worker in a facility or someone living in a community, to making sure that the environment is kept clean. That could be accomplished through fine splitting, making sure that those who participate in prosecutions receive half the benefit of the fine brought forward by the court.
There must be whistle-blowers' legislation, something that Parliament has talked about for a long time but must soon do. We have to have a super fund, the same as the United States, to clean up the past errors. Soon enough we will have to make moves on the international scene in terms of an international super fund to start cleaning up areas of the developing world that have been used as toxic and hazardous waste dumps and some other things during this particularly unethical period of human history-
There must be legislative, professional and ethical guidelines, something I will talk about later today. There must be a safe drinking water act. I understand the Minister plans to bring that forward this year. Canadians all look forward to it with bated breath. There also must be a clean air act. I would hope the Minister would move on that. There must be a national Act to protect endangered species.
The Minister knows, despite what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had to say, that this year there will be $15.8 million less available for Environment Canada than there was in 1984. We are not going forward in terms of the level of funds that are required. We require at least 1 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product directed specifically to the environment. I hope the Minister picks that up later today as his target and that of his Department.
Twelve per cent of Canada's land and marine areas must be set aside for conservation. Perhaps our generation and in fact this Parliament, may be the last to have the opportunity to do so.
It will be a pleasure later today to hear President Kaunda speak. There are many African nations such as Tanzania that have set aside 17 per cent of their land base. Our whole national parks system consists of only 1.3 per cent of Canada lands. Many developing countries have done far better than us.
Let me spend a moment on you, Mr. Speaker, because I issued this as a double-barrelled blow today: One, to the Minister and the Government for things they can do, and second, to the Hill. The very first place that the principles of the Brundtland report must be applied and implemented is right here on Parliament Hill.
The buildings and the grounds are known from coast to coast as a symbol of Canada's parliamentary democracy and should be formally designated an environmentally friendly zone. Every aspect of our operation should conform to the principles of sustainable development. This would entail the purchase of only recycled or environmentally healthy products, the use of unbleached paper products, the banning of plastic cutlery and styrofoam cups from all restaurants and cafeterias, the use of non-toxic cleaning products and the grounds of Parliament Hill should be maintained using environmentally sound pest management techniques. More trees should be planted, buildings and facilities should be examined and altered where necessary to provide everything from the removal of dangerous building materials to secure parking facilities for bicycles. Parliament Hill should
June 5, 1989

become a model of the sustainable community and an example for the rest of Canada and the world, of how Canada's elected representatives can put their own house in order.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 52 and to a letter you have received earlier, I would move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Don Valley North (Ms. Greene), that the House do now adjourn for the purpose of debating the unprecedented crisis and violence in the People's Republic of China.
One of the criteria. Sir, that you must use in deciding whether to allow such a debate is that the matter falls within the ability of Canada to do something about it. Our Government can do a number of things to indicate the outrage of Canadians generally at the senseless bloodbath in the streets of Beijing and horrors which appear to continue as we speak here.
First, there is the safety of all Canadians now present in the People's Republic. I understand that is an estimated 101 diplomats and dependents, 600 to 700 Canadian citizens and the indicated bedlam at the Beijing Airport.
Second, there is our ambassador and other officials at our embassy. Some or all of these could be called back to
Canada, at least until the killing stops, in order to show that Canadians are outraged at the treatment of nonviolent unarmed protesters.
There is our official assistance, which according to the Canadian International Development Agency as of this morning, last year amounted to $32.5 million in technical assistance and training.
Third, there is the concern of the estimated 360,000 Canadians of origin in China, many of whom I believe reside in your constituency, with both family in Beijing and elsewhere in China where violence is still occurring against dissenting civilians. Canadians of every origin must be fully in support of their fellow citizens of origin in China. There were demonstrations, yesterday, including in Vancouver where approximately 100,000 Canadians of origin in China live. There were demonstrations in Calgary, Winnipeg, Ottawa, and more than 15,000 people in Toronto alone. There are also many hundreds of students of origin in China studying in this country.
You are required, Mr. Speaker, to consider whether the situation constitutes a genuine emergency. No one in any country with a free media can have the slightest doubt as to the severity of the crisis.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-19, an Act to amend the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to place before the House today for second reading a Bill to amend the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program Act. The purpose of the Bill is to implement the decision announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his recent Budget to terminate CEDIP incentives on April 27, 1989, except for certain activities under way or required to be undertaken pursuant to written agreements as of that date.
It is important that we all understand the context in which the decision was taken to terminate CEDIP. Canada has a serious deficit problem. The national debt is growing more rapidly than our national income. Despite some tough measures by the Government over its last term in office, that debt is continuing to grow.
As Members of the House will know, as of April 1, 1989, at the beginning of this fiscal year, the debt stood at $320 billion. The Government has recognized the threat posed by the growing burden of public debt, and the 1989 Budget announced reductions in government spending affecting a wide range of programs including CEDIP.
These budget measures reflect the seriousness of the deficit problem. Tough action was called for in curtailing program expenditures, and difficult decisions had to be made. CEDIP was created in March, 1987 in response to the devastating impact uncertain world oil prices were having on the oil and gas industry in general and the economy of western Canada in particular.
We had announced as a Government the Western Energy Accord early in 1985, and it set in motion a process of deregulating the oil and gas industry within a
Exploration and Development
market oriented policy framework. This was welcomed not only by the oil and gas industry but by those producing areas of the country that knew we had to move toward a market oriented approach.
We also knew the devastation the National Energy Program had on exploration, on incentives, on initiatives, and on investment. We also knew the unfairness of it, particularly in the producing areas of our country.
Step after purposeful step was taken to dismantle the National Energy Program and to lift the weight of government intervention which had stifled entrepreneurial drive. The response from the oil and gas industry was immediate. They were true to their word. In 1985 records were set for industry investment and drilling activity. However, the collapse of world oil prices in 1986 from $30 a barrel to $10 a barrel cut short the renewal which had been taking place.
The Government of Canada was sensitive to the disruption caused by the precipitous fall in oil prices, and industry needed a bridge to get it across the short-term difficulties it was facing. CEDIP was that bridge. A number of Members on both sides of the House were active in developing the terms for that bridge.
It was introduced as a temporary safety net, a safety net designed to assist the petroleum industries and to maintain upstream employment and investment.
CEDIP provided cash when it was desperately needed to stabilize exploration and development activity. The program also provided time for industry to adjust its investment plans to meet market conditions. The program was especially designed to help that part of the sector facing the most difficulty, the smaller and medium sized companies, many of which are Canadian owned. It was for this reason that entitlement under the program was capped at $10 million in expenses per company per year.
I should also say that there has been criticism that this money has gone primarily to the large companies. I can show Members later that that criticism, at least in some measure, is not valid.
Let me describe how events unfolded since the program was announced. Clearly, CEDIP has been successful in its objectives. Current projections are that the

June 5, 1989
Exploration and Development
program will have provided more than $1.2 billion to industry over its life of little more than a year and a half.
It should also be noted that the Government and those who designed the program were estimating annualized costs of approximately $345 million or approximately $690 million to $700 million over the 24-month period. That cost is now projected to be $1,245 billion over the period of this program, that is, with the passage of this Bill.
The program will have supported over $3.7 billion in exploration and development activity, the bulk of that activity being in western Canada. For 1987 and 1988, the first year of CEDIP and the only one for which the deadline on applications has lapsed, industry will have been provided with $500 million in incentives, $150 million more than anticipated. It is also noteworthy that most of this increase was directed to those applicants spending less than the $10 million annual limit. It bears out that the program has benefited smaller firms more than the larger firms. In fact, roughly 59 per cent of the incentives for 1987 and 1988 will go to below limit applicants, even though such firms accounted for only 25 per cent of total exploration and development spending.
The Government believes that it is a good record, a record of accomplishments for the petroleum sector to which the petroleum sector responded after it had made very strong representations to the Government that it had to move toward a market oriented approach to the oil and gas industry. It has demonstrated the benefits of a less intrusive, more market oriented approach designed toward success.
The National Energy Program has been dismantled, as has the Foreign Investment Review Agency. The market oriented approach is also reflected in the initiative to deregulate gas markets, early removal of the PGRT, and efforts to open markets for oil and gas production.
We intend to stay the course in advancing the agenda begun last term, confident that a market oriented approach will best position industry to meet the challenges that come from the market-place.
What of the health of the oil and gas industry itself? Clearly all is not completely rosy out there in the oil patch. The first quarter of this year was one of the
poorest quarters of drilling activity in recent years;that at a time when CEDIP was available. A number of market conditions contribute to this situation, including transportation bottlenecks, low gas prices, and some uncertainty over how well and how long the current world oil price of roughly $20 a barrel will hold.
As well, we have witnessed a major restructuring in the industry through acquisitions and mergers which, in the short term at least, has reduced activity levels and led to a further rationalization of investment decisions.
Nonetheless, over the last few years industry has strengthened its over-all financial position. It has developed a cautious approach in taking on major investments. Many companies have reduced their debt load and have increased the efficiency of their operations through cost reduction and other means. They are better poised today than two years ago to deal with market conditions and to take advantage of opportunities as and when they present themselves.
The Government's policy of non-intervention does not mean the absence of responsibility or a role for government. Indeed, we will continue to work closely with industry in addressing its concerns with the market oriented framework.
However, faced with competing priorities, this Government must also choose courses of action which respond to the national interest. That was the case with the decision to terminate CEDIP.
The termination of CEDIP will save the Government a projected $80 million. We have instituted grandfathering provisions with a view to honouring activities under way or committed to underwritten agreements. This grandfathering regime will cushion the impact of program termination. Incentives will be provided on grandfathered activities through December 31, 1989 when the program will be completely terminated.
The grandfathering regime will help many companies. Yet, we fully realize that by asking the oil patch to contribute $80 million toward the deficit, some companies will have more difficulty than others in adjusting their investment plans accordingly.
What I want to emphasize is that it is money that the companies did not have, money the companies did not have to spend. It was an expenditure of the Government of Canada. I believe when I look at the incentives or the
June 5, 1989

projections as against the total amount invested by the Government of Canada that we have been fair.
We have made the decision to terminate CEDIP. I have said to the oil industry-and I have met with the industry and others in the mineral field-that it was not an easy decision to take but I believe it was the correct one. I have also been pleased with the response of the industry. The industry has been saying that while it would like to see in present circumstances possibly other decisions, it understands the over-all need by the Government of Canada to tackle both the deficit and the debt.
We know that the oil and gas industry would like to have had more notice provided on this decision. We also have to recognize that in a demand driven program, as this one was, decisions have to be made and they require a terminal date. It was for that reason that notice was not given. I think the House understands that as well.
I would thank the House for the time to explain CEDIP and Bill C-19. I would ask the House to demonstrate its commitment to deficit reduction by passing the Bill at second reading.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this Bill, because what the Government is proposing is one of the greatest injustices perpetuated on the oil and gas sector in many, many years. I say that knowing of the National Energy Program and that the Liberal Government suffered as a result of it. However, if they listen they will find out exactly what their Government is doing to the energy sector in western Canada.
The conventional oil and gas industry is now going through one of the most difficult times in its history. For the small companies, for the drillers, for the service industry, it is the most difficult time in its history. In the second quarter of 1989 the drilling industry was predicting that 171 wells would be drilled.This was its projection in March-171 wells.
Within one month, the industry reduced that projection by almost 50 per cent, to 89 wells drilled in the second quarter of 1989, which is only 17 per cent of the wells available for drilling in western Canada. That is almost half the number of wells drilled in 1988, which in itself was not a good year. That means that this year over last year, which was not a good year, there will be as
Exploration and Development
many as 6,000 fewer people working in the energy sector in Alberta and Saskatchewan.
In light of that, why was the Canadian Energy Production Incentive Program cancelled? Why was CEDIP cancelled? The Minister stated: "Well, it was not an easy decision but it was a correct one." It was obviously a sudden one for the Minister because he was in Calgary on April 5 of this year and said that this program would continue until the end of the year. Some 22 days later, on April 27, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his Budget said that CEDIP was to be cancelled at that very time. It was obviously a very sudden decision that was imposed on the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp).
I do not believe that the Minister of Energy would mislead people in western Canada. I think the Government is cutting the legs out from underneath the Minister of Energy and the whole oil and gas industry. We are seeing here an attempt to try to fix in the minds of people in western Canada that everything is going well in the oil and gas sector in western Canada. Nothing could be further from the truth.
The Government states that it is to save $80 million by cancelling the CEDIP on April 27. The drilling sector states that in order for the Government to save $80 million there is to be a reduction in spending of $450 million. They say that $450 million has to be spent for the energy sector to be able to claim $80 million under the CEDIP. One heck of a lot of activity in the western sedimentary basin is going to be cancelled at a time when it looks like there is to be 6,000 people out of work in the oil and gas sector. These reductions are to be in the sectors that can least afford to suffer these kinds of reductions in employment.
The Government is going to state: "Well, we spent $1.2 billion in a little over a year and a half. Aren't we great?" The Minister states that he was to tell us that it was not the major companies that received this funding,we never did receive that information. The Government spent $1.2 billion, over 85 per cent of which went to the large companies.
In fact, 90 per cent of the companies that applied for funding under the CEDIP received less than 15 per cent of the financing. It is absolutely incredible that the smaller companies, which in the Minister's own words

June 5, 1989
Exploration and Development
were targeted for the benefits of this program, would receive less than 15 per cent of the actual benefits of the program.
If the Government reduced the ceiling of the program from $10 million that would be available for a company to $1 million instead of cancelling it, it could still satisfy 90 per cent of the claims and save 65 per cent of the funding. Yet the Government will not do that at a time when activity in the western sedimentary basin in Alberta and Saskatchewan in the conventional oil sector is at the lowest it has ever been, with projections getting worse each passing day.
The Minister said that he has figures which indicate that the smaller companies received much of the benefits. I am asking the Minister to make those figures public. We certainly cannot get them through the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources because the Government, the Chairman, or somebody refuses to allow the committee to meet.
There have been two meetings of the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources thus far. The first was an organizational meeting. The second was also an organizational meeting which was held because the Chairman forgot to submit the seven names and alternates. Thus we had to have a second meeting to reappoint him as Chairman. That has been the sole activity of the standing committee. What a full calendar this committee has had. What a veritable brain thrust of activities is being contributed by the Government into the very important issue of energy, mines and resources. Of course the Government does not want the people of Canada to know the precarious state of the oil and gas industry at this particular time.
The Minister has said that we do not need CEDIP any more, that prices have gone up. The Minister and the Government know very well that the small companies are having a tremendously difficult time in obtaining funding and that they are still suffering from the time when they borrowed large amounts of money in the early 1980s when the banks were left with some bad accounts. These small companies are having a difficult time raising money. That is why CEDIP was so important.
It was important even though the Government reduced the amount from 33 and one-third per cent last
October and stated that it would reduce it again on the first of July to 16 and two-thirds per cent and then cancel it at the end of the year. At least it was something that the small companies could use for a projection. However, to cancel it at the date of the Budget left the small companies without an opportunity to take advantage of the phasing out period.
The Minister and the Government did this when they knew they were obligated under the regulations in the Act to give a six-month notification period of the cancellation of the Act. Yet the Government still cancelled the provisions of this Act at the date of the Budget without any warning whatsoever.
We do not have CEDIP any more. One could say that in its largess the Government has showered the oil and gas industry with opportunity to get out of this most difficult time in which it finds itself. One could say that it has done an awful lot. One could say that there is the Canadian Exploration Incentive Program. One may say that this is marvellous because the companies have the right to make application under CEDIP. However, CEDIP was set up for the mining industry. At the urging of some of the back-benchers from western Canada the Government included the oil and gas industry at the last moment.
However, it created a catch-22 situation for the oil and gas sector. The Government put in place an exploration definition clause which is retroactive. Now a company can drill for oil and gas and actually receive funding under the CEDIP. Later the Government can designate the result as not a bona fide well for exploration and ask the company to pay the funds back with interest.
How many companies will ask for a rebate under the program only to have to pay it back later on with interest? If that is help then it is akin to the sort of help one gives by throwing an anvil to a drowning man.
Let us consider other matters. Perhaps there is something that the Government has done to help the oil and gas industry and in particular small companies. There is in the Budget what is called the large corporations tax. It is a good idea to tax large corporations and make sure that there is something coming in from some of these companies that like to put money where Governments cannot get at it. I think that is good. However, once again in its ignorance of the oil and gas industry the Govern-
June 5, 1989

ment has failed to see the damage that it has done to small companies.
The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Andre) is in the House. He is from Calgary. He does not even know the damage that this measure is doing. If he does not know, what chance does the poor Minister of Finance have in terms of knowing anything about damage to the country and Canadians?
The fact is that if the Minister of Finance knew anything about damage to the country and to Canadians, we would not be in the mess we are in right now with this absolutely Draconian Budget that is devastating the small business sector and low and middle income Canadians.
The Minister of Finance in his wisdom has said that the junior resource companies, as he calls them, are not liable for this tax because it does not affect companies with less than $10 million in corporate capitalization. He says that in complete ignorance of the oil and gas industry. Any company in the oil and gas industry with less than approximately $25 million in capital would consider itself as an emerging player. I do not think it would be enough cash flow to sustain a company.
Independent and small oil and gas companies are small businesses with a capital risk exposure that would be considered insane by a small machine shop, for instance, in southern Ontario. There is no comparison to be made between small oil and gas companies and small manufacturing companies. Yet the Minister of Finance has refused to acknowledge that, or he has not taken the time to find out the differences. The Minister of Finance was the energy critic for his Party between 1980 and 1984. Yet he shows an abysmal ignorance of the oil and gas sector.
The capital base of a small resource producer is entirely different from that of a manufacturing company. The problem is that we now have this taxing of small oil and gas companies when they are not making any money. They are not working because they cannot borrow money. The Government has cut the knees out from under them with the cancellation of the CEDIP and other retrogressive tax measures. They cannot explore or do anything. Yet they are still paying this tax because they are companies with capitalization of over $10 million. What this amounts to is a tax on the assets of the company. It is not a tax on revenue as was the PORT,
Exploration and Development
which was hated in the oil and gas sector. This is a tax on the very assets of a company.
I wish to quote from a letter dated May 9 written by the Small Explorers and Producers Association of Canada. Regarding the large corporation tax it is stated: "It is really a tax on assets, productive or not, and is more oppressive than the hated tax on revenue, the PGRT, under the National Energy Program". So this is the opinion of the energy sector, of the small companies that the CEDIP program was supposed to help, saying that the Government's policies to the oil and gas sector in western Canada are worse than the PGRT was under the National Energy Program. I can imagine that there is not one company in western Canada which believed it would say that about something this Government was going to do relating to oil and gas, this Government that takes such pride in developing the western accord and the American oriented system.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp) says the Government cannot continue to give funding under the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program, under CEDIP, because it has developed an American economy in the oil and gas sector. This is the same market economy that will be financing Oslo, the same market economy that will be financing the Husky upgrader. This is the same economy that presumably will be funding the Hibernia project. This is the American economy of this Government.
When it comes to the majors and multinationals, it is not a market economy. When it comes to jobs in the western sedimentary basin, to the small producers, to the drillers, to the service industries, suddenly it is a market economy in the oil and gas sector. This is absolutely incredible. It is a sham being perpetuated on the small companies, the service industries and drilling companies in western Canada.
What is going to happen with this assets tax which is supposed to be something that the Government feels is not going to hurt western Canada? The small companies that are not generating capital and having to pay a tax on their assets will have to sell their reserves to pay the tax. There we have the master plan of this Government: Get rid of the little companies, the small little companies that are a nuisance that are actually doing one-third of all the drilling in western Canada in the conventional sector. Get rid of them. Have them sell their reserves to the larger companies. The Government will only deal

June 5, 1989
Exploration and Development
with the big players, the big guys, the ones that count with the Government. Then it will be as the Government's philosophy would have us believe that only the large companies can make it. The small companies cannot make it. The reason they cannot make it is because they are being sabotaged by their own federal Government.
We have seen what the large companies have done. We have seen this only too well. If the small companies are going to be forced to sell their reserves to the major companies, then, of course, there will be failures of the smaller companies and their reserves in the hands of the larger companies. This has been going on since this Government took office.
The Government is saying that the market system that works for the big companies is great and that it will generate more activity. The smaller companies are not drilling because they cannot raise the money. The banks will not give them the funding and the Government is taking away what incentive programs they had.
The question is, why are the large companies not drilling? Why is drilling down? These large companies that are declaring hundreds of millions of dollars in profit every year, why are they not drilling? The Minister stated that prices are supposedly up. So, why are they not drilling? Because they are not exploring for product. They are buying product through mergers. That way they can sit in their offices with their feet on the desk, lay off their geologists and seismic people, reduce their staff, save money and buy product. They just shuffle paper. This saves a lot of trouble. They don't have to get their feet dirty and muddy by going out into the oil patch to explore. They can just sit in their offices and buy and merge.
This is like a big monopoly game for these big boys. They just sit away while people in the service industries and drilling companies lose their jobs or go somewhere else. They can leave western Canada and perhaps go North to the pulp and paper industry. The prices charged by the drilling companies and service industries go down because so many of them have to compete for a smaller
chunk of the business. The actual standard of living for the people working in the oil patch, which was improving, has declined. They have to wreck their trucks on poorly prepared roads. They buy their own clothes. They do not sleep in mobile units now. Some of them sleep in their pick-up trucks.
This is what this Government is doing. It is fine for the big companies and the executives, but what they are doing to the workers in the oil and gas sector, Mr. Speaker, is a travesty.
Let me just give some figures of the mergers that took place. We have had six major mergers. There is the three-company merger of Sceptre, Oakwood and SO-QUIP which drilled 81 wells in 1987 and 116 in 1988. That group that was up 30 per cent in their drilling. That is one of the two increases. The other one was Husky and Canterra which drilled, in 1987, 154 wells and 185 in 1988. That is not to say what the situation is going to be in the first quarter. In week eight of this year as opposed to week eight of last year, the drilling in 1988 was 10 wells. This year with Husky and Canterra it is one well.
The merger of Amoco and Dome is an indication of what will happen. In 1987, those two companies drilled a total of 315 wells. In 1988, they drilled 256 wells; a decline of 23 per cent in drilling. In 1987, Esso, Sulpetro and Ocelot drilled 743 wells. After the merger in 1988, they drilled 407. That is a decline of 83 per cent. In 1987, Poco and Bonanza drilled 203 wells. Last year, it was 56 wells. That is a decrease of 262 per cent. In 1987, Westcoast and Canadian Roxy drilled 56 wells and last year, 45. That is a decline of 24 per cent.
Regardless of what the companies say when they merge-and they all say that this puts them in a better position to use the lands and to do more drilling-that the tendency is away from further drilling because they have used their resources to buy product. They are not drilling for product.
What about another tax, the Canadian goods and services tax? That is going to be very interesting because this tax is not going to apply for Canadian oil and gas that is exported, but it will apply for Canadian oil and gas that is consumed in Canada. This is something that is going to
June 5, 1989

be very interesting to the consumers of Canada when it finally hits home.
I hate to think that the Government would know so little about such an important resource sector of this country. The Government refuses to realize that by promoting the tendency away from drilling and exploration that it is going to eventually kill the conventional oil and gas sector in Canada, because as the activity is reduced, more and more people are going to leave the oil patch and go into the new pulp and paper activity that is being created in northern Alberta. They are going to go to the labour-short manufacturing industries in southern Ontario. They are going to get tired of sleeping in their pick-up trucks.
The small companies that cannot raise money are gradually going to go under. They are going to have to sell their reserves to pay this asset tax that the Government has imposed. That is not progress, Mr. Speaker. The catchword phrase that the Conservatives used between 1980 and 1984 was that the Government was picking winners and losers, when referring to the former Liberal Government. That is exactly what the Tory Government is doing right now. It is putting big bucks in megaprojects, and I am not opposed to that. If the Government wants to finance megaprojects that is its choice, but it should not be done at the expense of sabotaging the conventional oil and gas sector. The present Government criticized the former Liberal Government for diverting activity away from the conventional oil and gas sector, from the western sedimentary basin, and this is exactly what the Government is doing now, and to an extent and at a rate that was unprecedented during the National Energy Program.
The activity in the western sedimentary basin was never as low or as bad during the National Energy Program as it is today. It is still getting worse. How long can the oil and gas sector even keep a fraction of its employment if all the major companies are going to buy the reserves instead of exploring for reserves.
I cannot accept the absolute decimation of the oil and gas sector in western Canada. It is completely without any feeling on the part of the Government. Then I say to myself that feeling about people and about the regions of the country is not something the Government is very
Exploration and Development
strong on. I know first-hand what the Government has done to Atlantic Canada.
I can only hope that the Government changes its ways, that it puts back the CEDIP program with a ceiling of $1 million, services 90 per cent of the applications, in particular those from small companies, that it gets some activity going in the western sedimentary basin, stops stifling this activity and stops promoting higher levels of unemployment in the oil and gas sector. The only hope that we can possibly generate is that Members of the Government are going to change their minds because what they are doing now is counter-productive to the process and counter-productive to a healthy oil and gas sector in western Canada.

subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am still learning some of the intricacies of this institution and I appreciate your advice.
I am pleased today to rise in the debate on Bill C-19 which, in the view of some, would prematurely conclude the life of the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program Act. At the outset, I am delighted that the Minister responsible appears to intend to stay in the House for the entire debate. That is commendable, and I congratulate him for doing so. I would note with some astonishment that the only Members of the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources present for the debate are the Opposition Members.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT
speechtext: Order!

subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT
speechtext:
That is an observation on who is present, not on who is absent. I thank the Hon. Member. I find that absolutely astonishing. However, perhaps that is in keeping with the record of the committee to date.
CEDIP was first introduced effective April 1, 1987 to help the oil and gas industry overcome the decline in oil and gas prices and the impact of that decline on employment and investment, particularly in western Canada.

June 5, 1989
Exploration and Development
The second half of the 1980s have not been kind to Alberta in particular, and the western sedimentary basin generally. Living in Edmonton, I have seen the effects of the precipitous decline in oil prices at the time when Canada under Conservative Governments, federally and provincially, chose to go to a deregulated market. I have seen neighbourhoods devastated by unemployment. I have seen my own friends forced to abandon homes and move elsewhere. I have seen small businesses go bankrupt because communities they served no longer had the money to buy in those small businesses. I have seen what amounts to a devastation of entire communities in Edmonton, devastation which I am certain was reproduced throughout the Province of Alberta.
I have certainly seen an operating deficit in the provincial Government of Alberta, something which would have been inconceivable in the early part of the 1980s. I have seen the operating deficit in the Province of Alberta accumulate to somewhere between $6 billion to $7 billion in the fiscal year concluded March 31, of this year. We are looking forward to a provincial budget in Alberta on Thursday. Goodness knows what type of deficit we will find then, all because of the collapse in prices and hence the collapse of royalty and taxation revenues from the oil and gas sector.
There is no question that CEDIP was introduced to address the carnage in the oil patch and in the gas exploration industry occasioned by the collapse in prices. That is why all three political parties supported the Bill when it was introduced, and co-operated fully in ensuring its quick passage on June 10, 1987. The Opposition did chide the Government for taking so long to introduce it, given the devastation in the oil patch at that time, and pointed out that the Bill was in conflict with the Government's market-place ideology. I am certain that is a point that will be emphasized from time to time today.
As reported at page 6971 of Hansard. June 10, 1987, our then energy critic, the Hon. Member for Port Moody-Coquitlam (Mr. Waddell) stated:
I should like to say that I am cautiously optimistic that the Bill will work. It favours smaller companies. It focuses on grants rather than on tax incentives, allowing some of the smaller companies which do not pay taxes to benefit. It acknowledges the plight of small oil companies as a national issue. It is a national problem about which we all must talk.
It is still short-term. The long-term solution is to diversify the western economy-no mean feat but something which must be done-away from total dependence upon oil, but oil being a major part of it.
At the introduction of the Bill in 1987 it did enjoy the support of all Members in the Commons, and rightly so. It was a response, in part at least, to the devastation that gripped Alberta and the western sedimentary basin in general.
The point I wish to make today is that that devastation has not subsided. If anything, it has deepened. We all know that the price of oil in the last little while has gone up. The West Texas intermediate price has continually hovered around $20 a barrel. We also know that that has not translated into increased exploration and drilling activity in the western sedimentary basin. We may speculate as to why that is the case. The chief speculation seems to be that no one believes that price is going to stay there. Everyone believes that drilling undertaken now simply would not be economically sustainable.
I am in no position to quarrel with that estimation by the patch. I assume it to be correct. I assume that on the basis of straight forward market economics there is no good argument for extensive drilling and exploration at this time. It is the same situation as in 1986 to which CEDIP was the response in 1987.
Rig utilization was at a decade low in 1986 immediately before CEDIP was introduced. Only 35 per cent of the available rigs were drilling. In 1987 rig utilization was 37 per cent rising to 41 per cent in 1988. There is no question that CEDIP, and also some of the provincial programs did have a positive effect in the patch. For that the Government is to be commended. I congratulate the Government on that.
Spring is traditionally a time of low utilization. This spring has been much worse than expected. The president of the Canadian Association of Oil Well Drilling Contractors, Mr. Brian Krausert-by the way, hereafter in my remarks I will use the abbreviation of that organization, CAODC-recently stated the following. This is from the Edmonton Journal of May 26, 1989:
We have just come through the worst period in our recorded history.
The spring has been truly ugly.
June 5, 1989

At the end of May only 84 rigs were drilling in western Canada, a 60 per cent drop from the same period last year, a plunge the CAODC estimates has cost 17,000 direct and indirect jobs in the oil patch. Do not forget that this comes on top of 25 to 40,000 jobs lost as a result of the carnage of 1986.
The projections for the summer of 1989 were grim even before CEDIP was ended. CAODC forecast that only 40 per cent of rigs in western Canada would be drilling in the first quarter of 1989, only 29 per cent, about 153 rigs, in the second quarter, 28 per cent in the third and 48 per cent in the fourth. That was before the Budget and before CEDIP was prematurely ended. After the announcement that CEDIP was to be ended ahead of time, Don Herring, the managing director of CAODC said that even these low estimates would have to be revised. The Calgary Sun of May 12 states:
Now we will have to revise that figure downward.
Many companies are on the brink of bankruptcy and many oil and gas producers are holding back until June's OPEC meeting on quotas and prices hoping against hope that some firm commitment by the world's oil producers will be made to raise and hold up the price of oil, and hence of gas, at a level which will result in economic drilling activity in the western sedimentary basin. I must say that hope seems not to be shared by the forecasters in the majors and is perhaps a hope, we pray not, but perhaps a hope doomed to be dashed as a consequence of the results of that OPEC meeting.
The early cancellation of CEDIP simply means less activity and fewer jobs. There can be no question of that. The early cancellation of CEDIP represents the withdrawal of a planned $80 million investment in the western sedimentary basin. CAODC estimates that the maximum impact of this could be a decline in activity of a further 50 rigs representing a loss in employment of up to 1,500 people on the rig floor and up to 3,700 jobs at the lease.
I was interested earlier this morning to hear the remarks of the Minister when he said-I believe I have got this quote correct-"I have been pleased with the response of the industry". Now perhaps the Minister was speaking of a certain sector of the industry but that part of the industry with which I have been in contact has conveyed to me a response which I had assumed would not please the Minister, unless the Minister is enamoured of truly negative responses. For example, the Small Explorers and Producers Association of Canada wrote to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to express their concerns about the Budget and the early elimina-
Exploration and Development
tion of CEDIP. In their letter of May 9, Corey Heeren-sperger, the chairman of the SEPAC stated that:
The abrupt termination of the CEDIP program by the Government, which will be borne solely by the independent Canadian junior oil company, and the introduction of new taxes on the industry have eliminated at least $250 million in planned capital investment in the conventional oil and gas industry. It puts in jeopardy thousands of jobs in small exploration and producing companies as well as the service sector that conduct about one-third of the activity in the western Canadian sedimentary basin. It is unfair-
The thing we must bear in mind is that the cancellation of the CEDIP program now, the lack of any replacement for it either at the federal or provincial level, and continuing hard, low prices for oil can only result in the dismantling of the exploration and development industry in the western sedimentary basin.
That is not going to greatly hurt the oil majors that are continuing to reap substantial profits out of Canadian energy. There can be no doubt, when the price collapse hit in 1986, they simply transferred their profit-taking from their upstream operations, their oil patch operations, to their downstream operations, their refining and sales operations. The oil majors in consequence have not suffered greatly in the face of this devastating collapse of Canadian prices. There is no reason to believe they will suffer now. They have been able to maintain the very high pump price for gasoline in Canada that is the source now of their profits.
That cannot be said of the small independent Canadian companies that constitute the bulk of the companies engaged in exploration and development in the western sedimentary basin. They are going to be hit harder still in the face of the cancellation of CEDIP. They are going to go out of business. Thousands of jobs will be lost. Expertise will be lost. Capital equipment will be lost. These things will not be easily replaced. If I can issue one warning to Canada in this debate today, it is this. Beware of allowing the skill and capital that exists in the oil exploration and development industry in western Canada now to be eroded or lost because it will be needed again. There will be a time when again it becomes economic to explore and indeed becomes necessary for Canada's energy security to explore, and thus rebuild the

June 5, 1989
Exploration and Development
industry at that time from the paucious level to which it will have been forced.
It will be an extremely difficult and expensive proposition. We can avoid that in the future by maintaining what we have of the industry now. But in the absence of effective price supports, the only way we will be able to maintain that industry is through some kind of public support.
Whether or not a government is ideologically opposed to such support, to such intervention, is utterly beside the point. The question before us is the maintenance of an effective Canadian energy industry. That is the only question before us and the cancellation of CEDIP does nothing to maintain such an industry. In fact it actively harms that industry.
It is not just a question of the impact on the industry. It is not just a question of how oil patch workers and small independent Canadian companies feel about that elimination. They are indeed distressed by the elimination of CEDIP but I think they are also perhaps even more annoyed by the way the Government went about the elimination.
I would once again note the program was originally announced with much hoopla by the then Minister of Energy, Mr. Masse, in Edmonton on March 25, 1987. He announced that the program would start on April 1 of that year at a rate of 33-1/3 per cent. On October 1,
1988,	the rate would drop to 16-2/3 per cent and the program would eventually terminate on December 31,
1989.
Then came the run-up to the federal election. The Conservatives made announcements relating to Hibernia, Lloydminster, OSLO and the Vancouver Island pipeline. Small producers and Alberta MPs, we presume, joined together at that time to pressure the Government to modify the program which was about to decline in value to give conventional producers in the western sedimentary basin a wee bit of the sugar that was being sprinkled liberally over the other projects. By gosh, that announcement was eventually made. It was made by the Minister, who on September 30, 1988 announced that the program would be phased down less rapidly than originally announced. On October 1, 1988, the rate dropped to 25 per cent rather than 16-2/3 per cent and the drop from 25 per cent to 16-2/3 per cent would be
delayed until July 1, 1989 and that as planned, the program would continue until December 31, 1989. This announcement made it possible for the Minister to claim:
This-(delayed phase-down) will inject a further $80 million into the oil and gas industry.
This revision will lead to an estimated 300 additional wells and will maintain 1,600 "oil patch jobs''.
However, this extra $80 million announced in September before the election was taken away entirely when the Budget was announced last month, after the election. What was given one day was taken away the next, the principal intervening factor apparently being a successful election campaign.
This blatant manipulation was not well received in the oil patch. As was noted in a letter from Corey Heeren-sperger, Chairman of SEPAC, to the Minister of Finance on May 9, 1989:
Based on the Government's November election platform, we were shocked by the manner in which CEDIP was handled. Although the Minister of Energy told the industry in Calgary on April 5, 1989, that CEDIP would end (on December 31, 1989) as planned, this budget terminated the program three weeks later in spite of a negotiated clause in the CEDIP Act that was to provide six months notice of such a change. This action is hardly the encouragement needed to create more investment in western Canada. It is unfair-
I feel somewhat compelled to offer a small warning to my friends on the government benches. Manipulating programs, fudging rules, and not telling the whole truth is an approach to politics that the people of Canada will not tolerate for long. It is a very serious matter when the Government of Canada tries again and again to fool the people who elected it. As has been correctly observed, one can fool some of the people some of the time but keep it up and try to fool all the people and one will find oneself in trouble.
The cancellation of CEDIP will unquestionably hurt Alberta particularly and the western sedimentary basin in general. Even allowing the contention that "the deficit made me do it", the Government may have forgotten other alternatives that should have been entertained. If the Government really felt that cuts had to be made, even after announcing the extra $80 million just before the election, the alternative approach of restricting the cap on the program, which is to say the maximum amount of funds any one company could receive rather
June 5, 1989

than the proportion of expenses that could have been claimed back, deserved serious attention.
I do not know whether or not it was accorded serious attention.Perhaps someone sitting opposite could tell us that, but I would be most interested to learn the reason that proposal was rejected if indeed it was considered. It would have allowed the benefit of the program still to obtain where it was most needed, among the small producers and explorers, while cutting back on the over-all expense of the program if that was the principal concern.
I note that in the national context again we see that the energy market as such is not serving the needs of the Canadian energy industry. It is not serving the needs of the workers employed in that industry. It is not serving the long-term needs of the consumers who buy the products created by that industry.
The market is serving to destroy the exploration and development industry in western Canada. It is serving to eradicate the Canadian section of the industry. It is serving to foster non-productive mergers which in fact are further restricting exploration and development. It is serving to maintain artificially high pump prices in the face of low upstream prices so that the profits of the majors may be maintained at comfortable levels.
The market is not serving the Canadian people. The market is a hindrance. It is a positive problem for the Canadian people. It is only when we understand that we must regulate the energy market for the sake of the people who work in it, for the sake of the people who buy the product, for the sake of the long-term energy security of this country, that we will finally reach a point where we will not have to debate such matters as an incentive program here in the House of Commons and where they will not have to undergo such continuous debates in the Alberta legislature.
What I am saying, as I have been saying long before I was elected to this Chamber, is that we must have a regulated floor price for Canadian energy in Canada. That is the only long-term equitable solution to the problem of price fluctuations that will again and again, if left unchecked, devastate the industry and cause the massive waste of capital.
I realize that it is most unlikely that the Government will agree with me today, however forcefully it might find
Exploration and Development
I have made my remarks, but I would hope by continuing to make the argument in this Chamber I will, over time, contribute to a glimmer of recognition emerging on the benches opposite that perhaps there is reason behind this argument. Perhaps it is in the nature of the Canadian Confederation and its peculiar economic imperatives to require a regulated energy market. Perhaps the free market mythologies that so exorcize our good friends to the south are not directly applicable here in what has been called the northern empire.
This is a debate that will be carried on for some time yet. Perhaps I can just conclude my remarks by noting that this premature cancellation of CEDIP caught the industry unaware. subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am here today to speak to Bill C-19, an Act to terminate the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program Act. That program was put into place by the Conservative Government in 1987 to help small and medium sized firms in the oil and gas industry. The major objective was to encourage exploration and development of new reserves at a time of low world oil prices during a very difficult time for the industry.
I want to quote from Hansard on June 10, 1987, when the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources at that time spoke to the Bill. He said:
It will address the devastation experienced by the oil and natural gas producing provinces because of the drastic drop in world oil prices.
It did, by and large. Perhaps the Government is saying that now that prices are up-approximately $20 a barrel-

speechtext: They are.

subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT

But these prices certainly were not driven upward so much by market factors as by incidents such as the Exxon Valdez oil spill.

June 5, 1989
Exploration and Development
The industry has no confidence. No one in the industry believes the current price of $20 a barrel will be maintained. Therefore, there is no incentive for investment in the industry.
CEDIP is being cancelled at a time when capital expenditures in the oil and gas industry are at a very low peak. The Government is saying that it is going to be saving $80 million. What are the long-term implications of this saving when we consider that the spending of $80 million in this case would generate $450 million in expenditures in the gas and oil field? That means jobs, and jobs mean tax dollars.
When we look at the effect of these investments and the spin-offs, don't we perhaps think that the $80 million is not being saved at all? Actually, if we had invested the $80 million, we would be returning to the Government by way of tax dollars as much as the original investment.
It is not only that. Let us consider the impact on unemployment that will happen out West. Unemployment will rise. It will be a far bigger cost to this Government, although at this time the Government is saying it is pulling out of unemployment insurance. However, the cost in terms of Government assistance is devastating to any region. When one comes from a region such as northern Ontario, such as I do, one knows what happens when there is massive unemployment. We all know the cost, not just in terms of dollars but in terms of social costs. I would not wish that on any other area of the country.
It appears as if this Government is a Government of big business only. Let us note that all the promises and all grants in the megaprojects are intact. This is good, however, those grants benefit the large multinational corporations. What about the backbone of Canadian business, which is the small businessman? What about that small businessman? Do we have to sacrifice him at all costs? When we have a large corporation, especially in the gas and oil field, it can afford to move their operations to other countries where the business is more profitable. It can afford to wait.
What about the people? How do you explain that to the people of the western provinces? How do we say to them "you belong to this country also" when they are
being ripped off and when the jobs are going? It is a very difficult time. I do not understand why this Government is cancelling CEDIP. It could change it so that it would cost it a lot less and benefit as many people, especially the small independent businessman and the small business person out there. Not only is the Government going to cancel this program, but it is also bringing in the tax on large corporations. In the gas and oil industry, $10 million is not a lot of assets. That is a small corporation in that respect.
These small companies will not be compensated for the huge amounts of up-front capital investment that they are obligated to make to go into the business in the first place. As a result, many of them will go bankrupt. Many of them will just choose not to go into business at all. Therefore, it would all fall back on the large multinational gas and oil corporations.
I am wondering why-and I realize that it has nothing to do with the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) but that it has everything to do with this Government-the Energy, Mines and Resources Committee has had nothing but two organizational meetings. Is it because this Government feels that it is not interested in hearing what the people of Canada have to say about energy, mines and resources? It is appalling. As a new memberl cannot understand it. Other standing committees have met many times. Most of these standing committees have at least dealt with their Estimates.
There has been absolutely nothing, and no formal meeting is scheduled before September. Over and above that, there are no members on this committee from the government side who have been on that committee in the past.
Is it a signal by this Government that it wishes this committee to be ineffective? It is certainly being ineffective the way it stands now. I would certainly request that it perhaps gives some incentive to the chairman, who is a member of its side of the House, to call a formal meeting as quickly as possible. If the chairman is not capable or is not here to call a meeting, then it should ask its vice-chairman to call a meeting as quickly as possible.
It is extremely important that we not neglect-

You want to ask the Minister to stay out of this.

At any rate, it is extremely important that the committee meet as soon as possible. Considering that the chairman and vice-chairman of the committee belong to that side of the House, I think it might be in order.
I would certainly like to see CEDIP reintroduced, at least with a lower ceiling of $1 million per company. This would satisfy 90 per cent of the applicants and save the Government 85 per cent of the cost of the program. Perhaps the deficit could be helped in that way and still help the people in the constituencies out West. Believe me, when it comes time for another election, they will remember and they might be grateful if they could perhaps be given a bit of a boost, especially the ordinary, every day small producer.
Let us not heighten regional disparity. That is what this Bill does. I believe that the Government knows this. Perhaps that is why, on April 5 or April 6 when there was a speech by the Hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp), he stated that the Government would not terminate this agreement before December 1989 and that it would honour its commitment.
Not only did the Government not honour its commitment, but in effect it cut off the program as of April 27, despite a negotiated clause in the agreement that said that it would give them some six months' notice before terminating this agreement. It seems very strange to meto negotiate a clause of some kind that states "we are going to give you six months, fellows, to let you know well in advance" and all of a sudden, bingo, it is gone. It is not fair and it is not right, especially when the need is there, and the need is definitely there.
The Government is encouraging the megaprojects. I do not have anything against that. What I am against is the fact that we are forgetting the average Canadian. I would encourage this Government to change its way of thinking.

Mr. Speaker, my idea is to keep the thing going. That is why I am against cancelling CEDIP. In my area I have some experience as to what happens when grants are cut off to the small producers and the small explorers.
In the mining sector, which is what I am comfortable with, when we cancel incentive grants to small explorers we allow the large corporations to buy up all of the work that has been done by the small corporations and to stockpile.
These large corporations do not have to spend their money in a certain area if there is nothing going on in that country. They can afford to move their explorations to Indonesia or wherever they will. There is no guarantee that they will keep those jobs in the area. There is no guarantee that if they are not producing very much in that area they will purchase anything in that area. There are absolutely no guarantees.
I can tell all Hon. Members that the small explorers and the small business people are far more productive and more cost efficient than the companies which engage in large megaprojects. There is a much larger spin-off from every dollar that these small explorers spend in a community than the large megaprojects that in fact have not started up yet. There have been some announcements regarding them but they have not started up.
I like big corporations. However, I believe the backbone of the country is the small business man and the medium business man, not the large corporations that bail out as soon as they are not making a profit big enough. Large corporations only believe in huge profits;

the bigger the profit, the better. That does not mean they believe in people. They believe in profits where they can get them, be it in Indonesia, China, or wherever. That does not guarantee jobs in an area.
I want to see every area of the country benefit, not just certain rich areas like Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal. That is why I am fighting this measure. I believe the Government is forgetting one thing, that is, what Canadians are all about.
