speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in discussing Bill C-19 I must note, having listened to the Minister's speech, that even his best friends could not claim that he felt very inspired, very sure of himself, or really very motivated. He sounded unusually flat. He sounded as if his heart was not with the measure.
Strangely enough, I did not hear him making even one reference to the environment, not one reference to sustainable development. He certainly was concerned with the Budget. He certainly was concerned with market oriented approaches.
It seems to me that a Bill of this importance has to be dealt with in the context of the economy and in the context of the environment. The three are closely linked. As you know, Mr. Speaker, each one has an impact on the other two.
The importance of Bill C-19 is in what it does not say. It is important because it is surrounded by a vacuum. It is important because, as we debate it, Canadians do not know what is our long-term energy plan. Therefore, there are some questions that I would put to the Minister which need to be answered within the context of Bill C-19.
For instance, how long does the Minister think we can go on relying on fossil fuels while at the same time by the use of these fossil fuels, coal and oil mainly, we pollute
the atmosphere with carbon dioxide? We do this in the full knowledge of what that carbon dioxide does in terms of strengthening the greenhouse effect which in turn is reinforcing the trend toward global warming. Cancelling the exploration subsidies in the North, as is implicit in Bill C-19, is no doubt a welcome move in a sense although it was inspired not by environmental reasons. Does this mean that it is an implicit invitation by the Government to rely more on fossil fuels developed south of 60? Is that what it means?
Why in the name of fiscal responsibility does the Government cancel one subsidy for fossil fuel development while at the same time, as we learned today from the media, the Government and the Minister are vigorously defending massive subsidies to fossil fuel megaprojects? The two do not gibe in terms of long-term policy. There has to be an explanation given. If something has to stop subsidized fossil fuel development for the sake of the Budget, why not then cancel the very large commitments made to Hibernia, OSLO, Lloydminster, and the Vancouver Island gas pipeline which require investments not by the hundreds of millions but by the billions? There is here evidently a contradiction.
Does Bill C-19 mean an implicit invitation for the construction of more dams, more nuclear power stations and more C02 pollution from coal fired electricity generation south of 60? Why is this Bill introduced in the House in a vacuum, without a framework, without any of the ideas as to what Canada's energy future ought to be? Why therefore is the long term not on the Government's agenda? Does the cancellation of exploration subsidies mean that the Government intends to put in its place a policy of subsidies for renewable sources of energy?
After the decimation of what was in place until November 1984, which resulted in the cancellation of $40 million at the National Research Council alone on renewable sources of energy, it would be quite a conversion on the road to Damascus. We would like to believe that to be possible for the sake of the public interest.
Does Bill C-19 mean that with this Bill the Government is ready to move with energy efficiency, with energy conservation, intended for instance to capture that 30 per cent in efficiency on Canada's part as pointed out by the International Energy Agency, which sponsored an event attended by the Minister last week in Paris? Or, is this Bill the only policy thought necessary at this point in
June 5, 1989

time, unfortunately by a Government which is myopic, which is preoccupied with the short term, which is obsessed by a deficit and incapable of giving Canada an energy policy that takes the environment, the climate, human health and the long-term costs into consideration? These are the questions that we would like the Minister to answer when presenting Bill C-19.
When I speak of the word "costs"in the context of this debate, what I meant is the cost to our economy if we do not succeed in slowing down the climate warming trend, the so-called greenhouse effect, coming about as a result of the pollution produced through the burning of oil, coal, and the like.
Such costs, as we know, could be immense. There would be public works to protect Canada's coastal cities from rising sea levels, agricultural land becoming desertified as a result of gradual increases in temperature, forest acreage lost because of fires triggered by warmer weather and inevitable changes in the species of trees brought about by new climatic conditions.
It seems to me that in this policy vacuum, we are running the risk of being lured into embracing the nuclear option. We know what that entails. It entails risks. It has unresolved health questions and implied high costs. We know the Darlington nuclear station was originally scheduled to cost just over $7 billion. Then the cost jumped to $11 billion. Last week, we learned that it is now at $13 billion. We do not know yet the cost of permanent disposal of nuclear waste, the cost of decommissioning reactors and, as lately discovered and reported in an article in The Financial Post a couple of weeks ago by Stephen Probyn, the hidden subsidies in the form of unrealistically low discount rates for the capital invested in such plants.
To resist the nuclear sirens, so to speak, we must launch energy efficiency drives and renew the drive on energy conservation. We must do that because by postponing every year our ability to achieve the efficiency that other nations have achieved and in capturing the 30 per cent of energy losses incurred, as reported in a study conducted by the International Energy Agency, we incur substantial costs. Why such a drive is not initiated by this
Exploration and Development
Government is very difficult to understand. Is it lack of vision, inertia, or is it both?
Why is this Government approaching energy policies in such a piecemeal backward manner? Why does the Minister of Energy go to Paris rather than Calgary to make a statement-and I quote from his speech of May 30 which he distributed a few days ago. "While we are firmly committed to a market-oriented policy, we recognize that in its pure form, it cannot deal with so-called external environmental effects of economic activity". Why did the Minister not quote his speech fully instead of just half of the statement he made in Paris? The speech was quite interesting. He had the courage to make this statement abroad, but he does not have the courage to make it in Canada.
At the same meeting of the International Energy Agency, the Minister also said on May 30, and I quote: "We must pursue energy policy solutions available to us today such as energy efficiency improvements, while at the same time promoting sources of supply such as renewables".
Did we hear anything about it today? Did the Minister repeat his courageous and important statement at home? Why is it only good in Paris? Why is it only expressed across the Atlantic? Why does the Minister lose the courage when he comes home? We would like to hear it at home too in this Parliament.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has to accept the reality and the political fact-and I will explain in a moment why-that he is also a minister of the environment. He cannot ignore the commitment made by his Prime Minister to sustainable development. It is a commitment that the Prime Minister made a year ago and repeated last night at the National Art Gallery by way of a videotape, in both languages, in which he commits himself to sustainable development. This makes this Minister of Energy automatically a minister of the environment. Therefore, if the Minister of Energy does not pursue an energy policy that takes sustainable development fully into account, he makes the statement of his own Prime Minister hollow, empty and meaningless.
The Prime Minister of Canada embraced, in August of 1988, the Brundtland report. He declared himself on the side of sustainable development. Therefore the Minister of Energy, if he intends to follow the leadership ex-

June 5, 1989
Exploration and Development
pressed by the Prime Minister, should fall in line with that policy direction, but he does not seem to, and C-19 certainly does not give us any indication or direction.
Through the Prime Minister's statement, the Minister has received his orders from the Prime Minister, who stressed again sustainable development in the Speech from the Throne just a few months ago. This mandate, Mr. Speaker, is being ignored.
Together with this Bill today, the Minister of Energy was expected to offer an environmentally sustainable plan, a broader picture, an indication to Canadians that he and his Government have a clear idea as to where we should be going with energy between now and the year 2030, if you like, to ensure clean and safe sources of energy and sustainable for present and future generations. That has not happened with Bill C-19.
We would like to think that this Government has a long-term agenda. If it is limited to Bills like C-19, we will continue to raise, from this side of the House, the imperative necessity that the Government of Canada, at the present time directed by the ideology of the Conservative Party, has a duty to consult Canadians and to develop a long-term energy plan with a number of factors in mind which makes the development of such a plan more difficult than ever before. We have to take into consideration factors of sustainable development and climatic change which did not exist when we made plans in the past. Therefore, the task is multidimensional and poses a challenge. It seems to me that the Government of Canada cannot escape that responsibility.

I thank the Hon. Member for his question. The key word of course is the importance of "lead" time. Particularly in matters related to energy, lead time is a very important factor. I am sure that the Minister knows that very well.
What has struck me lately, both in reference to the previous Liberal Government as well as to the present Conservative Government, if in the last decade we had shifted the subsidies that we put behind exploration, particularly north of 60, for the discovery of additional sources of fossil fuels and had used those resources which in terms of funds were phenomenal, and I venture to guess that more than $8 billion in the past decade has been put behind exploration of fossil fuel research North of 60, and shifted even a modest portion of that resource, perhaps even half, behind photovoltaics, behind biomass, behind wind, solar, and other forms of renewable energy, particularly biomass and photovoltaics, that we would have done very well with the lead time required that the Hon. Now we have to stop for a moment, reassess our strategy, think of the long term. Bill C-19 disappears in an ocean of considerations that are much bigger and more significant, and come to grips with the lead time and ask ourselves, are we putting our money where we should put it? speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

speechtext:
that Bill C-4, an Act to amend the Energy Supplies Emergency Act and to amend the Access to Information Act in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as I have mentioned in the prior intervention I will require approximately 12 minutes, and I think that will be seen as an equitable distribution of the time available for the other two Parties.
The Energy Supplies Emergency Act was assented to on March 26, 1979. It is now more than 10 years and much has happened in this House since then. Certainly there will be few here who remember the occasion, even fewer who will recall what it was all about. However, I know that my critic and I were here. Before addressing the particular business before us today, I believe it would be appropriate to give Hon. Members an understanding of the origin of the Act, at least briefly.
Emergency, as we all know, is the sudden juncture of events demanding immediate action. The elements may be known but the timing of their concurrence is not. We can all think of examples, dramatic ones such as earthquakes or disasters at sea or other situations including fire or flood. In many of these cases, it was only afterward with perfect hindsight that the absence or
deficiency of contingency plans was sufficiently recognized and appropriate action taken.
The Energy Supplies Emergency Act itself has such a history, but as such it represents a determination to learn from experience through positive and corrective action. Its raison d'etre focuses on the possible disruption of the international oil market and its impact on Canada. It is therefore expressly designed to ensure that Canada has appropriate contingency plans and the instruments essential for their implementation.
I am sure Members will recall the international oil crisis of 1973 and 1974 or the so-called oil shocks as they were described from that time on. Some members of the OPEC countries interrupted normal oil supplies as a political lever. In fact discussions are taking place in OPEC as we discuss this issue today. Market panic followed with a sharp escalation in the price of oil as buyers competed for supply. Under the leadership of the U.S., a direct result of the situation was the signing in 1974 of the International Energy Program by 16 countries. Today it is made up of 21 countries. I have just returned from those meetings last week, and I want to say that the co-operation in the IEA is as secure today as when it was originally formed.
Countries are joined through the International Energy Agency in mutually supportive planning aimed at enhancing their collective energy and economic security. Canada is an original signatory to the IEP and an active supporter of the IEA. A major component of the agency's programs is an established emergency oil sharing system.
Canada's national response in 1974 when the IEA was formed was the passage of the original Energy Supplies Emergency Act. This Act established the Energy Supplies Allocation Board or ESAB, which is responsible for the Act's objectives and programs. Chief among those were programs to allocate crude oil and oil products and to ration gasoline and diesel fuel during a period of oil shortage. In addition, the board was responsible for fulfilling Canada's obligations in support of the IEA's emergency oil sharing programs.
When the crisis passed, the Act lapsed in 1976 under a sunset clause. The events of 1979-1980, that is, the Iranian revolution and the subsequent Iran-Iraq war, again caused oil market disturbance and rapidly escalating prices. Accordingly, the Government introduced the Energy Supplies Emergency Act, 1979 with similar but refined and modified provisions of the earlier Act. This time there is no sunset clause on the Act itself but only on the duration of the board's powers and programs in the event of their activation. In this fashion, the requisite
June 5, 1989

legal authorities are maintained against the sudden need to activate the planned response to a supply emergency.
Therefore, I think it is particularly noteworthy and of special interest to the House that the activation of ESAB's emergency powers and programs under the Act is a prerogative exercised only through a governor in council formal declaration by order of a national emergency or by reason of actual or anticipated shortages of petroleum. Further, this declaration is itself subject to the early concurrence of this House according to specified procedures set out in the Act.
Let me address one issue that may be raised in the context of this legislation, that is, the relationship between it and our obligations under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. It should be understood that our obligations under the FTA to share oil supplies in an emergency are likely to be much less than those required by theoil sharing system of the International Energy Agency which would be implemented using the provisions of the ESE Act. Under the FTA we can share any reduction in Canadian oil supplies due to offshore disruption through a proportionate decrease in oil exports to the U.S.
Furthermore, under the FTA there is no obligation to provide supplies to the U.S. There is only a requirement to make them available on commercial terms. On the other hand, as a member of the IEA and a net exporter of oil, Canada would likely be required to increase its supplies to other member countries including the U.S. in that type of emergency. With respect to oil supply emergencies, our IEA obligations are clearly more demanding than those under the FTA.
Therefore the resurrection of ESAB necessarily triggered a complete review of the emergency organization and programs. This led to passage in 1982 of a series of amendments to the Act for improvements to the allocation and rationing programs. These amendments reflected an intense period of consultation by ESAB with both the petroleum industry and the provinces and territories. These consultations were mainly achieved through the formation of two consultative committees, the Petroleum Industry Advisory Committee and the
Energy Supplies
Provincial Advisory Committee, and through consumer organizations and associations. This resulted in fully developed allocation and rationing programs that enjoy full support because they are recognized as realistic and compatible with industry and regional concerns. These committees continue to advise ESAB.
The programs for managing available supplies of petroleum and petroleum products necessarily must ensure fair and equitable distribution to consumers in all regions of our country. I believe therefore that Members of the House would benefit from a better understanding of how they operate.
First, it must be recognized that an international market disturbance would have a primary impact on the supply of crude oil. The programs are designed to use our western Canadian resources to support use in eastern Canada which is the area of import dependency. ESAB, with powers granted under the Energy Supplies Emergency Act, would activate a mandatory allocation program following a declaration of national emergency by the Governor in Council.
The terms have been with us for some time. Today, as I mentioned to the House, amendments are needed not only to continue with the program but to ensure Canadians that plans are in place in case emergencies take place. I could go through the amendments clause by clause to to clarify the definitions and the clause changes, but I do not have that time today. However, after second reading, if the House is so inclined, obviously I would want to discuss those terms with Members opposite in the legislative committee to make sure that Canada's interests are protected, our international obligations are met, and Canadians can be assured that the best plans are in place in case emergencies have to be met.

subtopic: ENERGY SUPPLIES EMERGENCY ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ENERGY SUPPLIES EMERGENCY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the words of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp) regarding Bill C-4.1 think we are of the same mind with respect to the need for legislation such as this to safeguard Canada in the event of an international disruption and to ensure that Canadians have a secure supply of energy.

June 5, 1989
Energy Supplies
I want to say one thing with respect to the International Energy Association. With relation to the Free Trade Agreement, it may not in any way restrict our obligations under the IEA, unless the determination is that we must share 7 per cent of the oil under the agreement with the International Energy Agency and the United States and the shortage occurs in the United States.
The trade agreement, as the Minister of Energy has said, does not require us to sell oil to the United States. It requires us to make it available. Of course that is splitting hairs. I believe 40 per cent of our oil now goes to the U.S. That is not going to stop. We have now created that dependency on Canadian oil in the United States. There are contracts which assure that that oil is going to be there. Of course, when there is multinational oil companies, the supply of Canadian oil will continue. It may not be at 40 per cent, but an increasing amount of our oil will go.
We are obliged under the International Energy Agency to share up to 7 per cent of our oil with other countries at the time of an international disruption. That amount of 7 per cent that we are to supply may or may not be with the United States. If it is with the United States it would merge with our obligations under the trade agreement. If not, the proportion we share with the United States would come after the 7 per cent that was made available under our obligation under the International Energy Agency. As a result of the trade agreement, we have guaranteed that more of our oil will go abroad. It is certainly not reducing our obligations under the agreement with the International Energy Agency.
The most important point I want to impress upon the Government is the issue of energy security in Canada. I think the Minister understands that nothing must be allowed to reduce the energy security we have in this country.
We are blessed with having a great deal of energy in Canada in various forms. The problem we face is to maintain that security in the event of a crisis, international or otherwise. It is very important that these energy supplies be available to Canadians, and I believe the Minister has said this will not be changed under this Bill.
The fact the clause seems to reduce the ability to make information available in a court of law is a subject that I think we can discuss in committee. However, I am pleased the Minister of State for Privatization (Mr. McDermid) is in the House along with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The Bill proposes to eliminate the role of Petro-Canada, and I will ask the Minister at committee why this is done. It appears to be a housekeeping measure to remove the mention of Petro-Canada so that when the Government introduces a privatization Bill on Petro-Canada this Act will already have been dealt with.
I believe that Petro-Canada's role according to Section 3 and Section 12 of the Act has been meaningful. It stated that one of the six directors on the board must be a member of Petro-Canada. That was a sensible provision, but the Government is deleting the need to have one of the directors as a representative of Petro-Canada.
I find that very strange, if Petro-Canada is to remain a Crown corporation. However, if it is the Government's intention to privatize Petro-Canada, it seems the Government will deal with this legislation before doing so. I hope that is not the case. I will give the Minister the opportunity to state whether there is another reason for this Bill in committee.
According to Clause 12, the duties carried out by the representative from Petro-Canada will be taken on by an official of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. I believe that Petro-Canada is even more important to this country now because of the trade agreement. While certain segments of the oil and gas industry and all segments of the energy sector in this country believe a continental energy sector exists, there does not exist a continental energy policy. However, we do have our own Crown Corporation involved in the energy sector which can give a very clear picture from its involvement in the market-place.
I believe that Petro-Canada had much to contribute in this legislation by being involved. That involvement is disappearing, and I am concerned about that. I will expand that in committee, but I wanted to advise the Minister of my concern in that regard.

subtopic: ENERGY SUPPLIES EMERGENCY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too will keep my remarks on this Bill mercifully brief. The Energy Emergencies Act, Chapter 89, was passed in 1979 to "provide a means to conserve the supplies of energy within Canada during periods of a national emergency caused by shortages or market disturbances affecting the
June 5, 1989

national security and welfare and the economic stability of Canada".
Those are very worth-while objectives with which I do not believe any one in the House could have serious quarrel. The existing legislation provides for the establishment of the Energy Supplies Allocation Board. In the event of actual or anticipated energy shortages as determined by the Governor in Council, this board would proceed to use its broad powers to administer a mandatory allocation or rationing program, which could include diverting oil or gas from pipeline companies, ordering Canadian ships into service as required, regulating imports and exports, subject to the Free Trade Agreement one presumes, and generally ensuring that the limited supplies in Canada get to where they are needed.
I will not go into the implications of the FTA for energy allocation in emergencies. I believe there will be other opportunities to do so as the current session proceeds through its natural life. However, I will just note that I share the concerns of the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) that the FTA has substantial implications for the allocation of energy resources in Canada within an emergency context.
Bill C-4 extends the powers of the board to regulate prices during a domestic emergency energy rationing program. Many of the changes that the Bill proposes are little more than wording changes and are, in fact, relatively unimportant.
However, there are a few proposals that I believe are important, even though at first glance they may appear not to be. I want to deal with three of them.
The first two concern Petro-Canada. Clause 2 has the effect of deleting from the Energy Supply Allocation Board, which currently consists of up to six people appointed by the Governor in Council, a representative of Petro-Canada. Clause 3 would amend the Act to delete from the International Energy Agency Canadaan appointment, being a Petro-Canada representative on that energy agency study group.
The International Energy Agency currently has a study group on energy questions, and current legislation stipulates that Petro-Canada is to be Canada's representative on that group, having responsibility to the board and to the Minister. According to the amendment, Canada's
Energy Supplies
representative on the international study group will not necessarily be a Petro-Canada official. Instead, our representative will be a board member who, given Clause 2, obviously could not be a Petro-Canada official or some other official of Energy, Mines and Resources.
I believe that this constitutes a stripping away of at least some of the public policy prerogatives currently enjoyed by Petro-Canada. Of course, this is consistent with the Government's ill concealed antipathy toward Petro-Canada. It is certainly consistent with its long range privatization project. If Petro-Canada is to be privatized, then it necessarily must be stripped of its public policy functions.
It will come as a surprise to no Member of the House that we in the New Democratic Party caucus greatly oppose any such moves to limit or in fact remove Petro-Canada's public policy function. As this caucus fought for and indeed compelled the Liberal Government to create Petro-Canada back in the mid-1970s, we continue to believe it has a vital public policy role to play.
That is why for us these two provisions in this Act are of some substantial concern. I, too, look forward with eager anticipation to the Minister's remarks in this regard in committee.
The third elementis certainly a closely tied one of equal interest to the Minister of State for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs (Mr. McDermid) whom I note is present. This is not noting an absence; this is noting of presence for the debate today. It is set out in Clause 5 of the Bill. Under the current unamended legislation the Board can now prescribe retail prices of controlled product and of printed material. The existing legislation states that printed material required for a rationing program would be handled by the Canada Post Corporation.
Under the amendment proposed in Bill C-4, and I quote, "any Department or agency of the Government of Canada" could be used for that purpose. This does not preclude the using of Canada Post, assuming that Canada Post is at the time of such issuance still an arm of the Government. However it again is a stripping away from a Crown corporation of a public policy function. In the absence of any strong indication to the contrary, it

June 5, 1989
cannot but be viewed, I would submit, as preparatory to a privatization in this instance of Canada Post.
It seems in fact that in this debate in principle at second reading we are debating two principles in this Bill. The first is that of the prudent allocation of energy resources in the event of an emergency shortage. To the degree that the Bill deals with that, I do not think any of us have any objection.
The second principle seems to be the preparation for the privatization, in part at least, of two Crown corporations. I must note that with that principle-

subtopic: STATEMENTS PURSUANT TO S. O. 31
STATEMENTS PURSUANT TO S. O. 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, June 4, 1989, we were all witness to the first free elections held in Poland in over 40 years.
This historic event is one in a succession of events that promises to lead to the democratization of Poland and guarantees major social and political change in that country. However, 40 years of oppression have resulted in considerable damage to the economy of Poland. Poland's foreign debt stands at between $30 billion and $40 billion. The country's ability to salvage its economy will depend largely on the flexibility of debtor countries to forgive or, at the very least, reschedule the payments in light of current events.
The West has an obligation not only to Poland but to all countries that are in pursuit of democracy to support in spirit and in action an ideology that though not perfect is far the best one designed to date by human mankind.
The West also has an obligation to re-evaluate continually its relationships with countries that penalize its citizens for expressing opinions that differ from those of their own Government.
In short, we should not be afraid to support those people who are striving for exactly the same things that we in the West have fought for and for which will continue to fight.

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
THE ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: LAUNCHING OF NATIONAL ENVIRONMENT WEEK IN CALGARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) launched National Environment Week to encourage Canadians to do our part to clean up the man-made mess that threatens our globe and jeopardizes our survival.
Calgary kicked off Environment Week yesterday with our annual river clean-up. It was a glorious day of sunshine that brought out thousands of Calgarians to scour the river banks, picking up garbage and cleaning out junk from the water-families with picnic lunches, community groups and individuals committed to a cleaner environment taking action to clean up our part of the globe.
The message of National Environment Week is awareness and action. There is no more time for study or delay. We must take action now as individuals, as communities, as provinces and as nations to stop the damage to our global home.

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is World Environment Day, the beginning of Environment Week in Canada.
Somehow the sense of urgency necessary to deal with our national and global crisis must be instilled in the political leadership of Canada and every country. Let me deal with the greenhouse effect for just a moment as an example.
The Minister this morning mentioned that one-half the carbon dioxide added to the atmosphere by human activity has been added in the last 30 years. In North
America, we have just 5 per cent of the world population but use 25 per cent of the world's energy and release over 25 per cent of atmospheric C02 and even higher levels of CFCs.
Our oceans are rising. Unless we reduce greenhouse gas production, oceans will continue to rise in direct relation to C02 and greenhouse gases. Entire nations such as the Maldives will be covered by the oceans as the ice caps melt.
The sense of urgency-where is it? In Canada, the Conservatives are closing the regional renewable energy offices and plan to give the fossil fuel industry billions of dollars in welfare to expand and prolong production.
Canada and the world must have action on the carbon cycle, action on reducing greenhouse gases, action on holes in the ozone and acid precipitation. That requires the sense of urgency which is lacking at every level.
Environment Day and Environment Week are appropriate for launching public education. However, let it begin here in this Chamber where decisions on environmental viability and human survival are determined every day by our decisions.

subtopic: MULTICULTURALISM
MULTICULTURALISM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today all three parties met with members of the Canadian Ethno-cultural Council to discuss issues of concern to all Canadians. The service this group plays as a co-ordinating body for ethnic minorities in Canada is indispensable to the maintenance of harmonious race relations in our country.

Since 1980, the CEC has headed more than 35 national organizations representing the cultural communities, all of which are dedicated to better race relations and the struggle against all forms of discrimination based on race and ethnic origin.
This group is inspired by values like equality, justice and fairness. By its very nature and because of the credibility it has acquired, the CEC must be a key player in the development of any Canadian multiculturalism policy.

June 5. 1989
In closing, I would like to thank all members of the CEC for their contribution to building a more open country where equal opportunity for all is a fact, not just political rhetoric.

subtopic: MONTREAL CONFERENCE ON AIDS
MONTREAL CONFERENCE ON AIDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the most important conventions of our time is now being held in Montreal. It is so important because it is about the scourge of the twentieth century, AIDS.
The attendance of the Prime Minister of Canada and the Minister of National Health at the opening of this international meeting is most eloquent testimony to the importance the Government gives to this leading problem.
By warning us not to expect miracles but emphasizing dialogue, co-operation and information, health specialists from throughout the world are showing us how to fight this scourge. To do this, and especially to preserve the dignity of those who have AIDS, now is the time for cooperation, not criticism; for supporting others in difficulty, not discrimination. Above all, we must put a major part of our effort into information and dispelling the falsehoods about AIDS.
In this regard, the Treasury Board's recent directives on protecting, hiring and accepting people with AIDS in the workplace could be a model for all businesses, whether in the public or private sector. In doing so, our Government has shown leadership.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all Members of the House will join me this afternoon in expressing our sorrow at the slaughter in China and in extending our sympathy to the Chinese people and their friends and relatives here in Canada.
The senseless and brutal actions of the so-called People's Army under the instructions of government authorities have resulted in the death or injuries of
thousands of young people. These youth are innocent of any wrongdoing. Their peaceful presence in Tiananmen Square over the last number of weeks has been exemplary for its non-violence. Their contribution to the Chinese political discourse has represented the highest ideals.
Through its inexplicable actions the Chinese Government has shown the world a most horrifying face. Its actions should be harshly condemned by all members of the international community.
For its part, the Canadian Government must examine the best way to communicate in the strongest possible terms our outrage individually as a country and in concert with others. Immediate attention must be given to the safety of Canadians in China, and the safety of Chinese students here in Canada who must not be put in the position of having to return to China against their will.
The Chinese authorities cannot long ignore the calls of its own people for greater freedom and democracy. Murdering their brightest and best is for fascists. The spirit of the revolution is surely toward democracy, if it is a living spirit and not something only of the past. Let it be said that the students have not died in vain.

June 5, 1989

Again, congratulations for a job well done.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a crime against humanity has been committed in the People's Republic of China. My wife wept as we watched together in disbelief over the weekend as a once peaceful demonstration turned into a blood bath.
There were gruesome television accounts of tanks and soldiers armed with automatic weapons roaring down the Avenue of Eternal Peace toward Tiananmen Square, trampling and shooting hundreds of student protesters whose only defence was the courage of their convictions.
The great Russian writer, Dostoyevski, once wrote that "compassion is the chief law of human existence". The ruthless and merciless People's Army showed absolutely no compassion in the mass slaughter of students, women and children.
Members of the Hamilton-Wentworth-Halton Chinese Canadian community, which numbers some 20,000, express their shock and horror at the abhorrent events in China. They express their outrage at the Government's brutal suppression of the democratic movement for reform. They call upon the Canadian Government to do whatever is in its power to persuade the Chinese Government to find a peaceful solution to the crisis in China.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, events in China have shocked and horrified Canadians. For over ten years, China represented a beacon of progress. China once offered a bold example to the Communist world by moving away from totalitarianism and responding to the will of its people. In two bloody days, that progress has been crushed. Today, the world watches as China reverts back to totalitarianism for a solution to its problem.
Canadians wonder how a nation that once taught the world to let a thousand flowers bloom could so brutally stamp out its own seeds of democracy. If China is to ever
truly be a people's republic, let it stop killing and start rebuilding the progress that it once made.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to record for my constituents and for freedom-loving people everywhere the anxiety and sadness of Canadians in response to the brutality and death which has been perpetrated by a repressive military force in Beijing over the past weekend.
This event is both a shock and a lesson for Canadians in that the freedom of peaceful assembly clearly enshrined in our Constitution does not exist for them. It is repugnant to all of us to see internationally recognized human rights violated in so brutal a manner as has taken place in Tiananmen Square.
A China in turmoil is a China in agony, and I want to confirm our democratic resolve in solidarity with the citizens of the PRC that our world history will not be ruled by guns but by peace and freedom.
The carnage of Tiananmen Square demands a response from our Government, a response which will show the students and other citizens in Tiananmen Square and the world that their hopes and dreams for freedom and human rights live on with all of us today in this House.

CONDUCT OF MEMBERS

Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada sent us here to govern the country and to address the very real and serious problems that face Canadians from coast to coast. Instead, for the past several weeks, the time of this Chamber has been taken up with the self-righteous indignation of Members opposite in their seemingly obsessive, if futile, quest to bring down a Minister or two over an issue which is at best of very limited interest to the public.

They simply do not care about the tempest in the teapot in Ottawa, and they are beginning to conclude that Ottawa doesn't care about them.
Lest this Parliament become totally irrelevant in the minds of Canadians, let us turn our attention to the real issues of real people. Let's get on with the business of Canada.

we can, as quickly as possible about the situation in China and consequently as to the most effective actions that we can take.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Minister is no doubt aware that many Chinese students now living in Canada and attending Canadian universities made some very harsh statements on Canadian television about their government and went so far as to openly condemn the Chinese leaders. Should some of these students prefer to remain in Canada instead of going back to China and an uncertain future, could the federal Government of Canada offer them political asylum?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO GIVE POLITICAL ASYLUM TO CHINESE STUDENTS IN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are aware of the situation, which may be somewhat uncertain, of a number of Chinese students here in Canada, and my Government colleagues and myself are now considering various arrangements, such as extending their right to stay in Canada and perhaps other ways of guaranteeing their safety.

subtopic: REQUEST AS TO WHETHER MINISTER SPOKE WITH WAN LI
REQUEST AS TO WHETHER MINISTER SPOKE WITH WAN LI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary. The Minister will recall that only a few weeks ago. Deputy Prime Minister Wan Li was in Canada on an official visit. He also met members of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade, and on that occasion he commented on the troubles that were starting in China, and he had been rather encouraging. He said he was prepared to act with all requisite understanding for the patriotic enthusiasm of the young Chinese. I would like to know whether the Minister had a chance to meet Mr. Wan Li, whether they discussed privately the situation in China and whether the Minister made it clear to the Chinese delegation at that time that Canada definitely

June 5, 1989
Oral Questions
would not approve of using the army to control the Chinese students.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST AS TO WHETHER MINISTER SPOKE WITH WAN LI
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, unfortunately I did not have a chance during the visit to have this kind of conversation, but Canada's attitude to the democratic aspirations and actions of the Chinese students was made clear to the Chinese authorities. We all hope that it will be possible to revert as soon as possible to a situation in which democracy can be encouraged, but for the time being, the main challenge for us is to have a detailed understanding of the events in China and to find out how Canada can first of all, help promote a stable situation; second, a situation that will enhance the safety of Chinese citizens; and third, a situation that will encourage democracy.

subtopic: CHINA-VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS
CHINA-VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate what the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said, not only today but during the weekend, in his condemnation of this horrific violation of human rights administered by the army in China, at whose instructions we may not know for some time.
I was a little concerned that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in his reference to the Security Council, indicated that we may have to wait a couple of days before the Government of Canada takes some initiative there.
Considering that it is appropriate to wait for a couple of days before we know the answers to a number of matters, we certainly know now that there has been an incredible violation of human rights and totally needless bloodshed. This is something that ought to be debated at the United Nations.
When we have seen past unacceptable circumstances there has been very prompt action by the Security Council, would he kindly tell the House why he thinks it is necessaiy to wait for another two days?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CHINA-VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party is quite correct in interpreting my remarks as suggesting that I wanted to be clearer than we can be in these circumstances as to what exactly is happening in
China before we take action in the Security Council. It might be prescriptive or it might be designed to try to encourage positive developments in China. I accept completely the view that it would be appropriate for Canada to act as quickly as possible to occasion a debate in the Security Council.
The Prime Minister and I have had discussions about that possibility this morning and we are examining it. We will be in touch with Ambassador Yves Fortier and examining the circumstances which would be most appropriate for Canada to follow. We intend no delay, but I am sure the Leader of the New Democratic Party and other Members of the House would want us to be as well informed as to the situation in China as we can be before launching that debate. Certainly I do not intend, by that answer, to suggest a delay.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE DEBATE IN SECURITY COUNCIL
REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE DEBATE IN SECURITY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to ask the Secretary of State to perhaps reconsider. He is acting, as all Members of the House are, with very good will to see what role an outside country can play in such horrific circumstances.
Would he not think it might provide precisely the kind of international pressure on the Government of China immediately, if they heard from the Security Council that there was a request for an immediate debate? If I can put it this way, I would like the Secretary of State to perhaps think this over. I especially point out that by demanding an immediate debate and insisting that the Chinese authorities come and justify what they have done, this may in fact force them to stop the violence sooner than otherwise would be the case.
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, we are considering precisely that factor and weighing it against the possibility that in the immediate aftermath of developments in China, there might be some wisdom in waiting a day or two.
Those are precisely the kind of factors that we are weighing because in the circumstances, all Members of this House and all Canadians would want action that Canada initiated to be as effective as possible. We do not simply want to register our horror and dismay at these developments, but also hopefully to be able to restore a situation that conforms to developments that many of us
June 5, 1989

hoped we had been seeing in China and that we had approved until these terrible recent events.

subtopic: SITUATION OF CHINESE IN CANADA
SITUATION OF CHINESE IN CANADA
speechtext: A third question, Mr. Speaker! The Minister suggested the possibility that the Canadian Government might decide to allow Chinese students who are here now to remain here for an indefinite period, perhaps. Once again, the Minister suggested that the Government had not yet decided, but that the Government is considering this option. My question will be very direct. Can the Minister guarantee that all Chinese students who are here now and are afraid to return to their country can stay here in Canada for an indefinite period?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SITUATION OF CHINESE IN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that is a direct question and the most direct answer I can give is that we do not intend to create or contribute to circumstances that might threaten the safety of Chinese students who are here in Canada. The way to safeguard or guarantee their safety remains to be determined, but this question is already being considered by the Canadian Government.

subtopic: POSITION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
POSITION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons.
Canadians want to know if our system of justice is responding to the so-called budget leak in a proper and ethical way. On April 26 the Government House Leader

June 5, 1989
Oral Questions
asked for extended sitting hours. After that was refused, the Budget was presented to the press.
On April 27 the Attorney General stated to the House that "there had been a theft of budget material".
The Department of Justice has since given advice to the RCMP and further has contacted Ontario Justice officials.
Has the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons acted in the best interests of the administration of justice in Canada, or has he acted in the best interests of his Government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: POSITION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are several questions there, but let me try two. In the first question I think my friend made an error. We tried to extend the hours of the House at about 5.40 on April 26.

subtopic: POSITION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You didn't tell us why.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: POSITION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, that is correct, because your House Leader wasn't here to tell.

subtopic: POSITION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The House Leader was right here. You didn't tell us why.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: POSITION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: POSITION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We subsequently came back and went to the opposition Leaders and tried to go back to the House, but we were refused that. Therefore, we made it public to the media.
On the question as to whether or not I acted in the best interests of the administration of justice, the answer to that is yes, at all times.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR PUBLIC REVIEW OF ACTIONS OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
REQUEST FOR PUBLIC REVIEW OF ACTIONS OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. A journalist and others have been charged in this matter. It is obviously before the courts. However, not all those persons who had access to the material have been charged.
If the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons is confident that he and officials of his Department have acted competently and ethically in this matter, I would ask the Minister of Justice if he believes
it is in the best interests of Canadians to ensure that the integrity of the system of administering justice in this country continue to be respected?
Would he agree that it would be useful to have a thorough and public review of how he has conducted himself as Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons to find out if Canadians can trust the fairness and the integrity of the administration of justice in this country in the light of what we have gone through in the last month or so?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend has indicated, the matter is before the courts. That is the place where justice should be done. I am convinced that it will be done there.

THE BUDGET
THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: TIME OF KNOWLEDGE OF STOCK EXCHANGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. First, I want to welcome him back to the House.
My question is about an apparent contradiction to which the Minister of Justice was unable to respond on Friday. If the Minister goes back to May 14, he will see that the Solicitor General told the House that from the outset the Mutual Life leak was under the investigation of the RCMP. On May 18 he stated that there was no
June 5, 1989

evidence of profiteering because of the Mutual leak or, indeed, the leak to Global Television.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance the following question: How could the Solicitor General say this on May 18 when representatives of the four stock exchanges are now saying that at that stage the RCMP had not notified them about the Mutual leak? In fact, they did not know about it until they heard about it from the news media five days later, after Mr. Masterman issued a press release.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)

subsubtopic: TIME OF KNOWLEDGE OF STOCK EXCHANGES

Mr. Speaker, I clearly informed the House that the RCMP Commissioner had told me then-and I can reiterate again today that the whole question of whether people could have profited from the public disclosure of a budget document was under investigation by the RCMP. As soon as the Commissioner saw fit to inform me that so far, at the time I informed my hon. colleague, there was no evidence or indication that anyone had profited, he informed me and immediately, at the first opportunity, I told the House. I believe it is important to reassure Canadians on that.
And the Commissioner assured me that this investigation was looking into everything. The RCMP is conducting its own investigation on that, on all the possibilities people had to profit. This whole part of the investigation is continuing.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that response is absolutely incredible when the RCMP had not even notified the four stock exchanges. I want to go after the Finance Minister on a separate question.

world, and that the Bank of Canada also intervened because of movement in the Canadian dollar.

subtopic: FAMILY VIOLENCE
FAMILY VIOLENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in June, 1988 the Government of Canada launched a very special initiative called Project Haven to support the development of additional emergency shelters for victims of family violence. Unfortunately not only in my own Province of Alberta but indeed all across Canada family violence is increasing.
Could the Minister of State for Housing tell the House what has been done to date on providing these shelters?

subtopic: FAMILY VIOLENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member is aware, in the summer of last year the Government announced a program to produce 500 emergency spaces or shelter beds for the victims of violence in Canada. There were to be 500 additional beds over and above what was already in place. That project has been proceeding. There has been

June 5, 1989
Oral Questions
a proposal call put out. In fact, some 45 of those 500 places were set aside for the Province of Alberta.
Unfortunately to date there have not been any applications from the City of Calgary, but the Department is expecting to issue a second proposal call and hopefully we will get some proposals from the City of Calgary.
There have been many proposals across the country. All the provinces, with the exception of Ontario and Quebec, are prepared to participate in this program for new spaces. Ontario and Quebec are reluctant to provide additional maintenance funding for these spaces, but we do hope they will participate as well.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR NATIONAL STRATEGY ON AIDS
REQUEST FOR NATIONAL STRATEGY ON AIDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Right Hon. Prime Minister. Yesterday the Prime Minister participated in an international conference on AIDS in Montreal and I believe learned first-hand of the agony and frustration of AIDS victims and those individuals working with them.
I want to ask the Prime Minister, in view of the seriousness of this critical situation: Is he prepared to tell the House when he will call a federal-provincial conference of Health Ministers?
When will he let Canadians, as well as the world, know the date for announcing a national strategy to address the situation of AIDS with its specific objectives, its courses of action, its time date and expenditure program? Can the Prime Minister of Canada inform the House on that most important initiative?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR NATIONAL STRATEGY ON AIDS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REQUEST FOR NATIONAL STRATEGY ON AIDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the policy of the Government of Canada involves the dissemination of information with regard to AIDS, funding research into treatment, making potentially useful and safe drugs available as rapidly as possible, protecting the rights and benefits of all employees in the federal work place, including those with
AIDS or HIV infection, and ensuring that all personal records are protected.
That would be the basis of an improved and strengthened strategy that would be announced by the Minister of Health and Welfare who, as my hon. friends knows, is presently conducting very productive consultations with members of the community interested in this problem.
He has had consultations with leaders of groups who are affected with AIDS, who are living with AIDS, and who have very special and important points of view to bring forward.
Yesterday at the conference I chatted with him and with people involved in this process and all seemed to be reasonably encouraged by the progress that is being made by the Government and other intervenors. I would look forward to that strategy in all of its facets being announced in short order.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DATE OF STRATEGY
REQUEST FOR DATE OF STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the Right Hon. Prime Minister that we in the Opposition want to participate fully in providing meaningful suggestions in order to address this particular situation. In point of fact, I have given that undertaking to the Minister of National Health and Welfare in committee as of last week. The Prime Minister must know that his own Minister of National Health and Welfare has said categorically that there is no national strategy here in Canada to fight AIDS.
In fact, in April, 1988 the Royal Society of Canada provided a blueprint, if you will, for a national strategy.
I want to believe that the Prime Minister is sincere and that he is committed. Would he please give Canadians a specific date as to when he will announce a specific national strategy for the fight against AIDS, with its objectives, courses of action, as well as its expenditure program?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DATE OF STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the Minister of National Health and Welfare, when he returns to the House after his participation at the conference in Montreal, will be able to provide my hon. friend with the specific date that he is
June 5, 1989

seeking. In fact, he has spoken to me and others about the co-operation from the Hon. Member in regard to development of a strategy in this important area.
I have received a letter today from Mr. Braff, President and Chairman of the Canadian AIDS Society, a part of which I share with my hon. friend and the House:
Mr. Prime Minister, the Minister of National Health and Welfare has noted that People Living with AIDS must be treated with respect and compassion. By allowing PLWA's to make their views known to this conference, you have shown this respect.
It is now necessary to continue the process of recognition and involvement of which Mr. Beatty has so eloquently spoken. People Living with AIDS are expecting many and great things as a result of this conference, as well as a result of the initiatives begun by Mr. Beatty. It is my sincere hope that we will be able to continue to work in a spirit of co-operation and mutual respect.
In acknowledging that, I acknowledge as well the support and commitment of my hon. friend speaking I am sure on behalf of all other Members of the House.

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
THE ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: U. S. TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS WASTEBILL-POSITION OF CANADIAN EMBASSY IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. Today is World Environment Day and, as Canadians, we should reflect on the fact that we are fast becoming the garbage dump of the United States in respect of hazardous and dry wastes.
Canadians were shocked to learn during the PCB-laced gasoline affair that approximately 140,000 metric tons of hazardous waste is exported from the United States into Canada every year. Last week, specifically Wednesday, there was a Congressional Bill moved in the U.S. Congress that would have placed severe limitations on the capacity of U.S. companies to send their waste to Canada and to other countries.
Under whose direction has the Canadian Embassy in Washington already begun lobbying against that particular Bill?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: U. S. TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS WASTEBILL-POSITION OF CANADIAN EMBASSY IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the House is aware, Canada-U.S. relations with respect to the transportation of toxic waste are regulated under an agreement and by an Act of Parliament.
These rules set very strict standards, which include obliging companies shipping toxic waste to Canada or to the United States to provide guarantees that there are facilities at the point of destination capable of treating the waste.
As for the question of additional U.S. legislation, Canada hopes that controls on movements of toxic waste will be reinforced as much as possible. I have just checked with my Department, and no one in the Department objects to the passage of new U.S. legislation. However, we will not let Americans set Canadian standards. Those standards will be determined by Parliament and we will do so independently and in accordance with environmental requirements.

subtopic: REQUEST AS TO WHETHER MINISTER HAS GIVEN CERTAIN INSTRUCTIONS
REQUEST AS TO WHETHER MINISTER HAS GIVEN CERTAIN INSTRUCTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we know perfectly well that Canada is becoming a garbage dump, whether we are talking about the Eastern Townships with discarded U.S. refrigerators all over the place or the matter of toxic substances.
More specifically, I would like to ask the Minister whether he himself asked the Canadian Embassy in Washington last Thursday-the same morning he spoke to our Committee, saying he was concerned about the waste issue-did he give the Canadian Embassy instructions to call the U.S. congressman's office to lobby against a U.S. bill that would put limitations on exports of toxic substances to Canada? We know, for instance, that these shipments include used refrigerators that are sometimes stored illegally in Canadian dumps.
During a friendly conversation with the Hon. Member last week, we indicated that we needed her help to make

June 5, 1989
Oral Questions
a technical correction in the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, and if she gives us her support, we will be able to regulate PCBs in solid waste.

EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: VISIBLE MINORITY TARGET IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. We on this side share the concerns of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council that systemic discrimination in the Public Service is continuing since there is a very low percentage of minorities employed in the Public Service and employment equity is not working.
Why has the Government established a target of employing only 3.1 per cent visible minority persons when 6.3 per cent are employed in the general workforce? Is this not a policy of institutionalizing discrimination rather than eliminating it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: VISIBLE MINORITY TARGET IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Treasury Board, together with the various departments and Crown corporations, has been trying for several years to reduce all forms of job discrimation in the Public Service and in Crown corporations.
Objectives have been set to improve the situation by reducing those barriers that prevent people in various groups from having access to employment in the Public Service or access to promotions. So far progress has been made, quite substantial progress, Mr. Speaker, but we want to keep improving our record.
I can assure the Hon. Member that measures are in place, in consultation with the unions, to improve the situation and raise the targets set for the departments and Crown corporations.

subtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET CUTS IN PUBLIC SERVICE
EFFECT OF BUDGET CUTS IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is disgraceful that under 2 per cent of the Public Service employees whom we employ are people of colour. Surely we can do better than that.
Budget cuts will result in even more public servants being laid off and therefore fewer opportunities for visible minority people to get into the Public Service. What will the Government do about this? Will it establish a special fund that will assist in achieving employment equity for target groups?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET CUTS IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, advisory committees have already been established with the President of the Treasury Board for each target group for hiring and promotion in the Public Service. I meet regularly with each of these advisory groups, which make very useful recommendations to us during their work, Mr. Speaker. These groups are generally satisfied with the progress made to date. In the last few years, they, like the Government, wished that progress were faster. With their help and the support of my colleagues, I am sure that I can improve the situation considerably in coming years.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN LEBANESE IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. It concerns the sad situation presently being experienced by those fleeing the violence in Lebanon.
The Minister's officials stated last Tuesday that up to 1,500 Lebanese people visit the Canadian Immigration office in Nicosia every week. Yet after making their way through the fighting to the Island of Cyprus, up to 1,200 people per week, fully 80 per cent, face immediate rejection while the lucky few face months of delay.
Will the Minister undertake to the House and Canadians today to review the immigration criteria with a view to increasing the numbers eligible to come to Canada from this war-torn country and to streamline the already over burdened process?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN LEBANESE IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Member and members of the parliamentary committee for their interest in this issue. It is a very important one.
June 5, 1989

Oral Questions
We have been speeding up the process for family class and sponsored relatives. That system is working. We check into this very carefully on an almost daily basis.
I should say that Canada has done more than any other country in terms of alleviating the situation in Nicosia. We have been taking more proportionately than almost any other country. Of course we continue to watch the situation and will continue to handle it as expeditiously as possible.

subtopic: PRIVATE SPONSORSHIPS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
PRIVATE SPONSORSHIPS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
