speakeroldname: Hon. John H. McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to present for second reading Bill C-17, a Bill to enact some tariff changes emanating from the Budget.

As Hon. Members can see, the Bill that we are tabling today is not voluminous. However, it is quite important for many Canadian companies, industries and taxpayers. The Bill will implement the changes to the Customs Tariff made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on April 27, 1989 as part of his Budget.

This Bill would essentially accomplish four things. The first group of amendments responds to requests from the private sector to take into account the evolving needs of Canadian business and industry. Specifically, duties are being removed on time recorders, vessels for scrapping, checking fixtures imported temporarily for manufacturing automotive production equipment, and here is one that has caused some smiles in the department, pheasant blinders and guards. I could get into that in greater detail if the House is interested. These goods are not available from Canadian producers and the duty removal will assist industries in their competitiveness.
The duty is also being reduced on low alcohol beer while the excise duty and sales tax are being raised to bring the treatment of imported low alcohol beer into line with that of domestic low alcohol beer.
Secondly, the Bill extends the authority to restore pre-harmonized system tariff rates. Members may recall that on January 1, 1988, Canada and most of its major trading partners converted their tariffs to the harmonized system nomenclature, generally known as the HS,
Customs Tariff
an internationally agreed system for describing, classifying and recording imported goods.
The conversion was complex for Canada because the customs tariff had not undergone fundamental revision for decades. A major objective, and I might say successfully achieved, was to ensure the change would not affect revenue. For major trade items, the conversion maintained the same tariff rate. Because of the complexity of the conversion, however, all individual rates could not be guaranteed to remain the same, particularly in the smaller trade areas.
Since a completely neutral rate conversion could not be guaranteed, the new tariff approved by Parliament in December of 1987 included Order in Council authority to allow the Government, during an 18-month period after implementation, to respond to requests to restore rates existing before harmonization. This authority was extended to be used to rectify only those changes injuring Canadian manufacturers or importers.
As a result of a number of representations indicating the business community has not had time to fully assess the impact of the conversion and present requests for restoration of previous tariff rates, this Bill would extend that authority for a further 12 months until June 30, 1990. This extension will enable the Government to continue to respond to those cases where the conversion has had a negative economic impact on Canadian manufacturers or importers.
This Bill provides duty free entry for a range of imports which have previously benefited from duty remission by Order in Council. As Hon. Members know, the Government has the authority to remit customs duties by Order in Council in situations where it concludes such action is necessary, an authority which is used primarily where the application of the tariff laws or regulations are having unintended and undesirable results for specific imports.
In the past, the House has expressed concerns regarding the use of this authority. The Government has taken steps to address these concerns through the tabling of all remission orders valued over $20 million, and a semi-annual report of all remission orders approved by the Governor in Council.
In a further effort to deal with these concerns, the Government is taking a comprehensive look at all remission orders to determine those which can be converted to statutory provisions in the Tariff and there-

June 5, 1989
Customs Tariff
by provide Parliament with the opportunity to consider them. Converting these items into the statute itself will provide the private sector with greater certainty regarding the tariff relief and will relieve the administrative burden which the remission orders place on the importing community.
As a result of this initial review, this Bill would convert to statutory provisions in the tariff remission orders providing duty-free entry for the following products: books and printed matter; satellites and satellite subsystems for testing, and articles for use in the manufacture of satellites and subsystems; materials for use in the manufacture of upper atmospheric research rockets; investigational drugs, placebos, and emergency drugs; machinery and equipment for the manufacture of original equipment automotive parts; chemicals and photomasks for the manufacture of semi-conductors; used foundry patterns, core boxes, et cetera, temporarily imported for the making of metal castings; xenon lighting equipment; lamp bulbs for the production of Christmas lighting sets, and laminated glass dinnerware.
Fourth and last, the Bill also extends the Customs Tariff prohibition of importation of pornographic, hate, treasonable and seditious materials scheduled to expire on December 31, 1989. This Bill would extend the prohibition indefinitely to ensure that such materials continue to be denied entry into Canada.
I have already indicated that although the tariff amendments in this Bill are few in number, they are important to the companies and individuals who will benefit from them.
It has been the policy of successive Governments to respond to the evolving needs of the business community and individuals by introducing appropriate tariff changes in annual Budgets. This Bill continues that process. I would ask that the House give it speedy passage.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join the Minister in speaking briefly to this Bill. Like him, I trust it will receive speedy passage. It is largely a housekeeping Bill. It rectifies previous problems of an administrative nature that have arisen in the implementation of our Customs practices. It recognizes the need to accommodate the requirements of business
to make further adaptations to the new tariff rates and practices.
I join the Minister in recognizing that importers may well require a further 12 months to accommodate themselves to new tariff rates that replace those in effect before the recent harmonization exercise. The harmonization exercise is part of a broader move by Canada toward adapting to more liberal global trading practices. We support the first part of the Bill to enable that process to go forward.
The conversion of certain remission orders to statutory provisions is equally welcome for those goods and products which previously entered the country duty-free. Again, the benefit should be to the business community and to the general prosperity of our countiy.
I noted the Minister's comments about the adjustments to the statutory tariffs in response to domestic concerns. I was glad that earlier in his comments he had referred to the more generous treatment of pheasants and their blinders. I regretted that the Minister in his brief comments did not also draw our attention to the fact that under this legislation mongooses will be allowed into Canada if imported by a zoological institution for display or study purposes. The mongoose, an admirable animal, able to dispatch venomous reptiles with great alacrity, is certain to be a welcome addition to Canada. I say that incidentally, in completely non-partisan terms.
Finally, I want to say a word about the extension indefinitely of the Customs Tariff prohibiting importation of pornographic, hate, treasonable and seditious materials. This is a difficult area. It is not easy for any Government to define or delineate what exactly is pornographic, hate, treasonable and seditious material. However, the Government has moved, I believe, in the right way to extend the present prohibition. There may be problems with it, but I think the move is the right one in the circumstances.
We on this side of the House welcome the introduction of the Bill. We are ready to join in giving it early passage.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to represent my Party in the debate on Bill C-17, an Act to amend the Customs Tariff. I will not
June 5, 1989

spend any time dealing with the harmonization component and the delay by one year aspect of it.
I wish to focus on the change that comes in Clause 25 which states innocuously enough:
Code 9956 in Schedule VII to the said Act is amended by striking out the words following paragraph (d) thereof.
A lay person reading that clause will not know exactly what it is talking about. This is the clause that deals with the change in how material deemed to be pornographic, hateful, seditious and treasonable under the Criminal Code of Canada is dealt with.
Currently, there is an annual obligation that the Government come back to Parliament to request the re-enactment of that particular piece of legislation. It has a lifespan of a year. This deletion change means that the section will permanently be in place and that the Government will no longer have to come back to the House for permission and approval. We question that.
First, we question whether this is the appropriate Act to deal with that aspect, in the sense that it goes beyond the normal rules of bringing materials in for the purposes of tariffs or taxation. This can really become a matter of the policy of Canada in terms of how it is to treat material that has been produced in another country, that is, a visual display, electronic, celluloid or in print which deals with pornographic, hateful, seditious and treasonable materials. It is the type of thing where we need that annual mechanism so that as a result of decisions made by the Government or employees of the Government-all we have do is to look back over the last few months and the Rushdie affair and how, as a result of one letter to one Government Department, a ban was placed on that book coming across the border for a short period of time. It was not a permanent ban. Maybe the use of the word "ban" is inappropriate. It was held up for examination even though it had been coming into the country since September of that year.
Without getting into the specifics of that, the concern we have is that by allowing for this amendment under the guise of changes in tariffs, we are making permanent the existing regime. Instead of having a full debate and an
Customs Tariff
amendment coming forward to deal with how Canada approaches this type of material coming across our border, and that is separate from anything that is produced here, we believe this is the wrong vehicle. We believe this is an inappropriate step in this day and age when we do not have a clear definition in legal terms, because of an act of this House and the inability of the Government to proceed with its Draconian definition, a definition that reflects community standards, not just in one community but across this land. It is a mistake to include this in here. At the very least, we will be arguing in committee for its deletion so that we retain the year to year review.
In any case, because of that provision and because we feel it is that important, we in this Party will be voting against the Bill at second reading. We will not belabour the point. We will not, to my knowledge, add any additional speakers, and we will not call for a recorded division. However, we want to go on record as being opposed to this Bill because of Clause 25.
I appreciate the House taking the time to hear from me. Perhaps in committee we will perhaps be in a position to see, on one hand, the rationale of the Government as to why it is included in this way as opposed to some other more upfront vehicle which clearly says "an Act to Amend the Criminal Code of Canada dealing with pornography", and deal with it accordingly and have it go to the Justice Committee or a legislative committee dealing with justice rather than the route it will follow now.

subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will take a few brief moments to make some comments regarding the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program which this Government unfortunately and prematurely terminated on April 27.
The program was announced with great acclaim just two years ago. At that time it was obvious from the Government's comments that it appreciated the Opposition's co-operation in helping it through the House and that it recognized the necessity for this program.
I wish to take a few moments to read to the Members of this House and to remind them of some of the comments made by Government Members at that time, keeping in mind that these comments were made less than two years ago.
On June 10, 1987 in this House, Mr. Jack Shields, who at that time was the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, spoke with respect to this Bill. He made some very interesting comments. He said:
I am sure all Hon. Members are fully aware of the problems the Canadian oil industry and the western producing regions experienced, particularly last year because of the dramatic drop in international oil prices.
He went on to state:
Hundreds of companies went into receivership and experienced bankruptcies. I believe we all appreciate the human and social costs of the situation.
This was a Bill that received a lot of unanimity, which is unusual in this House. In fact, it received a lot of support throughout this country as the Government consulted not only with the Opposition Parties but with representatives of the oil and gas sector. The Hon. Member at that time indicated:
There is now a mood of optimism in the oil patch that has not
existed for quite some time.
He also indicated again:
The purpose of these consultations and briefings was to ensure that the financial support provided by the Government would do the greatest amount of good while respecting the structure of the industry.
He went on:
- it is estimated that the program will attract up to $1 billion in additional investment in the petroleum industry and will create as many as 20,000 jobs in the oil and gas sector.
This was a Bill and a program that was widely accepted throughout this country, a program that was doing good and held a lot of benefit for western Canada, an area of this country that has, as Members know, suffered economically in the recent past.
The Member concluded his remarks, in part, by stating:
The Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program is a signal to thousands of workers in the oil patch in western Canada and the producing provinces that we recognize the importance of the oil and gas industiy and that we have confidence in its future.
Well, just as they sent a signal in passing the Bill, they have certainly sent another signal by withdrawing it so prematurely, something which is most unsatisfying and upsetting to western Canadians.
There was also a Member, Bob Porter, who was at that time the Member from Medicine Hat who in his remarks stated:
While all energy companies will benefit, it is the hundreds of companies in the service sector and the smaller oil and gas producers that will benefit most from this program. An important feature is the provision to allow oil and gas companies to offer flow-through shares which will attract capital and offer Canadians an opportunity to invest in exploration and development in this country.
He went on to indicate that some 2,000 wells would result in some 4,500 direct jobs and over 12,000 jobs in the service and supply sector. I quote again:
While the immediate benefits are obvious, it is vital that the expertise in manpower and technology that Canada's energy sector has developed over the last four decades is to be maintained.
This is a program that supported western development in the western provinces. It was a program that was developing jobs and securing jobs in western Canada. Now this Government has taken the initiative to pull away that program, to simply tell western Canadians that they are no longer important. "We are a Government that is concerned with other areas of the economy but not with western Canada." That is the message being sent by this Government, a message that is most unfortunate and most upsetting for Members. Western Mem-
June 5, 1989

bers on both sides of the Elouse are extremely disappointed with this procedure. As well, just before the last election, the Member for Calgary Southwest (Mrs. Sparrow) indicated that the incentive program was going to be phased out. I quote from Hansard of September 30, 1988. She stated: "The incentive rate would be dropping off and in fact it would be terminating on December 31, 1989".
The Member indicated at that time that the cap would remain at $10 million per company. She also indicated, and I quote:
The Minister has also recognized the number of jobs in western Canada that are totally dependent on the petroleum industry. This incentive means a further $80 million will be injected into the industry which will keep the rigs working, protecting jobs and helping replace Canada's depleting conventional oil reserves.
That was just prior to the election call. That was $80 million added into the program. That was of the so-called guarantees that this Government had put forth.
In fact, the Government at that time indicated during the election campaign that it had not made promises, it had made commitments. That $80 million was part of some $23 billion or $24 billion or $25 billion of so-called commitments that the Conservative Party said it had made to the Canadian people. After the election, this Government came back and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said that he was sorry, but these were not really commitments but' were actually promises and now those promises cannot be kept, and this $80 million is simply part of that.
One thing you have to give this Government credit for is that they are very good when it comes to using smoke and mirrors. We could all learn some pretty good lessons from them if we wanted to learn those kinds of lessons, except we on this side of the House are not interested in those kinds of lessons.
This Government came forth with many promises which were supposed to be commitments, turned into promises, which suddenly vanished when the dust had
Exploration and Development
cleared from the last election. This is a slap in the face for western Canada.
This is the Party that for years said it was the Party for western Canadians. It said it was the Party that was going to stand up for western Canadians, election after election, year after year. It seems strange now that they are in power and after they have their second majority that suddenly the West is not as important as it used to be. It is not as essential. I remind the Government that people in western Canada are observing this. Certainly these are items they will remember.
Nowhere in these quotes does one get the impression that perhaps the Government did not think the program was useful or needed. In fact, it was quite the opposite. It indicated that it was a good program. We on this side of the House indicated that it was a good program and that we supported the program as did the Liberal Party, the petroleum industry and the gas industry.
There are many small oil and gas companies in this country right now that are suffering. Certainly the major oil companies are. The Essos of the world are in no danger of going under, but this is a program that was designed to assist some of the smaller oil companies and to keep jobs in the service sector that was part of the oil industry. Now the program has been removed.
There were proposals that were put forth to this Government to not stop the program, not take away the money, but change it slightly. Maybe reduce the cap. Instead of a $10 million cap, reduce it somewhat so that the total amount of money is reduced but the smaller oil and gas companies could take advantage of the program.
In fact, as was indicated earlier, some 90 per cent of the oil companies and companies which applied for incentive grants received only 15 per cent of the income. Some of these smaller oil companies can use that money. They can use it at this time in their development. As the Government indicated in the last House, it is important to maintain that sector and to maintain its expertise in Western Canada. If it goes, it is gone for a long time.
It is this type of attitude and callous disregard that this Government is displaying to Canadians that is making Western Canadians and all Canadians very annoyed. It is a situation that Canadians are going to remember. It is

June 5, 1989
Exploration and Development
like the old adage that it is not the Opposition that defeats a Government, it is the Government that defeats the Government. This Government is doing a very good job of it. This is a Government that with its second mandate and the first time there has been a second majority in some 35 years in this country, now is taking a high-handed approach to the Canadian public. It no longer has to listen to the Canadian people. That is the attitude it takes.
I remind this House that there will be another election within the next four years and at that time, these are points that the Canadian public is going to remember.
I would like to also quote from a Globe and Mail article by Drew Fagan, who was published on March 20, 1989.1 quote:
For drilling companies across Alberta this has been the winter of their discontent. Although there are 525 drilling rigs in Western Canada, only 160 actually operated in January. And while in February the number increased to 245, that still represents a 33 per cent decrease over the corresponding month a year earlier. At first glance, the situation seems surprising, as the world price of oil has risen substantially in late last year.
That benchmark price is generally the major factor driving activity levels across the energy industry.
But oil and gas companies planned their drilling levels for the key winter season last fall, when oil prices were cratering. And the rise in prices, even though it has been in place almost three months, has met decided skepticism about whether or not it can last -
To finish the quote:
-other factors have also played a major part in making this winter
one of the slowest in the past decade in terms of drilling activity.
The oil and gas industry is in a period of uncertainty. Certainly they are waiting for the OPEC meetings in June to see what sort of pricing they can count on. They are planning their activities long in advance. For this Government to come along, knowing the situation that exists in the oil patch at this time and to simply cut the feet from under the oil companies is a situation that borders on arrogance. This is a Government that prides itself on consultation? This is a Government that prides itself in listening to the Canadian public?
This is a Government that has its own small network of friends. This is a Government that is concerned only with that small group or that small clique that is calling the shots for this Party. To be quite frank, it is something that we, on this side of the House, find hard to stomach.
Although the Government announced just before the election that an extra $80 million would go into the program, that $80 million was taken away when the program was ended prematurely, just five months after the election.
The Canadian Association of Oil Well Drilling Contractors recently tried to put meaning to the numbers by calculating just what the cancellation of CEDIP would mean to their members.
These figures are from the oil and gas industry which indicate that up to 50 rigs could work with the $80 million stimulus that is now lost, that employment on the rig floor would have been 1,500 people, and at least 3,700 jobs would have been provided. This is a significant number of jobs in Western Canada and a significant number of jobs in a region that is now facing higher and higher unemployment. It is a region of Canada that has been suffering a drought for the last few years. In fact, an indication of the Government's concern for the West is from the Finance Minister, who indicated during the Budget debate that he thought that people in Western Canada were recovering from the drought. The Finance Minister is certainly out of touch with Western Canada when he makes comments like that. It is not surprising that this sort of legislation should come through as well.
Given the continuing need to protect jobs in the industry, especially among the small contractors and service companies, one must ask what the Government plans to do to replace CEDIP. Its premature cancellation has every appearance of short-term political expediency on the part of the Government. We on this side of the House hope that a suitable replacement will soon be put in place.
We suggest to the Minister that, instead of cancelling the program, it is restructured in order that jobs in the oil sector will be secure, the jobs in the service sector that supports the oil industry will remain in place, and
June 5, 1989

that the expertise that is now in western Canada will remain there. Certainly, by lowering the cap from $10 million to $1 million or $2 million would go a long way in saving the Government money, which it claims it wants to do, but it would also go a long way to securing jobs.
A much higher cost is paid when jobs disappear. The Government may save a few million dollars on a program, but the indirect costs are significant. When direct jobs are lost, the spin-off jobs related thereto are also lost. Suddenly, the pressure on social programs and unemployment insurance programs rises at a very time when the Government is cutting the legs offof those programs as well.
We plead with the Government to take some initiative in dealing with average Canadians who are simply trying to pay for their mortgage and maintain some standard of living. However, the Government is ignoring that, has been ignoring it, and continues to ignore it. This Bill is another example of a Government that is out of touch, a Government that has lost complete control of its understanding of the nation's problems. That is why we are opposed to the Bill.

I was delighted to hear the Hon. Member bring up the question of the economic impact of the cancellation of the CEDIP Program in general in western Canada. The Hon. Member mentioned the drought and the spin-off effects of the loss of direct patch jobs. In Alberta, especially in northern Alberta, most of those who ostensibly make their living as farmers rely as well on off-farm income to keep their farm operations going.
It is a simple fact of life in agriculture, especially in Alberta north of Red Deer, the farm income itself is insufficient to fully cover the costs of the operation and allow a sufficient surplus to provide for a life of comfort and some dignity for the farm families still on the land. Therefore, off-farm income in the non-growing season has become a fact of life. As often as not, in Alberta, off-farm income means the oil patch. There are literally thousands and thousands of people who are registered as farmers for income tax purposes who, in the off-farm season, go to work in the oil patch, work on the rigs, doing the servicing, or even slinging the hash at the sites.
Exploration and Development
Those people rely on that employment to allow them to continue to farm.
The effect of the cancellation of the CEDIP for those people, because the number of companies out in the patch drilling and exploring will be reduced because the over-all level of activity will be greatly reduced, will be far fewer of those jobs available for farmers seeking off-farm income. What we are talking about is not only a program the cancellation of which will be very bad news for the oil patch, which it certainly will be, but we are also talking about a program the cancellation of which will be very bad news for the farm community. I am certain that will prove to be the case in northern Alberta.
I was wondering if the Member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Laporte), especially because of the natural gas activity that we know occurs in Saskatchewan, might comment on the degree to which the same might hold true in his province.

speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for his comment. He has precisely hit the nail on the head. Not only in Alberta and Saskatchewan, but in Manitoba, and I am sure in other areas of Canada, but in western Canada we have an infrastructure where each element is important to the survival of the entire infrastructure.
In Saskatchewan the family farm is the basis of our economy. That family farm structure also supports numerous communities. It supports numerous small businesses that rely on the family farm income. In the last few years because of the situation in agriculture in western Canada, many farmers are now seeking off-farm income. Certainly, the oil patch in Alberta and the oil and gas-related jobs in Saskatchewan have provided much needed extra income for the people of that region.
The federal Government and the Government of Saskatchewan have been talking about the need for diversification. This program was helping to maintain some diversification. By cutting that program, and the loss of jobs that will result from the loss of that program will have an effect directly on agriculture and the many small farmers who are trying to survive, many family farms will lose the extra income.
As my hon. friend mentioned, there are many people who work on the farms during the summer months and spend other months on the oil rigs or in the gas fields. This is one more area that will be lost to them, one more area from which they will not have the opportunity to derive extra income. It is extremely important in light of

June 5, 1989
Exploration and Development
the fact of the Government's attitude toward agriculture.
In 1985 the then Minister of Agriculture indicated that the Government would be putting forward a permanent drought program. It never came. The Government has been promising some answers for agriculture which have not come forward. Now we know that in the fall the Government will be introducing programs with respect to agriculture, but that program will be dealing with the bottom line. The whole social infrastructure is in danger of collapsing as the Crow benefit is changed, rail lines are removed, and as family farms become larger. Those jobs that are now being lost are very important to the people in that region. If the Government would think of the social and economic benefits that will result from that program as opposed to always considering the bottom line, the Government would reconsider that legislation if it had a mind-set to take that approach and view western Canada from that philosophical point of view.

subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to join in the debate this afternoon on the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program. This program has been veiy beneficial since 1987 when it was first established to provide incentives to the oil and gas exploration industry.
In 1986 the price of oil dropped precipitously from $28 or $29 U.S. a barrel to as low as $10 a barrel. The whole industry collapsed during the latter half of 1986. By 1987 this incentive program was brought into being to assist the industry, especially the small producers and it has been beneficial in that regard. It could have been better if the cap had been lower as our caucus has been recommending in that the benefits would have flown to the small producers.
We have to realize that something very dramatic in terms of concentration of the industry has taken place since 1984. At that time we had the National Energy Program in place which was an incentive program to bring greater participation by Canadian oil and gas industry into the industry and to exploit our oil and gas reserves. With the Government's removal of all those incentives, with the collapse of prices in 1986, what we
have seen is cash-strapped Canadian companies being bought up by the multinationals and a massive concentration taking place. This incentive program, especially if it had been restricted to $1 million for the smaller companies as the multinationals do not need it on the same basis, could have continued the development of small and medium-sized Canadian companies to prove up reserves and bring them on stream.
It is incredible that this program is being dropped at a time when the Budget seems to indicate that all the megaprojects are going forward. We are talking about a relatively small amount of money here, $350 million, and we are told that if this program were limited to a cap of only $1 million per producer, the cost would be dramatically reduced to only $80 million per year. It would meet 90 per cent of those who wanted to use the program. I find it amazing that for that relatively small amount of money in terms of jobs created and economic activity developed that the megaprojects, where we are talking about $4 billion or $5 billion for Hibernia and the upgraders and the tar sands projects, are apparently on stream. Whether that will actually happen or not is hard to say.
We are killing off this relatively small incentive program in the western sedimentary basin where we have small jobbers and exploration and development companies which could easily use it. They have their people and equipment in place. It is being killed off at a time when all the megaprojects are still on stream, or have not been cancelled formally.
I recently read a report by the Ontario Corn Producers saying that it is interesting that while the megaprojects are still on stream, for programs designed to encourage the development of ethanol plants using distress farm products or damage for farm commodities, there is no incentive there. In fact, a disincentive is there because of the cancellation of a number of farm programs such as the Advanced Payments Program which is beneficial to corn producers and to western agricultural producers. We seem to be favouring massive megaprojects over the small ones. I don't believe anyone is opposed to the megaprojects. They do bring on stream large reserves but at the same time small incentive programs like the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program are being wiped out.
June 5, 1989

You, Mr. Speaker, represent an Edmonton riding. We know how conscious you are of the some 6,100 jobs which have been lost because of the drop of 32 per cent in the first quarter of this year. We are told that only 70 per cent of the rigs in Alberta are operating today. We are told that if the DECET program is wiped out that another 3,700 jobs will be lost. This is at a time when agriculture generally has suffered in the West with loss due to drought last year and loss in the previous two years due to the international grain wars. All in all we are putting a heavy load on western Canadians at this time.
I know from your perspective, Mr. Speaker, that you are very concerned about this and do not want to see any action taken which would be harmful to the industry. We have to put this into the perspective of the cut-back in the federal-provincial agreements, the ERDA agreements because this has been an incentive agreement by the federal Government to the oil and gas industry. However, the provinces do have similar incentive programs where a portion of the royalties are foregone for a period of a few months to try to bring on stream greater oil and gas exploration and development. We have to be very conscious of the fact that we are selling massive amounts of oil and exporting it into the U.S. right now. We are making commitments well beyond the 25 year period in natural gas. Therefore there is a need to bring on greater and greater supplies and prove up greater reserves in the western sedimentary basin.
Rather than cancelling the program, we are suggesting to the Government that it should be lowering the limit from $10 million to $1 million. This would satisfy some 90 per cent of the applicants. It would save the Government some 85 per cent of the cost of the program. We recognize that this kind of incentive program and cash flow needs are not that great for the large multinational corporations. It is mainly for small exploration and development companies. We think for that reason it should be continued.
For instance, it has been estimated that under the CEDIP program, it would cost the Government some $80 million a year if they use the new proposed criteria which we are putting forward. The industry would generate some $450 million worth of activity and of course develop more gas and oil reserves. At the same
Exploration and Development
time it would create thousands of jobs just by maintaining this program but at a lower level.
The Government should think twice about this. In its own way, it is a regional development program for portions of Saskatchewan and Alberta. Usually in regional development programs, you need to have a system or a mechanism that relates to the raw natural resources of the area. Clearly this is the resource. When the Premier of Alberta spoke dramatically and in very harsh terms about this to the government in 1987, the government responded by bringing in the program, it was one that was useful.
At that time the federal Government had refused to provide a loan of several hundred million dollars or a loan guarantee to the tar sands operations at Fort McMurray for expansion and development. The Alberta Government did it on its own. Then this program came in and the Premier spoke strongly to see it established. The Government responded. The Government should look twice at this proposal before cancelling it completely. We are talking about saving unemployment insurance, and welfare costs. We are talking about people having jobs and the dignity that a job provides. We are not sure how much more anguish there will be in the farm sector this year because of the uncertainty about crops and so on.
The Government should reconsider this proposal when it goes to committee. It could reduce the cap from $10 million to $1 million and specify it for small and medium size oil and gas exploration companies. I think it will find that CEDIP can continue to play a useful role in creating jobs and proving up oil and gas reserves in the western sedimentary basin.

Mr. Speaker, question or comment. I was interested in a number of the Hon. Member's remarks with regard to the impact of the Bill and the Government's ideological bent in the oil patch.
How would the Member respond to the contention that the Government is not one that is reluctant to interfere in the industry, at least nowhere near as reluctant as it claims from time to time, but rather one with a consistent history of interference in the marketplace in energy, and certainly one with gigantic plans for

June 5, 1989
Exploration and Development
further interference in that marketplace? I am thinking in particular of the proposed programs for funding of the various megaprojects.
EIow would he respond to the contention that this is in fact a Government not shy of interference, not in reality opposed to interference but one that enjoys a predilection toward interference on behalf of a wealthy and powerful few in the industiy while maintaining its much more rigorous ideological commitment to non-interference in that realm of the smaller independent Canadian companies that constitute the huge majority of companies in the patch but do not control anywhere near the assets of the foreign majors? Could the Member respond to that?

subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member's inquiry. I believe he has perceived the situation very much as it is. A year ago when we were facing the prospect of a general election, the Government made one announcement after another. Hibernia was obviously a massive intervention, with $1 billion or $2 billion, if one counts both the grants and the loan guarantees that were proposed. The tar sands and the upgrader projects are examples of a massive involvement by the Government.
I am surprised that this very small program, CEDIP, would even be noticed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), considering the several billions of dollars under these massive programs which, as far as we know, are still on the table.
As the Hon. Member said, it seems that when we talk about massive programs there are billions of dollars to intervene to assist the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) in his riding, or to assist in the development of the tar sands plant in Fort McMurray, or to assist the Minister for International Trade (Mr Crosbie) to get re-elected in Newfoundland. However, when it comes to levels of funding of $80 million or $100 million, it becomes a question of market economy.
We have already seen a massive concentration of oil and gas reserves in the western sedimentary basin during the last four years. Before the crash in oil prices in 1986, these reserves were much more widely held by small Canadian companies, which was the purpose of the whole incentive arrangement under the National Energy Program. When the prices collapsed from $28 to $10 during 1986, these companies did not have the resources to continue for long and there was a massive buy-up. Now there is a concentration of those reserves into the names of the multinationals.
When one considers the purchase of Gulf Minerals by Petro-Canada, there certainly was no hesitation by the Government to intervene in the marketplace and buy up one of the largest Canadian oil and gas companies owned by Petro-Canada. What will happen with Petro-Canada is anyone's guess. I think the Member is generally correct that it is not as much an ideological issue as it is the size of the project. The decision of whether or not to intervene in the marketplace is whether the Government is trying to deal with a specific political situation or give specific advantage to a multinational. That seems to be the general direction the Government has taken.

subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate at second reading of Bill C-19, an Act to amend the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program Act. When I read my briefing notes and listened to Hon. Members, I could not help but think back to another debate in a previous Parliament about the ramifications of a government's step to eliminate flow-through shares, and the hue and cry that was created throughout northern Ontario in particular because of the impact of that taxation change and the very quick decline of investment in mineral resource exploration in my part of the world. I wonder whether the Government will have the same problems as a result of its decision about CEDIP.
This program was introduced, effective April 1, 1987, to help the oil and gas industry overcome the impact of the decline in oil and gas prices on employment and investment, particularly in western Canada, caused in large part by the decision of the Government to deregulate energy pricing and marketing. In other words, it decided to take from the industry the system of stability that was in place within Canada so that producers would know their rate of return and purchasers would know the cost. This gave people the opportunity to have a stable lifestyle in the same way as we argue in the House for marketing boards for agricultural products to give some protection to both producers and consumers.
June 5, 1989

The price of oil at the time was $18.45 a barrel. It dropped to about $13 a barrel and rose again to $20. The program initially provided a cash incentive of 33.3 per cent on eligible exploration and development expenses incurred in Canada, up to a maximum grant of $3.3 million on $10 million in expenses per company.
To help debt-ridden small producers, the package allows companies that do not pay taxes to issue flowthrough shares and pass tax credit money through to investors to help raise money. The program was expected to provide $350 million in assistance annually to the oil and gas industry.
A total of $1.25 billion was placed into the program from 1987 through to 1990. When the Bill was dealt with by this Elouse back on June 10, 1987, all three Parties not only supported it but gave it quick passage.
There were concerns raised at the time that the Government took much too long to bring the legislation in. In some ways it was after the barn door was open and the horses had not only bolted but were well past the next pasture. Also we pointed out that it was in apparent conflict with the Government's free enterprise philosophy. This is something, Mr. Speaker, that I know you are very familiar with and would be concerned about if you thought that the Government of which you were elected as a Member was doing something different than its philosophy seemed to suggest.
In any case, that is how it was perceived and how it in fact occurred.
At that time during the debate, my colleague, who is now the Member for Port Moody-Coquitlam (Mr. Waddell) stated: "I should like to say that I am cautiously optimistic that the Bill will work. It favours smaller companies. It focuses on grants rather than on tax incentives, allowing some of the smaller companies which do not pay taxes to benefit. It acknowledges the plight of small oil companies as a national issue. It is a national problem about which we all must talk."
It is still short term. The long-term solution is to diversify the western economy. This is no mean feat but is something that must be done away from total dependence upon oil, but oil being the major part of it.
Exploration and Development
That is a very important component. As someone who comes from Ontario, but that part of Ontario which is not part of Metropolitan Toronto or the Golden Horseshoe, distance is a major factor, as it is in western Canada. Yes, we have our resources. Ours are of the mineral variety as opposed to the oil and gas variety in western Canada, and the agricultural resources. We recognize the inherent reality in the way the country is structured. The resources tend to gravitate toward the metropolitan areas, where there is a much larger consumer demand, so that when you add the value you can sell it more readily at a lower transportation cost. The real challenge that Canada faces is how do we develop our structures and our systems to encourage the development of secondary and tertiary industries in Alberta, in Saskatchewan, in Manitoba and in northern Ontario, so that we can use the resources closer to where we live and work so that we, too, can share in that benefit.
On the energy side I think there is a much greater need to provide mechanisms to allow that to happen. Unfortunately, this Government has seen fit to eliminate one of those elements that in effect encouraged processing in the Province of Alberta, or processing in the Province of Saskatchewan. That is a regret. It just makes even more distant the day on which Alberta residents can see additional jobs created. Not just the drilling and the direct employment opportunities related to exploration and drilling, but additional processing, additional manufacturing that we think they should have without having to get into the battle of stealing jobs from one part of the country to the other. Create the wealth in western Canada, where there is wealth in terms of resources, and use that for the benefit of the people there.
Back in 1986, in terms of western Canadian rig activity, utilization was at a decade-low. Just before CEDIP was introduced, only 35 per cent of available rigs were drilling. One year later, utilization was only 37 per cent, rising to 41 per cent in 1988. This is still well under half of the rigs being utilized for exploration.
I gather that spring is traditionally a time of low utilization but this year's spring is even worse than expected. The President of the Canadian Association of Oil Well Drilling Contractors, Mr. Brian Krausert, recently stated in the Edmonton Journal: "We've just

June 5. 1989
Exploration and Development
come through the worst period in our recorded history. The spring has been truly ugly."
At the end of May, only 84 rigs were drilling in western Canada, a 60 per cent drop from the same period last year. This is a plunge the Association estimates has cost
17,000	direct and indirect jobs in the oil patch. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that if 17,000 jobs were eliminated in a Hamilton or a London or in Ottawa in the Province of Ontario over two or three months, it would not go unnoticed. In fact, to use the vernacular, there would be hell to pay. People would be clamouring in this House and in the Ontario Legislature for some action. Instead, because they are resource-based jobs, they are spread throughout and not any one particular community is hit by them. They are just bits and pieces around the provinces. It is an invisible kind of unemployment problem, Mr. Speaker, and because it is invisible it does not obtain the attention that is appropriate for the degree of impact, nor does it achieve or obtain the political sensitivity that I think is important for us to recognize. It is a very important situation.
Even before the projected ending of CEDIP, figures for the summer of 1989 were grim. CAODC forecast that only 40 per cent of rigs in western Canada would be drilling in the first quarter of 1989, only 29 per cent or 153 rigs in the second quarter, 28 per cent in the third, and 48 per cent in the fourth. That was before the Budget and before the end of CEDIP.
The managing director of CAODC, Don Herring, stated that after CEDIP even these low estimates will have to be revised. "Now we'll have to revise that figure downward." Many companies are apparently on the brink of bankruptcy. Many oil and gas producers are holding back until June's OPEC meeting on quotas and prices.
The early cancellation of CEDIP will mean less activity and fewer jobs. Early cancellation represents $80 million. CAODC estimates that the maximum impact of this is as follows: Activity for up to 50 rigs only, representing employment for up to 1,500 people on the rig floor and 3,700 jobs at the least.
The Small Explorers and Producers Association of Canada wrote to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to express its concerns about the Budget and the early
elimination of CEDIP. In its letter of May 9, the chairman stated: "The abrupt termination of the CEDIP Program by the Government, which will be borne solely by the independent Canadian junior oil company, and the introduction of new taxes on the industry have eliminated at least $250 million in planned capital investment in the conventional oil and gas industry. It puts in jeopardy thousands of jobs in small exploration and producing companies as well as the service sectors that conduct about one-third of the activity in the Western Canadian sedimentary basin. It is unfair."
Not only are oil patch workers and associations distressed at the early elimination of CEDIP, they are also annoyed by the way the Government eliminated it. The program was originally announced amidst much hoop-la by the then Minister of Energy back in 1987. He announced the program would start on April 1, 1987, at the rate of 33-1/3 per cent. On October 1, 1988, the rate would drop to 16-2/3 per cent. The program was scheduled to end on December 31, 1989, about six or seven months from now.
Then came the run-up to the federal election. The Conservatives made announcements relating to Hibernia, Lloydminster, OSLO and the Vancouver Island pipeline. Small producers and Alberta MPs joined together to pressure the Government to modify the program which was about to decline in value.
On September 30, 1988, the Government announced that the program would be phased down less rapidly than originally announced. I repeat, less rapidly. On October 1, 1988, the rate would drop to 25 per cent rather than 16-2/3 per cent. The drop from 25 per cent to 16-2/3 per cent would be delayed until July 1, 1989, and the program would end as planned on December 31, 1989.
This announcement made it possible for the Minister to claim, "This delayed phase-down will inject a further $80 million into the oil and gas industry. This revision will lead to the drilling of an estimated 300 additional wells and will maintain 1,600 oil-patch jobs". However, this extra $80 million was taken away entirely when the Budget was announced. Give one day, just before the election, and take away the next, when safely elected, seems to be the Tory motto.
June 5, 1989

This blatant manipulation was not well received in the oil patch. The Chairman of the Small Explorers and Producers Association of Canada in a letter to the Minister of Finance dated May 9, 1989 stated:
Based on the government's November election platform, we were shocked by the manner in which CEDIP was handled. Although the Minister of Energy told the industry in Calgary on April 5, 1989 that CEDIP would end (on December 31, 1989) as planned, this budget terminated the program three weeks later in spite of a negotiated clause in the CEDIP Act that was to provide six months notice of such a change. This action is hardly the encouragement needed to create more investment in Western Canada.
It is no wonder that the people of Alberta are beginning to wake up. That is why we now have for the first time a New Democratic Party Member from the Province of Alberta sitting in this House. The people of Alberta are beginning to recognize that they cannot trust the Conservatives, that the Conservatives say one thing before an election and do the exact opposite after. We need Members, such as our New Democratic Party Member, to ensure that the people of Alberta know what is really happening in the House of Commons and what their Government is doing for them and to them.
There are a number of other items that I want to talk about. If the Government really felt that cuts had to be made, even after announcing an extra $80 million just before the election, then the alternative approach-restricting the cap on the program, that is, the maximum amount of grant any one company could receive, rather than the proportion of expenses that could be claimed back-deserves serious attention. This would have given even greater relative support to the smallest companies. However, there is no evidence that this option was even considered by the Government. I am sure that my colleague in committee will question the Government as to whether in fact it did pursue that option as well as others before it arrived at the six-month early termination of the program.
There is really no substitute for a made-in-Canada floor price for oil to provide real stability for the oil patch in these downturns, and to provide employment stability for thousands of workers in the West. My constituents are the consumers of these products. They recognize that on the one hand there is a need for fairness in terms of the price they have to pay, whether it be at the pump or in their homes, no matter whether it is oil or gas. They also recognize on the other hand that the people of the producing provinces, both the workers and the compan-
Exploration and Development
ies, need a decent standard of living. They realize that they need to be assured of stable employment and therefore stable operation of the companies involved.
While I have gone to bat for my constituents before the Ontario Energy Board to make sure that whatever savings achieved by companies such as ICG Utilities were in fact passed on to the consumers and not just kept as additional profits for yet another mega-company, I recognize that there is a need for a stable situation in energy pricing in Canada. While eastern consumers can get energy at a reasonable level, it should not be at the expense of the economy of the prairie provinces. It should not be done at the expense of people who live and work in the prairie provinces. I support the approach that talks about a need for a made-in-Canada floor price for oil so that there will be some stability out there and so that the price cannot go below a certain amount. In that way those people may maintain their livelihood, as can the people in northern Ontario.
I would like to get the Government of Canada and the Province of Ontario to stop bashing my constituents and the rest of the people around northern Ontario by upping our taxes for fuel that we have to choose. We do not have the alternatives, such as urban transit, as there is in Toronto and other major cities. Then we would be able to take the pressure away from the consumers and allay the feeling that they are being gouged by all and sundry.
I mentioned earlier the intervention aspect and that this is a so-called free-market Government. I want to remind the Government and the people of Canada that in spite of the Government's rhetoric it does believe in interfering in the marketplace. It announced CEDIP in the first place. It announced its participation in Hibernia, Lloydminster and the Vancouver Island pipeline. Negotiations are still under way on some of these projects.
Mr. Speaker, do not let anyone say that the Government has an entirely market-oriented approach. No Government should have that approach. There is a role for Governments to play in ensuring stability so that, where possible, economic growth and wealth is not concentrated in only one part of the country. We have talked a fair bit about western Canada. There is no question that eastern Canada, the Atlantic region, has not had its fair share of economic growth. It is our role as parliamentarians to find ways in which we can ensure

Exploration and Development
that those things happen. That is why it is important that we debate legislation such as this to its fullest.
I look forward to seeing what the committee has to say about this particular Bill. Hopefully, there will be some changes in it, where appropriate, which will make it better for the people of western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in addressing Bill C-19, an Act to amend the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program Act, I want to start by concurring that my own experience matches in many ways those shared by my predecessor in this debate, the Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus). We are not a constituency with a component in the oil and gas exploration industry, but many of us within the West Kootenay region have been for over 100 years well versed in the difficulties faced by the mining industry. Considering the obvious comparison of what the changes to the whole flowthrough share mechanism has been over the last couple of years and what is envisioned by the legislation before us, we are only too aware of the type of adverse impact the termination of this program may have on an industry that in many ways is similar to the mining industry that we are familiar with in my area.
I want to begin by making a few brief comments regarding the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program which this Government terminated very early on April 21'. The program was announced with great acclaim two years ago. At that time, it seemed obvious from the Government's comments that it appreciated the Opposition's co-operation in helping the program through the House and that it recgonized the necessity for such a program. I want to read a few comments from some of the government Members at that time, keeping in mind that these remarks were made only one or two years ago.
I want to quote the then Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources when he said on June 10, 1987, referring to the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program:
This legislation will make possible the implementation of the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentives Program which my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse), announced on March 25 in Edmonton. I am sure all Hon. Members are fully aware of the problems the Canadian oil industry and the western producing regions experienced, particularly last year because of the dramatic drop in international oil prices. Just as an example of this, exploration and development spending in the western sedimentary basin plunged by more than 50 per cent and thousands of jobs were lost. Hundreds of companies went into receivership and experienced bankruptcies. I believe we all appreciate the human and social costs of the situation.
I am sure all Hon. Members will agree on the soundness of the measures provided by the Bill and the urgent need to support
Exploration and Development
recovery in this key sector of the economy. Just as an aside, let me say that, since the announcement of this program, there have been clear signs that exploration and development activities and plans as reported by the service sector in the oil industry have increased considerably. There is now a mood of optimism in the oil patch that has not existed for quite some time.
As an aside, I wonder, if that optimism was felt so strongly then, what the feelings are now in that same sector as a result of the Government's early termination of this program?
Going back to the remarks:
The Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program is as relevant to the imperatives of social justice as it is to those of economic development. I would like to emphasize that the provisions of the Bill are the outcome of lengthy discussions and consultations with representatives of the oil and gas sector and provincial Governments as well as with my Liberal friend from Cape Breton-The Sydneys and my NDP friend from Vancouver- Kingsway.
The purpose of these consultations and briefings was to ensure that the financial support provided by the Government would do the greatest amount of good while respecting the structure of the industry-it is estimated that the program will attract up to $1 billion in additional investment in the petroleum industry and will create as many as 20,000 jobs in the oil and gas sector.
He ended by saying:
The Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program is a signal to thousands of workers in the oil patch in western Canada and the producing provinces that we recognize the importance of the oil and gas industry and that we have confidence in its future.
If the implementation of that program was a signal to thousands of workers and to the industry that this Parliament and Government recognized the importance of the oil and gas industry and that we had confidence in that industry's future, then what is the signal given by this early termination of a program that was so welcomed by the industry and so overwhelmingly supported by all Members in the House of Commons?
Next, I want to quote the Member for Medicine Hat in 1987. The Member for Medicine Hat at that time is recorded on page 4589 of Hansard, March 26, 1987. He said:
Yesterday in Edmonton the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) announced the Canadian Exploration and Development Program. While all energy companies will benefit, it is the hundreds of companies in the service sector and the smaller oil and gas producers that will benefit most from this program. An important feature is the provision to allow oil and gas companies to offer flow-through shares which will attract capital and offer

June 5. 1989
Exploration and Development
Canadians an opportunity to invest in exploration and development in this country.
The drilling of 2,000 wells will result in 4,500 direct jobs and over 12,000 jobs in the service and supply sectors. While the immediate benefits are obvious, it is vital that the expertise in manpower and technology that Canada's energy sector has developed over the past four decades be maintained. This announcement should not be considered a short-term solution but an investment in the future security of energy resources for the benefit of all Canadians.
I want to go back to the last few words, that this announcement, that is, the establishment of the program, should not be considered a short-term solution but a long-term investment in the future security of that industry. Here we have the Government, after bravely announcing that this was not a short-term solution, coming in less than two years later and terminating, against the advice of many people in the industry, and closing it down. That is an example of short-term expediency, not long-term planning and certainly not the kind of consultation with an important area of the private sector in western Canada, that we should expect from the Government if it wants to appear to be doing the proper job for the long-term security of this industry and devout working Canadians.
I want to quote one additional source from Hansard. In a statement on page 19810 of September 30, 1988 of Hansard the then Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mrs. Sparrow) stated:
- the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) announced today an adjustment in the phase-down of the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program. The incentive rate from October 1, 1988. to June 30, 1989, will drop from 33-1/3 per cent to 25 per cent. As of July 1,1989, until December 31,1989, the rate will be 16-2/3 per cent. The cap remains at $10 million per company or related companies.
The Minister has also recognized the number of jobs in western Canada that are totally dependent on the petroleum industry. This incentive means a further $80 million will be injected into the industry, which will keep the rigs working, protecting jobs and helping to replace Canada's depleting conventional oil reserves.
Nowhere in these quotes from government Members does one get the impression that perhaps the Government does not think the program is useful, or that the program was needed or is needed today. There are many indications that the program is needed just as much today as it was two years ago.
I quote from The Globe and Mail article by Drew Fagan published on March 20, 1989 as follows:
For drilling companies across Alberta, this has been the winter of their discontent.
Although there are 525 drilling rigs in western Canada, only 160 were actually operating in January. And while in February the number increased to 245, that still represents a 33 per cent decrease over the corresponding month a year earlier.
At first glance, this situation seems surprising, as the world price of oil has risen substantially since late last year. That benchmark price is generally the major factor driving activity levels across the energy industry.
But oil and gas companies planned their drilling levels for the key winter season last fall, when oil prices were cratering. And the rise in prices, even though it has been in place almost three months, has met decided skepticism about whether or not it can last-
- other factors have also played a major part in making this winter one of the slowest in the past decade in terms of drilling activity.
Although the Government announced just before the election that an extra $80 million would go into the program, that $80 million was taken away when the program was ended prematurely just five months after that election. This is the Government that said it was in favour of long-term planning, not short-term giveaways.
The Canadian Association of Oilwell Drilling Contractors recently tried to put meaning to these numbers by calculating just what the cancellation of the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program mean to their members. As an addendum to their press release on the cancellation of the CEDIP, the association stated:
In terms of employment and activity the cancellation of CEDIP would have the following maximum impact:
(1)	up to 50 rigs could work with the $80 million stimulus that is now lost.
(2)	employment on the rig floor would have been 1,500 people and at the least. 3,700 jobs would have been provided.
This was was said with the following assumptions:
(1)	money would have been spread evenly over the year. This means to earn $80 million, operators would have spent $450 million.
(2)	average central Alberta well is $500,000, which means 900 wells could have been drilled.
(3)	average central Alberta well takes ten drilling days, or 9,000 work days are lost.
June 5, 1989

(4)	there are 240 days left in the year, and a rig could work 80 per cent of the time, or 190 days.
(5)	using 9,000 days and 190 rig days/rig = 50 rigs running full time.
That is a major loss.
Given the continuing need to protect jobs in the industry, especially among the small contractors and service companies, one must ask just what this Government plans to do to replace CEDIP. Its premature cancellation has every appearance of short-term political expediency on the part of this Government. We in the New Democratic Party hope that a suitable replacement will soon be put in its place.
There is an old saying that if it ain't broke, don't fix it. The saying that this Government perhaps should listen to is if it is working, don't break it. That appears to be what is happening here.
I mentioned earlier that this was a Government that, almost as an article of faith, says that it is a business-like Government and a Government that consults with industry, business and those on the ground floor of our economy. It is a Government that administers on a long-term basis, not simply for the short-term and with grab-bag expediencies.
This action by the Government in the cancellation of this program, in spite of all of their words just a few short months ago, puts the lie to those assumptions. This is not a business-like Government. This is obviously not a Government that consults with major companies, workers or with communities who are engaged in large areas of the private sector, at least not in Western Canada. They have forgotten their roots on the other side of the House. They have forgotten their roots with not only level-headed people in the business community, but they have forgotten their roots in that section of the country that gave them some of their strongest political support over the last one or two decades.

Exploration and Development
and other historic mining exploration and development areas across the country learned that. Because of the shenanigans, over flow-through shares and the up-again, down-again changes to those programs, people have found out that they cannot rely on the word of this Government when they say they are going to do something for the long term and will introduce a program that lets industry and investors know what the ground rules are for a significant period of time so that they can make the necessary adjustments to gain the maximum amount of revenue and support to those communities and to those industries.
One cannot operate a country this way. For those on the other side who say things are a lot better in the mining and oil industry than they were in the bad old days-and we know which bad old days they are referring to when they use those phrases-I would like them to realize that in good measure because of the changes to the flow-through shares mechanism regarding exploration and drilling in the mining industry that in my own constituency of Kootenay West-Revelstoke, which historically is one of the major areas in Western Canada when it comes to mining exploration and development, unemployment levels have gone up from some 10 per cent, 11 per cent or 12 per cent back up to 16 per cent and 17 per cent. In some cases, it is as high as 19 percent. We are again approaching exactly those same depths of unemployment as we had during the worst years of the resource debt in the early 1980s.
This is the Government that pledged to begin to change that in the resource areas of this country and particularly in the resource areas of Western Canada. They ignore those commitments at their peril. I ask them to reconsider both this legislation and their whole attitude.
One of those changes that they might also consider, and it is relevant to this particular area of discussion, is their decision to place both the mineral development agreements and the forest resource development agreements under the Western Diversification Fund.
Again, that is a short-term fund for particular companies and particular industries. It does not lead to the kind of long-term planning that is necessary both in the forest industry and the mining industry if we are to see stable and planned growth take place whether publicly or privately within those important sectors.

The resource communities of this country need a long-term commitment. They need long-term commitments from industry, from the labour force. Most importantly, to set the ground rules, they need to have some long-term planning and commitments from the Government that when a program is in place for a specific period that it should at least last for that long so that we all know the ground rules and begin to work to change our resource communities and our resource industries from the boom-and-bust cycle into long-term, stable growth so that we and succeeding generations can count on an increasing share of the wealth that this country can produce.
