subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak during this important debate tonight, and I want to thank you for allowing this emergency debate.
The violence of the events in China has shocked and saddened us all, and I am pleased that the motion presented by the Secretary of State for External Affairs received the unanimous support of the House.

The Hon. Member for LaSalle-Emard (Mr. Martin), who spoke earlier said that this was one of the evenings on which he was particularly proud to be a Member of Parliament. It is always a high point in the life of Parliament when we are able to come together as one mind and express on behalf of Canadians a particular view. Of course tonight what we have expressed, both in

June 5, 1989
the granting of this emergency debate and in the debate itself, and particularly in the unanimous resolution adopted by the Elouse, is the unanimous outrage that Canadians feel about the events in China.
I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) put it well, though, when he said that it should be clear to all who may be listening, both here in Canada and abroad, that what we are talking about here is an unequivocal condemnation of the actions of a particular Government in a particular time and place in the history of China. We are not talking about the Chinese people themselves. We begin this debate with a tremendous respect for the history of China as a civilization and for the Chinese people themselves.
We begin, I dare say, with a respect for the Chinese Revolution, something which many people have studied over the years and have recognized as not only a great struggle, but a struggle that has resulted in many achievements for the Chinese people. Many people have looked with awe at the ability of a country with so large a population to feed and provide for itself in a way that has been the envy of many other countries of the world. That is why what has happened this last weekend is a political as well as a human tragedy, that a revolution which begins with the long march and with so much struggle and passion for social justice should come to a point where the People's Liberation Army is firing on the people themselves.
I think a great many Canadians are saddened not only by the loss of life but by the tremendous and painful irony that that must be for all who have watched the struggle for justice in China and which has its antecedence in the Revolution and in the overthrow of the Nationalist Chinese regime, a regime noted for its brutality.
I also want to say that I wish the House had more of these kinds of opportunities to express our unanimous condemnation of gross violations of human rights. As someone else said earlier, we know that tragedies of this proportion sometimes happen without the world taking any notice at all, or taking very little notice. I am reminded of the genocide which has happened against
the people of East Timor, or the chemical warfare which the Iraquis used on their own people in Kurdistan, or the actions of the Chinese Government not so long ago in Tibet. The list goes on and on of events which do not receive the kind of attention that this event has.
We are glad that this event has received that kind of attention, but I think we also have a responsibility to say that there are many more occasions on which the House of Commons could unite to condemn human rights violations. Perhaps we should see this as a precedent setting move for further parliamentary action in the future, should such occasions arise. We, of course, hope they do not.
I would like to go over some of the things that have been suggested in terms of a Canadian response, things which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has covered. I would like to just speak for the record as to how we, in the New Democratic Party, view some of the areas which we have to concern ourselves with as a result of the tragic events in Beijing.
It has been suggested that Canada-and my Leader raised this in the Question Period earlier today-call for a debate in the Security Council. It was also suggested earlier that a self-understanding of the United Nations may well prevent the kind of full debate that one would like to see in the United Nations.
I am told that the Security Council's mandate has to do with conflicts between nations rather than within nations. If that is the case, as I believe it is, in many respects that is a very serious limitation. It is a limitation reflected in the statement by the Secretary General today. It is only a paragraph long. It says that this is essentially a matter within the domestic jurisdiction of a state, and he urges utmost restraint. It seems to me that more should both be required and permitted within the context of the United Nations than now seems possible.
I urge the Canadian Government to explore every opportunity, as it said it will, to see how the moral suasive powers-I think that is the way the Minister put it-can be used to put pressure on China in this instance to make sure, first of all, that the killing does stop and, second, that the road to democratization which China
June 5, 1989

was on and which the students so ably represented is a road that is resumed.
Some people have called for the immediate withdrawal of the Canadian Ambassador to China. Certainly this is something that the Government must consider in the days ahead, particularly if it becomes obvious that those who ordered the troops on the students are solidifying their power in the country. Although, as you know, we are not sure. I do not think anyone is sure at this point just exactly what is happening in China. There are strong indications of conflicts within the People's Liberation Army itself. It may be some time before we know who it is appropriate to speak of when we are speaking about the Government or authority in China.
In any case, this traditional gesture of protest is something the Government must consider, but we appreciate that in the next few days and perhaps for the next little while this will be a judgment that will have to be made. Having the Ambassador on site may well be something that will be useful in terms of advancing the security of Canadians who are in China, although as the Minister said, it may well be that all Canadians will have to be evacuated from Beijing and not just the Ambassador in the form of a withdrawal.
With respect to Chinese students in Canada, I was glad to hear the announcement by the Government as to how to deal with the predicament in which many of those students find themselves. The point is well taken that the Government must now begin to think about what it will do with respect to those students if there is a long-term problem. Even if things were to return to an acceptable state in China, these students may still have a long-term problem in terms of having identified themselves as people who were afraid to go home and who may have stayed here longer than they had originally planned. There are some long-term considerations with which the Government will have to deal with respect to Chinese students here in Canada. We urge the Government to do everything possible to facilitate both the safety of the students in terms of staying here, or in China, should they eventually return there.
This past weekend I was at the New Democratic Party convention in Manitoba. Everyone was upset to hear
what had happened in China. What struck me and even made me feel old for a moment was how upset the Manitoba Young New Democrats were, how upset students were, and how upset students around the world are. They feel an identity with those students in China.
Whether they have ever been in China, or know Chinese, or whatever the case may be, they identify with those young people who for so many weeks now have gathered in Tiananmen Square in a non-violent, idealistic and courageous way. I was struck by the way that young Canadians identified with those students.
Not so long ago I was a student. I remember the events of 1970 when students were fired upon at Kent State University. I believe at that time only four students were killed. This obviously was not something ordered by the national Government. It was an order that came from much lower down the totem pole than that. Yet that event, along with others, so eroded the moral credibility of the policy that the American Government was following at that time in Vietnam that it was not very long before that policy crumbled altogether.
It did not bring on an election victory for the students in 1972, just as this much more massive, tragic, and hardly even comparable event may not bring an immediate victory for the students and what they are seeking. However, I think that I can say with confidence that this much blood will not be shed in vain. This much blood is never shed in vain when it is the blood of the non-violent which is shed at the hands of the violent. Always out of this kind of violence comes a victory that may not be apparent today, and it may not even be apparent in the months or years ahead. We hope that it will be readily apparent in the near future. However, I am confident that this much blood of the non-violent shed by the violent will not be shed in vain, just as the blood of incomparably fewer students in previous situations in other countries was never shed in vain.
Those who know me know it is not my habit to say complimentary things about journalists, but a word needs to be said about many of the Chinese and international journalists who have brought us the coverage of events in Tiananmen Square that they have over the last few days at great risk to life and limb. It is the type of event that gives one a certain respect for the profession when journalists are willing to persist in obviously dangerous

June 5, 1989
situations so that word and image can get out to the world so people can know exactly what is going on.
There is an irony here that should not be missed. People are doing a lot of talking about the hardliners. In this context, if I understand it correctly, the hardliners are the people who want to see the economy of China westernized. Deng Xiaoping and others have become known for their economic reforms. In that sense they have not been hardliners when it comes to economic ideology. It turns out that they have been hardliners when it comes to political ideology. It is important to say that because so often the concept of being a hardliner is used with a broad brush and implies both political and economic rigidity which in this case is not an accurate way of describing what is going on.
The task for the western world will be to drive home the point, particularly if the so-called hardliners, in this case the people who ordered the troops on the students are the people who emerge victorious from the struggle which is now going on from the chain of violence that they set in motion, not only in rhetoric and motions here in the House of Commons, however important they may be, but to drive home the point in practical and concrete actions about how much offence is taken by the world at what has happened in China. At the same time China must not be driven into isolationism and hostility toward the rest of the world. That will be dangerous for us all. In this I do not care one whit about who happens to have investments in China or joint ventures. I am not talking about the economic dimension. Economic matters should always be subordinate to larger moral and political values. I am talking about the fact that we are dealing with one of the largest countries in the world, a country which, if things go awiy in China, can affect all kinds of things which are either progressing well at this point or have the hope of progressing well.
Recently I had occasion to speak to the Asia-Pacific Foundation in Vancouver. It was an opportunity for me to have a good look at many things that are happening in the Asia-Pacific region. One of the things one was delighted to note was that it was an era of reconciliation and so many old enemies were reconciling. When I spoke in late April it was just previous to the first visit by a Taiwanese Minister to the mainland since the revolution.
China-Japan relations are warming, Russian-Chinese relations are warming, Russian-Japanese relations are warming, and the Southeast Asian countries are trying to find a solution to problems in Indochina. Without a China that knows its mind it maybe very difficult to solve the problem in Cambodia. All of this will have a profound effect on a great many international situations that are important to us all.
Therefore it is incumbent upon all of us to think very carefully and of course it is even more incumbent upon the Government because they are the ones who have to act, but it is incumbent upon us to think how we react to these events. Whatever we do, we have to do actual things. We cannot be guilty of saying our piece tonight and being done with it. Whatever we do, we have to do it from that sense of outrage which is unanimously shared by Canadians, and particularly shared by Chinese Canadians and others who have had the good fortune to visit China over the last few decades. I notice that people who have been to China in the last decade or so have had a special pain in their hearts about what has gone on there. I believe that speaks well of the Chinese people. It speaks well of the hopes that many have had and should still have for the future of China. China as a civilization and as a nation has been around for a long time. It will be around for a long time yet. What those students were after, and what I believe in great measure they will have achieved by their deaths, will yet come to pass.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a great distance between our country and China in geographic terms. There is a great distance as well between the Chinese and most Canadians in cultural terms. There is no distance between us whatsoever tonight in the shared emotional response to the tragedy that is unfolding in China.
This century which in so many ways highlights steps of human advancement and progress, is also the century of the most unspeakable horrors inflicted by mankind upon other humans. It is perhaps one of the most discouraging things for people around the globe tonight to see on the news that has just been broadcast, the unfolding events in China. The often hoped for sense of progress towards civilized methods of government, orderly and peaceful methods of resolving differences, in fact represents a stage of human progress. It is black chapters like the one
June 5, 1989

that is being written now that bring us up short with the realization that too often the veneer of civilization is just that, a very thin veneer.
As this tragedy unfolds as one more chapter in China's long history, it is perhaps very important for all of us in this country and elsewhere around the globe to make a distinction between the people of China and those who are currently in authority in China and have set in motion this chain of events.
It is very clear that China with its centuries of rich culture and human endeavour has a very great deal to teach the rest of the world. But China has nothing to teach the rest of the world about how to deal with political change. What we have seen in the last two days represents the most complete and abysmal failure of a government to respond to change within its own country. When the point is reached where armed soldiers turn and fire on unarmed civilians within their own country, no more greater statement of bankrupt political thinking could be made than that which was carried by the signature of those machine guns firing and those tanks moving along the Boulevard of Eternal Peace.
The Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) when he spoke earlier referred to events in Europe, particularly in Hungary in 1956. I was 11 years old in 1956 and delivering newspapers on my paper route door to door. After several days of seeing photographs on the front page of The Toronto Telegram showing students in running shoes with Molotov cocktails in their hands up against the heavy-booted soldiers and the steel-plated tanks moving through the streets of Budapest, I became very depressed and for a number of weeks was inexplicably in a state of melancholy. I feel the same sense tonight, and I mention Budapest in 1956 for two reasons.
First, because that image of students standing before those tanks as the troops of repression swept into Hungary is a direct parallel with the scene that Canadians saw just a few moments ago on national television. They saw students standing before tanks in the streets of the capital city of China with nothing but their human bravery and their commitment to their beliefs in democracy against that awesome military threat that was only feet and inches away from them. Therefore we see a parallel in a sense.
If we are to see some similarities between now and 1956, let us see another one. In retrospect, many people saw Budapest in 1956 as a time of lost opportunity because coming from the people was a strong drive for political freedom in a communist controlled country. The West did not respond at that time because the West was preoccupied with other activities; the French and the British in the Suez and the Canadians also in the Suez crisis. The Americans were preoccupied in 1956 with electing their popular general, Dwight Eisenhower, as President.
There were many other distractions. It was only in retrospect that many people regretted that there had not been a greater sense of the historic moment so that those within Hungary could have felt appropriate support.
We are now witnessing another moment of history. It is more than right for all of us to stand here as representatives of an outraged Canadian populace and give expression to the justifiable horror which we all feel. It is not only right, it is necessary that around the world those who are democrats express that feeling unequivocally.
Beyond expressing outrage, I am saying that we must be creative in how we are viewing this unfolding situation in China. Most assuredly this is another historic moment. There may be opportunities if we think creatively, if we view the situation with an open mind and listen especially to those forces within China which in some form or other we can assist at this time. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Transcona spoke about the ironies in this situation and the distinction between who are the hardliners and who are not the hardliners. Following on his line of thinking, I believe it is very important that we do not at this time fall too easily into putting labels and categories to a situation that is extraordinarily complex.
Using all of the resources of our country, including not only Canadians with experience in China but many who are now Canadians of Chinese background, and being open to all the possibilities that this situation presents, we must speak as we are tonight and act as a Parliament as we are tonight. However, in the days ahead, as this chain of events continues to unfold, we must look for ways that we can, as one of the world's countries that has a very special relationship with China, continue to support those forces of democracy and those forces of

reform within the country. To do less might very well mean that in 10 or 15 years we would look back and see that an opportunity had been missed.
The upheaval that is currently taking place in the communist world is truly remarkable. Events are happening these weeks and months that two years ago people would have thought quite impossible. Certainly in the example from China, in contrast to the example in eastern Europe, we are seeing that economic reform must be accompanied by political reform.
For these reasons I join with other elected representatives of the Canadian people to stand in the House of Commons of Canada tonight and express, as all others have, support for our resolution which unequivocally condemns this brutal use of force against the peaceful populace of China, to issue our call to the authorities in China to cease the senseless killing, and to adopt immediately a course of dialogue with the Chinese people.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be impossible for me to improve upon the moving words that have been spoken by so many of my colleagues from all corners of the House tonight about the tragic massacre which has occurred in China over the past few days.
However, I want to take this opportunity to add my voice on behalf of my constituents in full support of this unanimous motion of condemnation against the senseless and vulgar decisions taken by the Chinese Government to slaughter its own citizens. Surely such actions demonstrate the total vacuum of leadership which exists in China at this time, and surely all the world deplores any system of government that must resort to violence as the final measure of its incompetence and its inhumanity.
Yesterday in Fredericton, New Brunswick, a peaceful and orderly demonstration was conducted by Chinese citizens to express their shock, anguish, and anger over the events that had just taken place in Beijing. They were joined by students, both foreign and Canadian, and by local citizens of several cultures and languages, in a community expression of sympathy for those who suffered and of outrage that this world is capable of such atrocities.
That demonstration in Fredericton cannot help but cause us to realize how truly fortunate we are in New Brunswick and in all of Canada to enjoy a system of democracy that is so stable, so secure, and truly so peaceful. It surely cannot help but cause us to reflect upon the values, the challenges, and the opportunities which we are privileged in this country to pursue in the future building of our own great nation.
After watching the horrors of China this weekend, surely we shall realize how blessed we are to have the chance to join with the many people of Canada, with the several world cultures that make up our population and the official languages of our population, in one magnificent, unified nation.
I am moved by the accord that exists in this House tonight condemning this unspeakable scene from a country so far away. I cannot help but be brought back close to home and express the wishes others have expressed here tonight, that such accord as we feel on this subject will move us on to other subjects closer to home, that we shall remember this evening and be moved to make this House more an instrument of progress and resolution, reconciliation and peace in building our own great nation.
It is a privilege, as the Member of Parliament for my constituency, to rise in the House and be able to express the sadness, the dismay, the anguish, and the anger of the citizens whom I represent over the atrocities that we have seen this past weekend and to express the wish that the unfolding of these events will in due course move us to greater goals and pursuit of the unification and strengthening of our own country.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise in my place tonight to join in this emergency debate on the situation in China, I am aghast when I think of the terrible atrocity that has taken place.
Television and mass media bring these events much closer to us than ever before possible. Yet the horror we have seen on our TV sets is in reality magnified one hundred times for those who find themselves in the middle of it. I simply cannot understand why this has happened.
Television has brought catastrophes into our living rooms before: mass genocide in Jonestown, airline disasters, Bhopal, Ethiopia, but this one is different. Over the last month we have watched student calls for reform blossom into a full-fledged movement for democracy.
June 5, 1989

Now we see the Government's attempt to crush it, a brutal, sadistic, deliberate, unprovoked, unforgivable attack on its own citizens.
This carnage is like nothing we have witnessed since the Second World War. Indeed, it is the first time in the 40-year history of communist China that the Government has turned its guns on its own people. This is a state driven human slaughter. It has happened when global expectations for peace and freedom are at an all time high.
Yet, it is an avowal of failure. Because of its actions, the Chinese Government has not crushed the movement for democracy. Far from it. The blood of the student protesters and their civilian supporters will give impetus that will shake the Chinese Government to its very foundation.
There are many questions on our minds this evening. The first of these is about what the Government in China will do next. Another is about what we in the outside world can do. Certainly there is little encouragement from these Chinese officials, whereas yesterday we heard their promises that this was only the beginning, that more needed to be done to bring what they call dissidents in line. We must condemn the actions of the Chinese Government. We must offer our voice of condemnation to that of the world reaction.
If the Chinese Government could order this course of recent events, perhaps Canada should re-examine our expansion of trade with China. In 1988 there were $2.6 billion in exports from Canada to China, nearly double the $1.4 billion of the previous year. Chinese imports to Canada rose from $812 million to $955 million in 1988. China needs Canadian knowledge and technology to propel it into the 21st century. For most Canadians, respect for human rights is as important as technological advancement. We must demonstrate this belief through our trade policies.
In this trying time of world drama and tension, it is a blessing that with our country's wonderful system of democracy, our three political Parties chose and were able to conduct this emergency debate this evening. I personally feel so exasperated at being so far away, so much appalled and yet so unable to help. Many people globally have expressed their shock and horror. Now is
our moment to do something with our emotions and turn them into actions. It is Canada's moment to help turn world-wide opinion into nation-wide action.
We have heard so many pleas from people in China that reporters must get this story out to the world. We now know that they have and it is our turn to get our message in the strongest possible terms to the people of China, to tell them-no, to show them-that our heart and our thoughts are with them.
In my own riding of Nepean, over 2,000 people are of Chinese ethnic origin. Over half that number consider the Chinese language their mother tongue. That 2,000 figure in my riding is exceeded only by one other Ottawa area riding and represents almost exactly one-quarter of the persons of Chinese origin in all Ottawa area ridings. To put that in perspective, one out of 100 national capital resident is of Chinese origin.
The immediate concern of all Canadians, particularly Chinese Canadians, is for the safety of their family and friends in China. Our concern, however, is also for the future, the future of China and the future of Hong Kong. I join my colleagues and all Canadians in calling on the Government to use any measure at its disposal, be it diplomatic or economic, to indicate clearly to the Chinese Government that we will not tolerate nor easily forget such abhorrent action.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great sorrow that I rise to take part in the emergency debate on the events of the past weekend in China. The actions of the Peoples Liberation Army, in their crushing of the pro-democracy movement, can only be described as crimes against humanity.
The horrors that all Canadians witnessed on their television sets over the past couple of nights are completely repulsive to the human mind. Canada's reaction to these atrocities should be swift and conducive to the magnitude of the crime committed by the People's Republic of China against its own people.
We can trace the roots of the unrest to the initial reforms set out by Deng Xiaoping in the late seventies and the early eighties. The former premier of the Peoples Republic of China set out a brave agenda for the economy of China that would turn the isolationist tide that characterized that nation's foreign policy for the better part of 40 years.

June 5, 1989
Premier Deng seemed to infuse a breath of fresh air into the stagnating Chinese economy. Unfortunately, this political stalwart has outlived his welcome and has exercised a rational vengeance against his own people. We have learned from various media sources that it was upon his order that the Chinese military violently dispersed the youth demonstrations in Tiananmen Square.
I say that this is the most reprehensible action that a political leader can take against his own people and should not go without strong international retribution.
The demonstrations in Beijing are a result of the rising expectations precipitated by the economic reforms of the past 10 years. The Government of the People's Republic of China seemed to be opening up its doors to allow foreign investment and greater free market interaction so as to facilitate a more rapid pace of economic development.
As a result of the successes of this policy, the Chinese people demanded what seemed to be part of the natural progression towards freedom. They demanded that justice and equality be part of the Chinese communist system. They demanded that rules of fairness and equity be followed by the upper echelons of the Communist Party and that no one should profit from their position within the state system.

Mr. Speaker, thousands of Chinese gave their lives for these principles. As Canadians, we cannot afford to take for granted the principles of freedom enshrined in our Constitution. In fact, we should become very much aware of them as a result of these recent events.
The expectations of the students in Beijing were heightened by the political reforms taking place throughout the Communist world. Since the Soviet Union was preparing for its first democratic election in over 70 years, the Chinese people could not remain unaffected by this new attitude. Unfortunately for the Chinese, glasnost has not yet reached the People's Republic of China.
Instead of forging ahead and preparing for a more democratic system, the Chinese political elite decided it was better to protect their entrenched positions within
the system than to secure the freedom and prosperity of the Chinese people.
Mr. Speaker, political changes in China have always come through the student activist wing. During the past few weeks, the whole world was able to witness that the massed students on Tienanmen Square were peaceful, only demanding their basic political rights and the principles of freedom. That is why the violence shown by the government was in no way justified.
Unfortunately, Deng Xiaoping and Li Peng preferred to use brute force instead of showing understanding and initiating some kind of compromise, faced with this movement for freedom and democracy.

All Canadians looked on with dismay as the statue erected in the square called the Goddess of Democracy was destroyed by a tank over the weekend. The image of armed vehicles roaring up and down the Avenue of Eternal Peace in the heart of Beijing could only make one think of the paradox that China is today.
On the other hand, we have the youth of China. The students at these universities represent the best and the brightest of the Chinese people. The youth of the country are being sacrificed for the political ambition of an ever ageing gerontocracy. For the first time since the Communists have taken over Mainland China, innocent civilians have been victims of their own Armed Forces. As a Canadian, I find this fact most reprehensible.
This is indeed a heinous crime. Estimates of the casualties in Beijing range from 500 to 3,000 people killed and up to 10,000 people injured. China has not seen such absolute bloodshed for decades. Instead of joining the trend toward global peace and understanding, the Chinese Government has shown its true colours and has demonstrated that it will not tolerate any challenge to its totalitarian political power. The fact that the people being shot were unarmed and being passive in their resistance heightens the revulsion at this deed.
Students, women and children being shot at random is simply unacceptable in today's world. The immediate evil tactics of the Chinese Government will not be forgotten by our world. Stories emanating from Beijing are indeed horrible. One unconfirmed incident, as reported by The Globe and Mail, told of 100 people linking arms to act as
June 5, 1989

a human barricade against the oncoming tanks. Soldiers then opened fire against these unarmed civilians killing scores and injuring many others.
A second wave of people stepped over their fallen comrades to act as a second barrier against the armoured column. To everyone's horror they, too, were mowed down. News reports from Beijing indicated that many were killed or crushed by the tanks. Others reported that indiscriminate shooting by soldiers killed many innocent bystanders.
Through any examination of the facts the truth is undeniable. The political leadership of China must be held accountable for the crime it has committed.
As one of my Party's spokespersons for multicultural-ism, along with my colleague the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Mills), I am particularly concerned for the Chinese population here in Canada. The shock to many Canadians who still have family and friends in Beijing must be enormous. I hope the federal Government will co-operate to the fullest of its ability to alleviate any undue anxieties these people may feel. I also hope that the federal Government assists these people through whatever means possible to send necessary aid to their people in China who desperately need our support in their struggle for democracy and freedom at this time.
I am also concerned with respect to how events in China will affect Canada's refugee system. It is highly likely that the events of the past weekend will create a new tide of immigrants from Hong Kong who are ever more fearful of the colony's reunification with the mainland, as well as from the mainland as prospects for political reform grow fainter.
I hope that the federal Government treats these anticipated cases with great care and compassion. Canada should open its doors to those refugees from the turmoil in China who will obviously be affected as a result of their involvement in the student demonstrations.

The Canadian Government must consider the options open to it. As a country that cherishes the sacredness of
human life, as well as the basic rights of freedom, we must make known our anger very clearly. The Canadian Government must first recall its representative to the People's Republic of China as a sign of disapproval. It should also consider the possibility of economic sanctions to express the horror felt by Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, Canada should use the opportunity provided by its seat on the United Nations Security Council to gain the support of other states for unanimous condemnation of the reprehensible acts of the Chinese Government. It is high time that this Government used Canada's good reputation as an involved country and passed a firm resolution on this subject.

China is an ancient land that has in its history endured much hardship and oppression. The events of the past weekend demonstrate that this unfortunate trend will continue and, according to some reports, expand to other cities.
I hope that the Government of the People's Republic of China reconsiders its decision to crush the peaceful demonstration. Until the time when this wrong can be corrected, I hope that the Canadian Government and the global community take the strongest measures possible to condemn this horrible act.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just when we thought the world had taken a small tentative step out of Churchill's broad sunlit uplands, hope has turned to heartbreak, exultation to dejection.
How did it happen? What happens now? What should Canada do? What should Canadians and China do?
When I heard the news that the tanks had moved into Tiananmen Square I was in Drumheller to get a progress report on the Canada-China dinosaur project, a joint venture of our two countries that has as its objective a travelling exhibition which will, if all goes well, attract some 12 million visitors in the great cities of the world and show the palaeontological resources of our two countries which have yet that one other item in common.
A visiting palaeontologist who was in the Drumheller region on the weekend from the People's Republic of

June 5, 1989
China had a son who was demonstrating in Tiananmen Square. He was full of anxiety as to his son's fate.
Since the Second World War there have been notable public uprisings of this kind. There was one in 1951 in East Germany, in Budapest in 1956, and Tibet in 1959. There was the one in the Prague in the spring in 1968. There was that wonderful moment in February 1986 in Manila when an 82 year old grandmother with the power of prayer and a flower stopped a tank which had rolled out of the barracks. In the words of Jaime Cardinal Sin: "People power defeated the weaponry of the oppressor".
Now, in 1989, we have the slaughter in Tiananmen Square. What has led to the uprising? What has led to the tyranny which put it down?
I am told that there is a dichotomy in Chinese society between the urban and the rural population. Life is more difficult in the cities. Prices are higher. There is crowding and tension which leads to a good deal of anxiety. There is, of course, the yearning for freedom, a yearning for political freedom and perhaps more economic freedom. It is a yearning which might to our eyes and our ears be somewhat naive and idealistic.
I had the opportunity this afternoon to speak with Professor Leslie Green, a distinguished international jurist, a Professor of International Law at the University of Alberta who just in the last seven days has returned from lecturing at Beijing University and at Harbin University in Heilongjang Province of northern China. While in Harbin, Professor Green was asked questions about human rights by the Chinese students. To quote the Professor directly:
-their questions were excellent. Let me give you an example because I think it reflects the student mentality in the area.
The question posed to the professor was:
In your country, Professor, if students wish to demonstrate, do they need Government permission?
Professor Green replied by pointing out:
- in Canada you don't need government permission but the police have to approve your route, and if you deviate from the route they will push you back. They didn't like that answer, they had been led sort of by western reaction to assume that all students have to do is come out and everything in the garden will be lovely.
They also said to Professor Green:
- in your country, if a visiting dignitary, a head of state comes, and wants to invite people to dinner, will the Government interfere if he invites a leading dissident?
You may remember, Mr. Speaker, that that is what happened with President Bush. Professor Green replied:
-I don't think it would happen in Canada, because the Chief of Protocol of External Affairs would ask to see the guest list in advance, and I think that is correct. They didn't like that answer, either. So you can see the sort of temper they were in, but they asked their questions the way that wouldn't embarrass me.
Within the Chinese society and the Chinese culture students have traditionally had a special place. The scholar has had a special place, as the incubator of tomorrow's intelligentsia.
Another factor which I believe has led to this tension in Chinese society is something that perhaps no society is immune from. We see it on our own continent, that is to say a resentment of the life-style of a leadership elite.
We also must examine the role of the western media both in the encouragement of liberation movements and sometimes in their collapse. We look back to the Budapest situation of October of 1956 and there is no doubt that in that situation there were broadcasts by liberation radio organizations in Western Europe which led the Hungarian people to the belief that if only they threw off the Soviet oppressor the western nations would soon come to their rescue. Of course, that was not to be. The West chose not to act in Hungary in 1956.
So we examine in the age of television what role the western media, playing to a western audience but bringing the picture directly out of the Forbidden City and Tiananmen Square from Beijing into our own homes, may play in interacting with the attitudes of the students themselves.
Professor Green again had some comments to offer. He said:
When marshal law was declared and the western press made so much of the non-action of the military, the presentation of flowers and the hugging and the sitting crosslegged without weaponry, would have been the sort of thing to lead the government to assume that this was the beginning of something more than just a student protest. I also had the feeling from what we could see and sense that it was dying out, that if the government would have sort of let it run, it would have subsided quietly. Again, the students were a little unreasonable. You couldn't really expect the government to agree
June 5, 1989

that the conversations between government and student leaders would be televised to the public.
Yet, paradoxically, the students told Professor Green, both in Beijing and Heilongjang, thank God for the BBC, because that wonderful public broadcasting organization which had established such a great reputation for reliability during the Second World War and the years since then was the main source of the students for active accounts of what was happening within their own country.
Are we going to have another Budapest, another night of darkness? I asked Professor Green that question this afternoon when we discussed the situation in Beijing. He said:
I think to a certain extent, that is what has happened in China. And I am not blaming the western press. What I am saying is that with their reactions, with their comments rather than straight reporting, they may have encouraged the students to go a little further to make more extreme demands and to terrify the government into believing that what was starting as a pure passive resistant demonstration by youngsters, which could be disregarded and allowed to wear itself out, was becoming the beginning, the seeds of the civil war.
So we listened tonight with great concern and apprehension when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) reported that minutes before he spoke reports had come from our embassy in Beijing that there were reports of some civil strife among military units in various parts of China.
Canada's interest in all of this is, first of all, human and humanitarian. I share the sentiments of other speakers tonight who are horrified by the unnecessary use of force that has taken place and the blatant disregard for human rights.
In Alberta and British Columbia over the last few years, as indeed in other parts of Canada, there has been a blooming of activity with China, joint ventures, delegations constantly going, the twinning of communities. My own City of Edmonton is twinned with Harbin and the Province of Alberta with Heilongjang.
The Middle Kingdom is truly the centre of gravity of the world's population. It began with the missionaries, as the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition pointed out tonight, and continued with Norman Bethune. Alvin
Hamilton first sold wheat in China and we led many of the western democracies with the Trudeau Government recognition of the PRC in 1970 and leading its sponsorship for UN admission later on.
Canada has $36 million of overseas development assistance with China, $771 million worth of imports into Canada, and double that in exports to China. The Chinese have built our country, our railways, our service industries, and many are active in our professions and in Government. We now have a Lieutenant Governor of our western-most province who was born of Chinese parentage and who came as an immigrant to this country.
So what should Canada do in this situation? First of all, we endorse the resolution. Second, we must give comfort and reassurance to the families of Canadians in China. I am pleased at the rapid action of the Government in ordering a plane sent to Beijing for those who are unable to get out through civilian airlines.
We should offer a haven in Canada to those Chinese who seek it, be they students or refugees. I submit that finally, and I say this with great regret because of my deep interest in the Canada-China dinosaur project of the Ex Terra Foundation, we should withhold the hand of new co-operation from the regime responsible for the slaughter.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to address this veiy serious matter, a matter that has left us and the world thunderstruck. As one who has experienced the peace and tranquillity of the Chinese people, a peace-loving people, I would like to urge some caution and restraint in the handling of this matter which, while I quite readily concede has affected lives, nothing we can say or do will reverse what has happened. What we can do and what we should do remains very important, not only to other lives, but as well could quite well prevent the rebirth of a cold war between Canada and the People's Republic of China. Our international diplomacy and our international diplomatic maturity is currently at test.
We have a peaceful and friendly existence with the Chinese people, it having lasted over a period of many years. That in itself is worth life. Our friendship is of value to them as is theirs to us.

June 5, 1989
The indiscriminate taking of life that has occurred is something that should be condemned and every human being, every father, mother, sister and brother, has a right to take issue with what has happened in Beijing. Perhaps at the beginning of our day tomorrow it would be appropriate to observe a moment's silence to acknowledge the sacrifice for peace and democracy that those young Chinese students gave.
We should make the point that we would hope that some day every government in this world would be democratic and would provide for an individual's right to speak, to be heard and understood. We make this claim as an attempt to strive toward a more perfect life and to do so driven by peaceful motivation. It is most unfortunate that a segment in this world has not complied with our basis for the attainment of individual human rights.
What exists is a breach in what appeared within a natural flow towards the attainment of individual status and accomplishment and the opportunity for people to feel better about themselves and to some day soon attain those rights and privileges which we as Canadians enjoy and perhaps sometimes take for granted.
I want to give some history as to my involvement with the People's Republic of China. It was at the urging of our local Chinese community that the City of Regina began the pursuit of establishing a twinning relationship with a city in the People's Republic of China. It was, as well, with the urging of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities that this move be encouraged and undertaken as a measure for, not only economic development for municipalities all across Canada, but as well for an opportunity to assist in providing the People's Republic of China with some of the municipal technologies that we had available that could provide them with a better life. As well, and perhaps even more importantly, there was the opportunity to establish a relationship, to build bridges, to make friends, to build trusts so that we might both mutually enjoy each other's peace. It was often theorised that the button to the bomb would not be pushed by your twin.
This pursuit was followed to the point where the City of Regina was twinned with the City of Jinan, Shandong Province in PRC. This relationship and trust was extended further, to the point where the City of Jinan agreed to exhibit at an industrial trade show to occur in
Regina during the months of July and August at the Regina Buffalo Days Exhibition.
The trust that was required was enormous in that they are, without any guarantees, bringing a display that they hope to sell that is worth somewhere in the order of $150,000 to $200,000. This does not include the freight, set up, tear down and commitment required to bring this display to Canada. I now believe that this exhibition to be in jeopardy and I am therefore anxious that dialogue commence as quickly as possible.
This exhibition is the faith that the Chinese people have placed in us and is not something that we should take as a commitment given lightly. Therefore I would encourage that those of us who have comments about the situation do so in a manner that is constructive, compassionate, and which will not seal the doors to a renewed friendship that was so long in the making. Kindness and understanding can retain this friendship. Arrogance may lose it. Spontaneity may weaken it. Diplomacy may be the only tool we have to retain this relationship.
Mr. Speaker, I urge the support of the motion that conveys our concern with the loss of life that has occurred, our compassion and sympathy for the relatives of those who are the survivors, our support for the continuation of the establishment of human rights for those living in the People's Republic of China in a peaceful way, and our support and encouragement to those who participated in Tiananmen Square who did so with the resolve of the attainment of their pursuit in a peaceful manner.
We should be sending to the People's Republic of China our expression of continued interest and concern and hope that the Chinese Government seek a speedy truce to the civil conflict and continue in a fashion which encourages dialogue and rejects bullets. We should not be acting out of haste. There are no medals to be won by being first. We should act carefully, with determination, and with the objective to assist in the resolve of this turmoil facing the world's largest population.
We should offer our prayers to the effort and cause of those who lost their lives and to those who continue the pursuit. I entreat Members of Parliament to be diligent and understanding, to have the peaceful goals of the Chinese people as our goals as well, to cast aside aspirations for being on the front pages of our newspa-
June 5, 1989

pers, to pursue that which can be done in the true spirit of Dr. Norman Bethune, and to seek no other gratification other than knowing that we can continue to be leaders in striving for world peace.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak and condemn the inhuman acts perpetrated by the Chinese Government against her own people. I understand the aspirations of the Chinese people who protest for freedom. I cannot fathom the insanity of action by the Chinese authorities.
Indeed, Beijing's Tiananmen Square will henceforth stand in world history as a slaughterhouse for innocent civilians whose only aspiration is for the betterment of their own people, for the dignity of their families-the very foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world.
The brutality which the military has used in quelling the forces of democracy is horrifying indeed. Civilians of all ages and from all walks of life are being slain. All are being sacrificed because they had the courage and determination to pursue the universal goal of freedom. The catastrophe in China affects all human beings irrespective of race, religion or political allegiance. In Canada, our collective indignation is symbolized by the unanimous consent and agreement of all political parties to debate this issue in the House of Commons tonight and I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your consent.
We must not only speak as enraged democratic people, but also in consciousness of the many Chinese Canadians who must feel particularly shocked by the events in Beijing. Chinese Canadians have participated fully in the economic and social growth of our country and have helped build some of our most important national institutions.
What is behind this sudden surge of support for democracy on the part of the students? This is a question that must be examined. Why suddenly are these students protesting against the political party that has ruled their lives all along?
Basically, China has given her citizens new economic freedom but has denied them political freedom. The current Chinese leadership believed that economic reform would be enough. They believed that the Chinese
population could be seduced by the importation of consumer goods and would be apathetic to the demand for political freedom. The authorities were wrong.
The demonstrations by these students signalled to conservative Communist Party members that they were wrong. The demonstrators called for specific political reforms; for increased funding for education which would make it possible for more Chinese citizens to escape poverty; for the publication of the income and assets of top party leaders to provide public accountability and prevent corruption; for the support of liberal policies and greater democracy; for open dialogue between the students and government that would be open to the public and broadcasts uncensored on national television. Above all, they called for the freedom of the press, speech and assembly, values which all societies in the world strive for.
Instead of granting the desired pday olitical freedom, the Communist Party acted desperately to preserve their control at the expense of human lives. By setting the military on unarmed civilians, the Chinese leaders illustrated that they are barbaric, without a heart and who govern without consent. They obviously adhere to Mao's maxim that power grows from the barrel of a gun and ignore that true power emanates from the people.
This morning, Beijing Mayor Chen Xitong warned that the Government and the Communist Party had reached the end of their patience, and I quote: "If anyone continues their resistance, they will be severely punished."
It has also been reported that Deng has said, and again I quote: "Even if they're functioning out of ignorance, they are still participating and must be suppressed."
It is the people of China who have reached the end of their patience with Chinese leaders who are ignorant. They are ignorant of the needs of their citizens: the need for political freedom and for personal independence. Indeed, the very basic need to live and to be free to live.
The concerns that these events cause us are many. We are concerned about the lives of the protesters in China as well as the Canadian citizens whose lives may be in danger.

June 5, 1989
The brutal way in which the Chinese Government is reacting to the quest for political freedom also makes us realise that the political, social and ethical values for tolerance, of the need to protect human dignity, which we see as a given in Canada, have not yet spread to the leaders of China.
We must also be concerned about the future of the citizens of Hong Kong. The poor example set in Beijing in the past couple of days bodes ill for the people of Hong Kong after its integration with China in 1997.
We must also be concerned about the future of Chinese students currently in Canada. They must never suffer because they have expressed indignation about the way their government is treating Chinese citizens.
Government over-cautiousness as a response to the violence in China when human lives are involved is in itself a threat. Inaction on the part of other countries might encourage the Chinese Government to proceed with its use of force in the belief that it will not be punished on the international scene.
I therefore salute all freedom-loving governments and peoples who unite to condemn the inhuman acts of the Chinese authorities. Our Government must ask China to take note of the lessons of successful revolutions, of solidarity in Poland and of the victory of Corazon Aquino in the Philippines. The signals that we send to China now will have a far-reaching effect beyond China and might encourage democratic forces in other oppressed countries. We must apply diplomatic and economic pressure, including asking for an emergency Security Council session of the United Nations. This will send a clear message that the international community stands behind the students and workers, the men and women, the youth and the elderly in China who have sacrificed their lives to obtain a universal human value-freedom.
Now is not the time to worry about our trading relationship with China. The urgent priority is to take action to stop the bloodshed. Economic considerations must be subservient to consideration of human lives. We must provide moral support for the oppressed and suppressed people of China, and signal to the Chinese authorities that we condemn their actions. We must tell
the Chinese leaders to react with tact and not tanks, to give goods and not guns.
I add my voice and those of my constituents in Winnipeg North to those in the House who have expressed deep indignation at the unspeakable action of the Chinese authorities. By our united action we demonstrate to the whole world and, more importantly, to the freedom-loving people of China that we Canadians are committed to freedom, justice, and peace for all peoples. We are behind them. We love and care for them. Indeed, we ask the Chinese Government as we demonstrate tonight in Parliament to give her people both life and liberty.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak about the tragedy of this weekend's massacres in Tiananmen Square. The past months and years have been especially hopeful for the world. We have witnessed glasnost and perestroika, the hopeful talks for arms reduction, increased international trade and global integration, and a spirit of openness is being felt throughout the world as we address problems such as environmental degradation and the AIDS threat.
In the past week alone we watched students gather in Tiananmen Square to fight for democratic reforms. In another part of the world, the people of Poland have participated in their first semi-democratic election. People gathered in Montreal this weekend to talk openly and candidly about the AIDS threat.
After the malaise of the last years caused by arms escalation, increased cold war tensions, and the poverty of the Third World, our generation has played an important role around the world in returning hope to mankind and nowhere more so than in China where, in the last six weeks, students took it upon themselves to demand that democratic reforms follow the Government's economic reforms.
The student movement in Tiananmen Square owes its beginning to the strength and courage of a few young men and women who understood that democracy does not just happen. It is built, and the price of reform is hardship and self-sacrifice. They soon discovered that their strength and courage, camaraderie and character were contagious.
By Sunday morning Beijing time, Saturday morning our time, the dreams that began in the hearts of a few idealistic students had permeated men, women and children of all classes in Beijing society. People around the world watched as they fought in unison to prevent the Chinese army from removing them from Tiananmen Square. I watched on television as a woman on the street explained very matter of factly that all they had to do was
June 5, 1989

explain to the armed soldiers moving in on trucks that they, the soldiers, were people first and that they should not attack the students. For a while, the world was transfixed awaiting reform somewhat anxiously. Perhaps we were too complacent. Perhaps we should have been encouraging the students and supporting them rather than waiting.
We as Canadians have a history of looking outward. One of our former Prime Ministers, a personal hero of mine, Mr. Lester Pearson, was awarded a Nobel Prize when he saw tensions grow in the Suez Canal region and he provided a release valve. Canadian peace-keeping troops have been awarded the Nobel Prize for their ongoing peace-keeping missions around the world. Those peace-keeping missions reflect the Canadian notion of duty to brother. We have a glorious history; at least we have had a glorious history. As has often been said in times of crises, the price of democracy is eternal vigilance. Perhaps it slipped our minds that the welfare and the future of the Chinese students was inextricably bound to our own, that we too had to stand up to be counted in this time of reform.
Perhaps our caution was justified and our reluctance to hope for too much was vindicated. The bloodshed of the last few days has set the world spinning. Yet despite ourselves, despite the distance between our two countries, somehow we were bound to the fate of the Chinese community at the other end of the earth. Because we are tied to the situation, it is now incumbent upon us to act unanimously in condemning the Chinese Government. We cannot shy away from the situation twice, not when lives have been lost. The hope that was dashed from the students who were demonstrating peacefully, and that hope which was dashed from ourselves, must be reclaimed. And it shall be, for hope springs eternal in the heart of man.
In order to achieve this end, in order that the lives of the young students were not lost in vain, it was imperative that a unilateral resolution be passed immediately in the Elouse. I congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) for acting so promptly this evening. It is imperative that we commit ourselves right
now, openly and honestly, to use any powers we may have to stop this violence.
Canada has a very special tie to China, and a very special relationship. China's increased international trade has benefited us greatly. Canadian exports to China nearly doubled in 1988, rising to $2.6 billion from $1.4 billion in 1987. Imports from China rose to $955 million in 1988 from $812 million the preceding year.
We have a history of relations with China stemming largely from early and continued Chinese immigration to this country. We owe our Chinese community a great deal, not the least of which was the construction of large tracts of the trans-Canadian railroad. At times, as we all know, we were less than honourable to the Chinese community. But we have grown as a nation and we have grown to respect one another. In my own riding of Broadview-Greenwood, the Chinese community is vibrant and dynamic and a tremendous asset. The Lee family in the housing community, Maiy Shih looks after health care, King Wong works diligently with the seniors, Y.S. Pong works with the youth, the Lum family, Dennis Leung, the students of Riverdale Collegiate and Eastern Commerce, these people are all making contributions to our economy, our culture and to our way of life. The pain they are feeling is our pain just as the pain of the international student organizations is and that of those who believe in fundamental human rights.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like other Members in this House that tonight, I rise with great sadness and frankly great anticipation. Much that is very important has been said here tonight. I intend to be brief, and like the Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), perhaps a little personal. I too have had the opportunity to travel in China. I have travelled in China twice for extended periods of time. I stand here tonight, having viewed the events of the weekend, and having, as other Members have done, watched the footage tonight and heard the analysis. My greatest concern is for the people of China, but not just for their safety. The people of China are willing to make their own decisions and sacrifices. I am concerned for the spirit of the Chinese people, a people that has had a long and proud history, that has a great culture which has found its way through

June 5, 1989
much of eastern Asia. But while that history and culture are well-known and strong, they are full of strife. It is a history that is full of conflict, foreign invasion and foreign imposed conflict that has led to much hardship, not the least of which has been in the last 80 years.
Despite that, they are a people who are dedicated to their families, who love and cherish their children, a happy people, a people that love fun, jokes, that love to play games and as my friend my Hamilton East said, a terribly inquisitive people, a people of great searching for knowledge, for education, a people who want nothing more than the ability to make their own decisions, to have discretion in their lives and to have the responsibility for those decisions. While there has been some economic reform in China, there has not been the political reform that is so essential to reinforce it. Sadly we in North America have had a picture painted of that great country that I am afraid is inaccurate.
Perhaps if I might be a bit pejorative, the American media has painted a picture of a country that has not come as far as our friends to the south would like perhaps, but it is a country that would like to come that far some day. I am particularly concerned when I think of the people of Shigatze in Tibet that had 20,000 monasta-ries and today has 34 as a result of the Cultural Revolution. There are people who walk hundreds of kilometres to observe their religious practices in a society that does not understand the Chinese, the regime that has been imposed upon them. The Chinese do not understand the lamism of the Tibetans. We have seen death and bloodshed.
My friend has talked about the students in Shanghai who walk up to any foreigner and say hello, how are you, where are you going, what are you doing, what is your name, are you alone, who are your friends. I think also of a very old man who came up to me in a park in Shanghai and said, you are going the wrong way. In a park on a sunny morning at 11 o'clock there is no wrong way but this man wanted to speak English. He had not spoken English for 20 years. He was taught English by a forestry company and he spent 15 years working for an agency
relocating Jews who were in Shanghai after the second war. All he wanted to do was talk to someone from outside to learn more.
I spent four days on a boat going from Muhan to Chong King and for two of those days I was the only non-Chinese on the boat of 800 people. The curiosity of the people that came to watch this not terribly slim, blond, bearded, left-handed foreign devil use chop sticks-all there was was curiosity and an urge to know. They wanted to know why I did not wear two pairs of pants like everybody else wore against the cold. They wanted to know what they could about Canada, anything they could find out. I spoke very little Chinese and they spoke no English, but in two days there was a remarkable exchange of information.
The spirit of those people despite the state, and perhaps in spite of the state, wants to move ahead in terms of knowledge, in terms of understanding. They are an inventive people who know that with their own resources can make their lives better and better for their children. What we have seen in the last three or four days is a repression of that spirit. If that spirit is what is broken, then China, and I would say the world, would be the losers for it. If that spirit if not rekindled and supported by the Members of this House, the people of Canada, the people of the western world, we cannot expect them to come on their own. This motion and the sentiments of all Members of this House bring that moral support that is so essential.
In closing, I spoke a few moments ago with an American friend who taught for a year in Shanghai. At the end of the phone conversation, he said to me, the old leaders used their benchmark as having participated in the long march. The new leaders will comment that they were in Tiananmen Square.
