subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the previous speaker from Newfoundland, I think when you hear of a tragedy to another nation and you have had a chance to have a relationship with individuals and with that nation itself by visiting it and coming to know it, indeed you have a very special feeling when the nation stands in turmoil as China stands tonight.
I can remember only too well sitting and talking with students in China at their universities in larger groups and in smaller groups in their dormitories. They were the same kind of questions, the same kind of young people you would find at any university in Canada with the same hopes and aspirations for their nation. In fact perhaps in China this group is more special because they have only been learning about freedom and liberty in the sense that we know it since 1978. As I listened to them talk about freedom and try to understand what freedom and democracy meant, as naive as they may have been, their hope and their enthusiasm for freedom and democracy and opportunity was contagious. As they told us about this, we started to feel the great hope of the young people for their China. One could feel the power of that new found liberty alone beaming from the eyes of these new young warriors of the reform generation. These young people were only 10 years old in 1978 when things started to happen in China. Each year of their life has been a new opening, a new growth and a new sign of hope.
How my stomach turns tonight in revulsion as I think about how the bayonets of a ruthlessly led military have poked out the brightness of their eyes, the passions of their hearts and now treads on the spirit of China. It is a spirit that was beginning to feed the nation. It is a spirit that was beginning to industrialize the nation and provide new opportunities, a higher standard of living and
greater opportunity for all Chinese. That spirit has been trampled.
After the shock, the horror, the anger and the pain, we stand in the House tonight to cry out in frustration with the world: "Let the carnage stop now". I wish I could believe it would. As we speak tonight, let us honour the memory of those who died. Let us honour not just those who died but those who are dying in hospitals throughout China tonight. Let us honour not just those who are dying tonight in China but those who will die in the next days.
This is not the end. It is the beginning in China, hopefully to a renewed China.
In tribute to these martyrs let us turn away from the anger and passion of the moment and look ahead toward a stable China that is at peace with itself and within the world community. Condemn, yes. Sanctions, yes. Review our policy and express our outrage. Let us do all of these things, but do not burn all our bridges. We will need those bridges to help rekindle the brightness of their eyes and the passion of their hearts and their spirit.
A stable, free prosperous China must be the goal of this Parliament and the result we are trying to project from this debate. If we are to be part of that, while we condemn those who have caused or condoned these atrocities, we must also buttress the bridges of those friends so many of us in this House and across the world have started to make inside China. They need our moral support and our strength now like they have never needed it before. We need a strong free China restored in order that peace and prosperity will prevail throughout the entire region.
Two weeks ago we welcomed Wan Li, the chairman of the National People's Congress. We talked with him and his group of Parliamentarians about reform, about hope for their nation.
Tonight, many of us, as members of the Canada-China Parliamentary Association, have been invited not to be here tonight but to be at the Chinese embassy with the ambassador and his staff to celebrate another in-road, the establishment of the Canada-China Parliamentary Association.
When he phoned me this morning in Vancouver and we talked about the reception tonight, I was quite angry. I had been up watching the news and I saw these things

June 5, 1989
happening. My first reaction was to cancel the whole initiative, take a stand.
As I listened to the ambassador, I could hear the anger and sorrow in his voice at the tragedy of his nation. I could begin to understand the suffering that must be going on in the embassy among those who spend their lives trying to build bridges to us in Canada. I realized that we must not cancel, that we must postpone. We must postpone that so it can be one of the bridges on which we will start to rebuild, pending a renewed China moving toward freedom and prosperity.
Through its actions, the Government of China has learned and taught many hard lessons. It has demonstrated the fragility of trust and co-operation between itself and the world, and between ourselves. Out of respect, Canada has largely accepted China's counsel on the region, in world bodies or discussing international politics. We have even turned a blind eye occasionally because we have developed a trust in its view. But it has damaged that.
As I turn my blind eye a 1 ittle bit toward the remote region of Tibet, I wonder if history may show us in default for benign apathy and neglect when we should have investigated and should have raised that issue more aggressively in the international forums of the world.
China is important not just to Canada, it is important to the world. It is more important than it was 10 years ago. It is a powerhouse of the world, economically, socially, and politically. It is in turmoil now.
That turmoil has left a large vacuum. There is the Chinese-Soviet initiative on Kampuchea. How will China exert controlling influence over the Khmer Rouge to prevent another blood bath in the killing fields of Kampuchea? Will the front line states of Vietnam and Thailand fill the vacuum or will ASEAN collectively pull together to prevent another civil war in Kampuchea?
Let Canada begin to prepare its part in a peace-keeping mechanism so that we will not sit here again for another night on a debate on Kampuchea. Instead, we will begin making the peace.
In 10 minutes it will be morning for us. It is 12:45 p.m. in China right now. It would be my hope that as we
condemn China in this resolution, we would also unanimously pray for the safety and reform of the reform leadership, young and old, inside China, that China will know peace and prosperity, and will return to fulfil its rightful and full role in our international community.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this is probably one of the most emotional debates of my 10 years in this House.
We join unanimously in all parties to condemn the present leadership of China that has brought about such carnage and violence against the young students in Tiananmen Square in Beijing. These were students who were demonstrating peacefully, not to overthrow the Government but to demand a hearing, more freedom, and an end of corruption of high officials.
We pay tribute to these students tonight, many of whom died for their cause. The massacre of fellow citizens by the People's Army will never be forgotten in Chinese history or in the minds and consciences of all who uphold human rights.
We in the New Democratic Party support the position taken by Canada as outlined by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) tonight. Canada has strongly protested the carnage and violence. It has taken steps to protect Canadian nationals in China. It has extended visas for Chinese students in Canada, has suspended certain bilateral events and it has supported the statement of the U.N. Secretary General calling for restraint.
In my remarks I want to briefly mention some of the information that I had, having consulted with leaders and friends in the Chinese Canadian community in order to bring their views to the House tonight. I might say that we learned about an hour ago that the People's Liberation Army now has moved into most of the major universities in China. Most Canadian Chinese people that I spoke to are stunned, are very concerned at the bloodshed and totally condemn the Government actions in China. They condemn the infringement of human rights, the taking of human life and the fear of security for persons who were involved in the demonstrations or those who supported the students. Canadians of Chinese origin oppose the violation and the slaughter. Many
June 5, 1989

demand the resignation of the present leaders for their incompetence, their corruption and as one friend said: "their craziness".
My contacts in Vancouver stress the strong need for continued monitoring of violations of human rights. Some are preparing to donate blood as are persons in Hong Kong. Other aid is difficult to plan at this time until things stabilize. The Chinese Canadian National Council whom we contacted has met with External Affairs asking that Canada demand an emergency meeting of the U.N. Security Council, urging close monitoring with the withdrawal of diplomats and economic sanctions if this becomes necessary. I must say that I think many of us will agree with earlier statements in this House, however, that it is important not to isolate China and to do everything positive to support progressive change.
The Chinese Canadian National Council ask that Canada use every means possible to stop the massacre and to influence world opinion to return China's leadership to sanity.
I want to conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by urging Canadians not to allow the carnage and violence which we have seen on television, and which has been so intolerable and upsetting to all of us, the kind of repression that leaders in China have promoted, to prejudice us against China and all that has been achieved by this great country.
China's civilization began thousands of years ago and is the oldest civilization in the world. The People's Republic of China in the early days of Mao Tse-tung, and I was in China in 1973, learned how to feed 1.2 billion people who were starving. This was a miracle. They developed health services and universal child care services, and care for children and respect for the elderly that Canada might well emulate. It is tragic that Deng Xiaoping who introduced economic reforms and normalized foreign relations should be the one to condone the repression of rights and the brutal massacre of Chinese students. We must remember that there were other moderate leaders, like Zhao Ziyang, whom we hope will rise to lead again.
Canada and China have a special friendship. For me, I must say, it is symbolized in a memory that I have of a little girl whom I encountered by accident in 1973 when I was visiting a village on the outskirts of Shanghai. This little girl was sitting at a table of children playing teacher. I asked the interpreter what she was saying and
I was told that she was saying: "You must serve the people like Dr. Norman Bethune."
Many of my constituents and friends in Vancouver East can trace their families back 12 generations in their villages in China. I join them in deep sorrow tonight which I know they must be feeling. China has always survived and overcome disasters in the past. The people of China are strong. I cannot help but feel that the spirit of the courageous students in Tiananmen Square will rise again and that a long march will commence to renew a peaceful revolution that will lead to human rights, justice and greater freedom in the great country of China.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we know a special kind of horror when we see those who would bring a message of refusal to acquiesce any longer in the leaden monotony of an oppressive regime; those who would bring a message of greater freedom and deeper humanity and a richer future; and those who would bring these things in the spirit of peace and non-violence and love, when we see them gunned down on the orders of evil and barbarous men, utterly corrupted by their contemptible thirst for unyielding power. I first knew this horror in 1970 when I saw on television, and heard on the radio and read in the newspapers of the gunning down of four students at Kent State University of Ohio, and the gunning down of six black students at Jackson State University in Mississippi. I hoped then never to see such hateful barbarism again.
However, I have seen it again, over the last 72 hours on a scale that dwarfs those crimes against its own citizens committed by the Nixon administration.
There are three stages, I think, in our response to this all but unimaginable tragedy. First, we cry out in horror at the staggering inhumanity of the events we see before us. Then we cry out in anguish with the pain and the fear that those events evoke. Then we cry out in rage that all basic tenets of justice and humanity should be so obscenely brushed aside, that mass murderers should stride through the squares and avenues of one of the

June 5, 1989
world's great cities with cold, ruthless state sanctioned determination. Our responses across this country run the gamut.
I would like to read a couple of quotes that were reported in today's newspaper. Today's Edmonton Sun stated that more than 200 emotional Chinese students and their supporters staged a rally at the University of Alberta. The article states at that rally: "Medical student John Zhag said his wife-a doctor in Beijing-spoke over the telephone yesterday about her experience in Tiananmen Square.
"First they used clubs, then they used bayonets", said Zhag. "Some people stayed there, so the soldiers used machine guns."
The article continues:
As Zhag's wife took cover, a neighbour's 14-year-old daughter had her head shot off at the neck by what the wife believes was an explosive bullet -
And the Edmonton chapter of the Chinese Canadian National Council yesterday denounced the government of Deng Xiaoping and Premier Li Peng in telegrams to the United Nations, Ottawa, the Alberta government and the City of Edmonton, said chapter president Ken Kwan.
"We call upon three levels of Canadian government and the UN to take immediate action against the Chinese government,'' said Kwan.
The following is a quote from the Edmonton Journal:
Ken and Maylee Kwan quietly fastened banners to Edmonton's China Gate, then placed flowers at its base.
"Putting flowers here is our way of expressing our sorrow,'' explained Ken Kwan, a 34-year-old landed immigrant. "My heart ached, literally."
I received the following letter today. It is dated June 5. I received it this afternoon. It reads as follows:
Dear Ross:
I and my family are very worried about our friends in China. Over the past five years we have come to know well a number of Chinese students posted to the Alberta Research Council and to the University of Alberta. Because these men were not allowed to bring their families to Canada, they "adopted" my children as substitutes. In many ways they have become like uncles to my two little girls.
We fear that these men and their families, if they have not already been harmed, will become the victims of future purges. It would be a double tragedy if this were to happen. They have already lost a decade of their lives because of the "Cultural Revolution".
We want the Canadian government to do more to protest the slaughter of China's best and brightest. A simple statement of the Canadian Government's "shock" is not enough, in our opinion. At the very least we expect the Government of Canada to grant asylum to any Chinese students now in our country.
Yours sincerely,
Bob Brunelle, Becky, Robin, Elizabeth
Tonight in this Chamber and across the country, we join in pain, rage, resolution and hope. We hope fervently that the beleaguered Chinese people may find quickly an end to the violence and to the Government of these murderers who launched this violence. We hope for wisdom and justice on the part of the Canadian Government as it represents all of us in these dark hours and days.
We resolve to redouble our efforts in aid of those brave, terribly brave Chinese students and workers whose vision of a free, democratic socialist China still shines brightly through the darkness which seeks to envelop that unhappy land.
We will all progress. China will be free. Elowever, why must the price be so painfully high?

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a sense of obligation on behalf of the constituents who I have the honour to represent in this Chamber that I rise to join my colleagues from all sides of the House in a fine moment in this parliamentary democratic tradition to condemn the Government of China for its brutal actions in the last number of days. Not to be moved by the footage which we have seen on our television screens would be almost impossible and bordering on the inhuman.
Just over one hour ago on CBC's The National it was particularly moving to witness the courage of the one individual who challenged a tank and who, in the end, overcame. The savagery and butchery that we have seen and the death of innocent defenceless students was indeed deeply and profoundly moving. When life is snuffed out in the manner that we have seen it, no one man or woman, no matter how powerful, how rich or how strong can condone that type of brutal action. Yet when it happens to young people, young students who are standing up for principles that they and we in this
June 5, 1989

country deeply believe in, I think the feeling runs deeper. We feel a deeper sense of loss, not only because their hope came to a premature end but perhaps, more important, because they will not be able to share in that day when China will finally see its way to re-establishing the dignity that belongs to each and every one of us by right and not by privilege as anointed by the state.
When I was watching the mobilization of troops and armed vehicles moving in on the people in the square, I was reminded of very similar scenes not too long ago in Manila when the same type of human uprising was taking place. People were mobilizing and standing up for freedom. The response of the Filipino regime was to mobilize the tanks, the guns and the artillery. In that particular experiment, the people won. The people silenced the machines. The people silenced the guns. "People power" won.
I remember being in Manila shortly thereafter and buying a T-shirt with the illustration of persons lying in front of a tank with a victory sign and stating: "People power rates". I had a hope that somehow in the Chinese context we would have the same ending, the same victory, that the people would be able to silence the tanks and the guns. Elowever, unfortunately, that was not to be. The ending to this particular chapter was very different. It was very dark and sad. It is for that reason that this evening in this Chamber is so important.
We all know that we live many miles away from Beijing. To be precise we are 7,000 miles away. Yet it is as important for us to speak as we are in one united voice so that this ripple, hopefully, will join the other ripples around the globe. In the end we will have a tidal wave of public opinion which will render a measure on Chinese society, particularly on the Chinese Government.
On the one hand this public opinion will begin with a ripple this evening, started in the House of Commons in Ottawa, Ontario, Canada. It will find its course around the globe. It will send not only strength to the people who have had the courage and the conviction of their principles to stay the course but at the same time send a message to the Government of China that we will not tolerate or condone such action.
Indeed, our voice of frustration, our voice of disgust and of anger must be expressed loudly and boldly. In the face of such action it would be morally irresponsible for nations which call themselves progressive and civilized to turn a blind eye to developments on the face of the globe. If history has taught us one thing, it is to be vigilant and not simply to be silent in the face of conflict and controversy. If we condone it through silence, it is far easier for similar events to be repeated. Therefore, it is important not only to register a comment on what has happened but, hopefully, to avert what may happen in the days and weeks ahead, to inform the Chinese Government through this international understanding that there must be a better way.
While China lost many young sons and daughters, the civilized world as well, including Canada as a member of that international community, suffered yet another setback. While the scenes are fresh in our minds and China has occupied and dominated public opinion in the last number of weeks, we have other tragedies around the globe every single day. We rise in our place one day and talk about the situation in Lebanon. We rise on another day and talk about the calamities in the Soviet Bloc countries. On another day, it is the question of refugees in Latin America. This time, unfortunately, our thoughts and our minds have been registered on China where Chinese citizens, students who mobilize peacefully as human beings, have been made enemies of their own state, strangers in their own home, refugees in their own backyard.
How many are there in the world? We talk today of perhaps up to 3,000 individuals who perished, 10,000 people injured, scores of others intimidated, pressured and tortured. Yet there are some 10 million to 15 million people in the world today who are on the move. Therefore, I hope that through this action in the House today, and I commend the Government and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) for showing expeditious leadership and a sense of grace, it is my deep hope that the outpouring of world opinion will move the Chinese government, not the army, to revisit its own conscience, to express its guilt, to admit and recognize that it erred, and to reinvest once again its trust and its confidence in its own people.

June 5, 1989
If it does that, then at the veiy least the lives that were quickly spent would not have been in vain. It is through those deaths that would have set in motion the ultimate catalyst, the ultimate force that will trigger a dynamic return to dignity and respect for human beings and the ability to express themselves in liberty and freedom. For this, I commend and congratulate all my colleagues for showing Parliament and Canadians that we can rise to the occasion and affect the life, changes and movements of the world around us.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
I must express today the horror that the people of my riding have expressed as they viewed the events of the last 48 hours in Tiananmen Square.
I must say that never before in the history of mankind has this kind of tragedy been brought so quickly into the homes of each and eveiy one of us. Nowadays, we have almost instant telecommunications. We have out in China reporters who are every day, and this minute, risking their lives to bring us what is happening. We must make every effort to ensure that our media is ever free to react and to report courageously the events that are around us. We may not always like what we see, hear or read, but it is essential so that we may govern and shape our future accordingly.
I react today to this horror in many different ways. First, I react as a mother and as a parent. I have children of university age. As a parent, I know that after having nurtured them through childhood, taught them as much as I could, now they are in fact shaping their future, the future of our country. We may not as parents always agree with what our children do, but we must always respect them, for they are our future. To have them cut down so savagely is a horror that only someone who has lost a child could really understand. As such, I want to offer my condolences to all of the families of those who have been slain.
I react also as a woman. It perhaps strengthens my resolve as a parliamentarian that we do need more women in politics. I cannot help but believe that had there been women in power in China right now, we would not have had this senseless slaughter. Somehow I have to believe that women would never allow this kind of thing to happen. I believe that we value life very highly.
I react also as a parliamentarian. I am very proud what we in this House have accomplished today by joining together to condemn what is happening in China. We must impose some sanctions, but we must also be very wary not to harm those whom we seek to help. It is a great dilemma for any Government.
How anyone can condone the slaughter of their best and brightest is absolutely impossible to understand. But there is one thing in which I have great faith, and that is that somehow, some day, those who have not been slaughtered, those who have been spared, will rule China. So there is hope.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, world public opinion, it can be said, is horrified and saddened by what has happened in China. Exercising raw power, the state has established its authority, and it has done so through violence, killing, repression, and with the use of brute force. This is a hard blow to civilization. I would describe it as a step backward in the evolution of humanity.
Why does the conflict of ideas have to be resolved through the taking of lives, one inevitably must ask? How can the rulers in China assume, on behalf of the people they are supposed to represent, that they have the mandate to repress and steamroll the population when dialogue and peaceful change seem to be the processes leading eventually to a solution? I don't know the answer to those questions, but those are certainly questions that trouble me.
So we are involved tonight in this debate in which we are all converging to the same conclusions with the hope that this Government will find the wisdom and the strength and the foresight in the name of decency and in the name of the values we cherish, to make some difficult decision and perhaps suspend the pursuit of Canada's economic interest in China until the present regime is replaced by people who respect the lives of their own citizens. We have to call on the Government from this side of the chamber to put human interests before economic interests and even to go so far as to stop government-to-government aid. This is not so much because we believe in the effectiveness of sanctions, but because this is the only way we can express the frustration, shock and moral indignation of what we have seen and heard through the media over the last few days.
June 5, 1989

Canada evidently has a role to play in the world community. The United Nations definitely offers a forum to Canada to advance some of our ideas. Inevitably, thought goes to the forum of the United Nations as the place where matters of this kind ought to be resolved. We know that technically this matter cannot be raised there because the Government of China is part of the Security Council. Nevertheless, ways must be found to raise this matter at the United Nations because that is the only body where international indignation can converge, can find full expression and generate the pressure that maybe will have impact on the present ruler in Beijing.
Therefore, we have to find ways of registering, through this Parliament, a message which only parliamentarians can register and, with the help of parliamentarians in other jurisdictions, mount a campaign that will eventually cross the oceans and reach the sensitive nerves of the decision-makers in that great country of China.
We are all saddened by what has happened. Words are inadequate to express the emotions. Others have expressed them here tonight and others will speak, but it is clear that from all sides of this House the strong political will is emerging that something must be registered beyond the scope of speeches with the decision-makers of Beijing to bring them to their senses.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to join my voice to all Members of this House in denouncing and condemning the officials of the Chinese Government for their flagrant disregard of human life. In this emergency debate, we are addressing the turmoil in China, the danger it poses to Canadians in China and the consequences for Canada's relationship with that country.

Mr. Speaker, I believe it is important to recall what the debate is about. It is on a motion which reads as follows:
That this House, noting that:
the relationship between Canada and the People's Republic of
China is important to Canadians and has been of benefit to both
countries over the past many years:
authorities in the People's Republic of China have directed the armed forces of China to attack the unarmed civilian population of Beijing in contravention of all humane principles of conduct;
the students and citizens of Beijing were peacefully advocating democratic principles and human freedoms as is the fundamental right of all peoples of the world: and
the authorities of China resorted to the use of excessive and indiscriminate armed force on a scale and scope which appalls all Canadians and has resulted in the tragic deaths of large numbers of innocent civilians; therefore unequivocally condemn this brutal use of force against the peaceful populace of Beijing and call upon the authorities of China to cease this senseless killing and immediately adopt a course of dialogue with the people of China.

We are outraged by the violent suppression of freedom of expression, violence against unarmed students resulting in the tragic loss of life through brutal force. This violence and bloodshed has shocked all democratic societies. We saw, in Tiananmen Square, unarmed students and civilians who formed human barricades through their sheer will to stand up for democracy in the face of incredible odds. We saw raw courage on the faces of students fighting for issues which we take so much for granted here at home: freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, freedom of the press. We saw the most uncivilized, brutal approach by the Government. We saw complete disregard of the necessary standards of human conduct in a civilized society. We have seen this horrendous story unfold before our eyes.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that we should express our respect and appreciation to all members of the press and electronic media who are really responsible for bringing this painful experience of the students and indeed the Chinese people into our daily lives. We must thank them for their courage and their presence on the scene, and also for having stayed there to make us aware of this dramatic situation.

I believe that the members of that profession of journalism-all journalists, reporters, cameramen, audio-visual men-those brave crews who have brought this unfortunate, regrettable, unthinkable uprising to the world stage require our respect. They have shown us the face of youth thirsting for a more democratic society while maintaining pride in their country and their heritage, the vision of the tanks rolling down the Avenue of Eternal Peace, the destruction of that symbol of democracy referred to as the goddess of democracy. We have

June 5, 1989
seen the tears and felt the horror, the anger, the hope and the hopelessness. All expression of human emotion have entered our homes on our screens because of these professionals. They have brought the unerring eye of the camera to bear witness to the horrors, to the killings, to the unfairness of this struggle.
These reporters have shown a commitment to their profession, to responsible reporting, to the courage of their convictions that have of course shown the kind of concern for human rights that is the only way the world could have seen and now express their total repugnance for these acts.
There have been genocides, atrocities, unconscionable aggression and mass loss of life around this world that have not been addressed, but left in silence because these visual reports, these scenes, were not available. The doors were closed. The media had no access and so no one spoke out. It was like a complicity of silence. Often that is not really so. It is just the absence of our fearless, competent journalists to report and so bring the pressure of world censure to bear.
We are grateful to all these very brave people for staying and for facing the risks in the name of democracy.
Canada's daily journalistic broadcast through Radio-Canada International in English and Chinese is vital and all the more so right now. Canada is a tempering, calming, sobering voice of influence and can bring solace to those mourning their loss because they know we are watching, listening and speaking out.
The killing must stop. These very sad scenes demonstrate that Chinese authorities have lost their moral authority. They have violated fundamental principles of human rights. The brutality of the dark side of human nature has unfolded before our eyes. We are outraged, shocked and revolted at these despicable actions. This tragedy has touched the hearts and homes of millions of Chinese.
We as Canadians have to review our stand and determine whether or not and when to take economic and political sanctions, if the situation does not change. We do not want to push the Chinese people back into isolation and a more closed society. We do not want to bring more suffering. However, this maintenance of our political and economic contact should be conditional upon a change, and a move for a peaceful and respectful solution to the needs of the Chinese people by a caring and open Chinese leadership.

I say to the anguished families in mourning, be comforted because in spite of the great sorrow you feel now, your loss will not be in vain; freedom will definitely triumph.

To all the families whose hearts and homes have been touched, know that the torch has been passed to you and that in the end democracy and freedom will survive. Be assured that these brave young lives which have been snuffed out will not have been in vain. You and they have given hope to millions of Chinese and to the citizens of China. They shall be remembered and their dreams will one day become a reality, for you and I know that repression cannot forever be subdued.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight Members of the House meet to debate in emergency session the significance of the events which have just taken place in Beijing, and to articulate the reaction of Canadians.
Why is this important? Why do we call this emergency session? Perhaps the first reason is the sheer size and importance of the Chinese population of over one billion. Another is the shocking number of casualties on the weekend. Last is the stark contrast between the ideals manifested by the peaceful demonstration in Tiananmen Square and the brutality and loss resulting from the armed intervention.
We in the House represent more than 300,000 Chinese- Canadians. We must record the common sense of sorrow and fear for the future felt not only by Chinese-Canadians but by all of us.
June 5, 1989

As we watch events unfold, we see human rights, often taken for granted by us, disregarded and violated by a misguided military force. Those rights include the right of peaceful assembly, and the right to life, liberty and security.
History shows us that few places in the world have escaped the pain and sorrow associated with growing democracy. Revolution has little regard for life, and usually renders life subordinate to power. Canada itself has known its Papineau Rebellion, the Mackenzie revolt in Upper Canada, and the Riel Rebellion. Each was in its own way a building block of our nation and spilled our blood. Most of the democratic freedom we have today has been bought and paid for with the blood of those who fought the battles of revolution and liberation, liberation from tyranny, oligarchy, and fascism.
However, what is perhaps so cruel about the blood of Tiananmen Square is that it has been shed at a time when men and women around the world could rejoice at progress in achieving democratic change without the bullets and the bayonets. Such changes can be seen to be taking place all around us, for example, in the Philippines, in Poland, and in the U.S.S.R. We pray that the people of Panama may yet attain the democratic change they seek without armed struggle. That is why we find the events of Saturday night so cruel.
We collectively must record our justifiable disgust and condemnation of those who ordered and carried out this brutality. We must hope that the blood that has been spilled and the life that has been lost will cause all citizens of the People's Republic of China, on all sides of the conflict, to pause before more bullets fly, pause before there is more retribution and bloodshed and seek out peaceful means of resolving the current political conflicts.
That is the only road that will truly fulfil the goals and justify the sacrifices made by so many in all the rebellions, revolutions, and wars that have preceded us.
I call upon the Government to tangibly manifest the indignation of Canadians at the violence in Beijing, and take steps to assist wherever it can in bringing about a peaceful resolution of this disturbing conflict.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is 12.35 a.m. and this evening Members from all sides of the House rose to disapprove of the Government of
China's action against its own people. I am no different. I am fortunate and happy to be a part of the House and part of this democracy, one of the best democracies in the world. It is a model democracy. I hope that some time Canadians have the opportunity to travel abroad in order to compare our democracy with what exists elsewhere.
Nothing can stop the people from voicing their concerns, nothing at all.
Over the years the Chinese people have become known as achievers. With close to one billion people living in China they have managed their own affairs peacefully and from time to time have been forced to voice their concerns. The Chinese revolution was a decision of the people at the time. Today, from what I am able to see and hear, the Chinese people have once again set their minds to achieving democracy.
On Sunday I attended the demonstration in front of the Chinese Embassy. I saw a group of students who exemplified a peaceful and non-confrontational approach. Those were students here in Canada who spoke out in support of their colleagues in China. I was somewhat disappointed when I saw the Government of China, and I have the opportunity to know the Ambassador here in Canada, use its own army to fight its own people. I was disappointed when I saw the armed forces moving in in order to crush a peaceful movement conducted by a group of peaceful students. That criminal act committed by the Chinese army cannot be tolerated. We in Canada have to exercise everything that we can in order to stop it.
Many people spoke about the possibility of economic sanctions. What we have to keep in mind is that if we take those actions we do not want to harm those who need our help the most. We do not want to harm the Chinese people. When the Canadian Government supplies assistance through our programs, we supply it to the people and not to the Government. We hope that our assistance goes to those who need it in those countries.
Because we are part of the United Nations and we occupy a very important role on the council, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has suggested, we should exercise our role and use all means possible for us in order to ensure the Chinese Government stops its action.

June 5, 1989
I wish to commend the Hon. Secretary of State on his speech today in the House in response to questions from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). I am veiy proud to be part of this society that not only speaks of democracy but exercises democracy.
I would like to commend the members of the Chinese community who were out in full force on Sunday in support of the Chinese people. I also want to congratulate members of my community who are anglophones, francophones, Italians, and people from all walks of life who marched on the embassy in order to voice their concerns in support of the Chinese people.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS CRISIS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak today with great sorrow. One has to have had first hand practice or knowledge of things that happened to share not only in speaking but in sorrow. In my early days, my parents fled a dictatorship from the country of my birth to come to my home country which is now Canada. Relatives of mine were lost in the Polytechnical Institute in Athens, Greece, in 1974 when the Government of the day decided to do what the Beijing Government did a couple of days ago. In 1974, the Government of the day in Greece overran peaceful students and killed hundreds of them.
I have a large community of Chinese people in my riding. My heart, thoughts and sorrows go out to them. At this particular time, as we speak, there is a vigil at some churches. I would like to take my turn here today along with my colleagues and Members of this House to condemn the happenings in Beijing. Canada must take a positive step in order to send a strong message to the Beijing Government. One has only to watch the news and speak to people to see unarmed students run over by tanks, cut down in cold blood. What did they have to protect themselves? Just their bodies. Thousands of people were killed and thousands wounded. The cameras were only able to show us part of the realization, perhaps only one-fifth or one-tenth of what happened.
It is not over yet. As we speak at 12.45 on this debate, the killings still continue. I shudder at the thought that at this particular moment, a bullet is flying at a student and a student's body is just about to fall.
We have to commend the reporters who brought this to us. In 1974 when things like this were happening in my country of birth, it was 24 to 48 hours before we learned anything. But in this age of fast telecommunications, we are able to find out first hand. I join with the rest of my colleagues and condemn those killings in Beijing.
All Canadians of Chinese origin are watching with horror as the events unfold and friends and brothers are being killed. The price of democracy is a high one. In many countries the price of democracy has to be paid with thousands of lives. In this particular instance, we were told one time that 63 students were killed, at another time 2,600 were killed. I am wondering what the real number was. You can watch on television and you can see the smoke going up in Tiananmen Square. What were they burning? Were they burning people's bodies? How can anybody stand there and think that people were being burned, not even given a decent burial. I shudder.
The price of democracy is indeed a high one. The students are paying as we speak with their lives that price of democracy. I hope that the price of democracy not only in China, not only in Panama, South Africa and other parts of the world comes soon as we on globe of ours are able to stand up one day and say that we indeed have the best democracy. It will be a long road. A lot of sacrifices will have to be made. I guess history will take a look at Tiananmen Square and say that this was part of the sacrifice. How much longer, how many more mothers, how many more fathers have to sit there and shudder? I join my colleagues and I condemn what happened in Beijing.
